items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Panel remarks at the 2026 ASSA Annual Meeting, 'Thoughts on the U.S. Economy and the Year Ahead'
items.quote: If all of that happens, then some modest further adjustments to the funds rate would likely be appropriate later in the year.
items.summary: Paulson said she is cautiously optimistic on inflation, expecting the tariff price-level shift to run its course in the first half and run-rate inflation near 2 percent by year end. She views the funds rate as still a little restrictive and said the trends argue against tighter policy. The labor market is bending but not breaking, and if inflation moderates and the labor market stabilizes, modest further cuts later in the year would be appropriate. She discussed AI-driven productivity as a possible reason for strong GDP with weak hiring.
items.score_note: Policy still a little restrictive, labor risks elevated, modest further cuts later in the year in her baseline; no urgency, so -1 not -2.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' live interview (Reuters report)
items.quote: I do think there's a risk that the unemployment rate could pop from here
items.summary: Kashkari says inflation is still too high and its risk is persistence as tariff effects take years to work through, while the unemployment rate could 'pop' higher. He guesses policy is pretty close to neutral and says the Fed needs more data to see whether inflation or the labor market is the bigger force before moving in either direction.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks, policy near neutral, wants more data before moving 'whatever direction is necessary'. Time from the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview with MNI
items.quote: as long as we keep policy at what I think of as materially too tight, we're reducing my growth expectations in the future
items.summary: Miran said the FOMC needs to cut substantially in 2026, that he wrote down 150 bp of cuts for the year in the December SEP (up from 100 bp), that underlying inflation is about 2.3% once shelter and portfolio-management distortions are removed, and that the labor market has weakened in large part because of Fed policy.
items.score_note: Says policy is materially too tight and wants 150 bp of cuts this year.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Year-end reflection essay "2025" (LinkedIn/X)
items.quote: At the same time, it appears likely the Fed will be inclined to ease to push real interest rates down.
items.summary: Dalio says the Fed and the incoming chair will likely be biased to push nominal and real rates down, which supports asset prices and inflates bubbles, though he doubts easing will be as large as priced. With nearly $10tn of debt to roll, he finds long bonds unappealing and expects a steeper curve. He calls the AI boom an early-stage bubble.
items.score_note: Expects an easing bias from the new chair/FOMC, but says easing may be less than the market discounts; so -1 rather than -2.
items.ai_quote: obviously the AI boom that is now in the early stages of a bubble had a big effect on everything

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'Tuning In: 2026 Outlook' (Richmond Fed posted text)
items.quote: But going forward, policy will require finely tuned judgments balancing progress on each side of our mandate.
items.summary: Barkin says the 175 basis points of cuts brought the funds rate within the range of neutral estimates and were a bit of insurance for the labor market. Both sides of the mandate bear watching: unemployment has ticked up and inflation has been above target for almost five years. He wants clean data after three months of missing or low-quality releases. He notes demand is narrow, resting on the AI ecosystem and wealthy consumers.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks, policy near neutral, no lean on the next move. Time from the Richmond Fed media advisory, not the speech page.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria'
items.quote: I think we've got to cut more than 100 basis points this year
items.summary: Miran said policy is clearly restrictive and holding the economy back, that underlying inflation is within noise of target once housing and portfolio-management quirks are adjusted for, and that well over 100 bp of cuts will be justified in 2026.
items.score_note: Explicit call for more than 100 bp of cuts this year.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: California Bankers Association Bank Presidents Seminar (virtual): 'Modernizing Supervision and Regulation: 2025 and the Path Ahead'
items.quote: A simple solution would be to adjust thresholds by nominal GDP, which includes both economic growth and inflation.
items.summary: Supervision and regulation agenda (tailoring, thresholds, supervisory reform). No monetary-policy content in the prepared text.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: New York Times interview (published January 8, as quoted by Reuters)
items.quote: I have in my mind a decision
items.summary: Trump told the New York Times on Wednesday night that he had made up his mind on the next Fed Chair but had not discussed it with anybody; he called Hassett 'certainly one of the people that I like'. Reported by Reuters in a story on Bessent's Minnesota remarks.
items.score_note: Fed Chair selection only; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks before the Economic Club of Minnesota
items.quote: at a certain point, the Federal Reserve must also do its part to spur investment.
items.summary: In prepared remarks Bessent said the White House can only do so much and the Fed must do its part to spur investment. He said the Fed needs 'merely an open mind' and cited Greenspan resisting premature rate hikes in the 1990s tech boom. In Q&A he said a Fed Chair decision was likely later in January (Reuters).
items.score_note: The text posted on treasury.gov says the Fed 'must also do its part'. Press reports of the remarks released that day (CNBC, relayed at themortgagepoint.com/2026/01/08/treasury-secretary-more-fed-rate-cuts-are-only-ingredient-missing-for-stronger-economy/) quote him: 'Cutting interest rates ... is the only ingredient missing ... Which is why the Fed should not delay.' That wording is not in the posted text. Scored -2 on the explicit call for cuts; would be -1 on the posted text alone.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, Bloomberg Television 'Surveillance'
items.quote: I'm looking for about a point and a half of cuts.
items.summary: Miran said he is looking for about 150 bp of cuts in 2026 to support the labor market, described policy as restrictive and put underlying inflation at about 2.3%.
items.score_note: Explicit call for 150 bp of cuts this year.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Bloomberg TV, The David Rubenstein Show (aired Jan 8; quotes via Fortune/Yahoo write-up of Jan 9)
items.quote: They print money, devalue the currency, and create an artificially low interest rate
items.summary: On the $38 trillion national debt, Dalio says countries that essentially go broke always print money, devalue the currency and hold interest rates artificially low, hurting bondholders. He says future generations will repay the debt in devalued dollars and recommends TIPS and 10-15% gold.
items.score_note: Left unscored: a long-run debt-monetization thesis (governments print money and hold rates artificially low), not a view on the Fed's policy-rate path at this time. Sub-collector had proposed -1 forecast. Describes the historical playbook (print, devalue, artificially low rates) as what will happen; a structural forecast, not a call on the next meeting.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post ordering $200 billion of mortgage bond purchases
items.quote: This will drive Mortgage Rates DOWN, monthly payments DOWN, and make the cost of owning a home more affordable.
items.summary: Trump said he is instructing his representatives (using Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac cash) to buy $200 billion of mortgage bonds to push mortgage rates down. No statement about the Fed's policy rate. Source is the trumpstruth.org archive, which reproduces the post in full.
items.score_note: About mortgage rates via GSE purchases, not the Fed's policy rate; no usable Fed-path content.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Reuters interview, Savage, Minnesota
items.quote: So I think the idea is to roughly match the Fed, which has been pushing the other way.
items.summary: Bessent told Reuters the administration's $200 billion of Fannie/Freddie MBS purchases is meant to roughly offset the about $15 billion a month of MBS rolling off the Fed's balance sheet. He said the purchases would lower mortgage rates only indirectly, through the MBS spread over Treasuries.
items.score_note: About offsetting the Fed's MBS run-off through GSE purchases; no statement on the policy rate path.

items.speaker: Bill Ackman
items.occasion: X post (later deleted) replying to Trump's call for a one-year 10% cap on credit card interest rates, plus follow-up post
items.quote: The best way to bring down rates would be to make it more competitive by making the regulatory regime more conducive to new entrants and new technologies.
items.summary: Ackman called Trump's proposed 10% credit-card rate cap a mistake, saying lenders unable to price for losses would cancel cards for millions and push them to loan sharks. He said the goal of lower card rates is worthy but should be reached through more competition and lighter regulation for new entrants.
items.score_note: No view on the Fed policy rate; about a consumer credit price cap and credit availability.

items.speaker: Raphael Bostic
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (until 2026-02-28; non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Radio interview, WLRN 'The Florida Roundup' (recorded Friday Jan 9; WLRN write-up posted Jan 12)
items.quote: Inflation is too high. We have to get it under control, and we need to be laser focused on making sure that everything we do is contributing to that,
items.summary: Bostic says inflation remains the bigger concern of the two mandates: PCE inflation at 2.8 percent is 50 percent above target and he worries people will lose confidence the Fed will get to 2 percent. The job market is cooler but not necessarily weak. Reuters' account of the same interview adds that he doubts labor markets are heading toward greater weakness.
items.score_note: Inflation risk clearly dominates and he stresses focus on it; no explicit call for a hike.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Podcast conversation with Kyla Scanlon and Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin (transcript on Kyla's Newsletter)
items.quote: We’re not in a place where we’re making large policy moves.
items.summary: Daly said the Fed cut to offset a softer labor market while inflation still prints above target, and that policy is now in a fine-tuning phase: a stone's throw from neutral for some forecasters, with a little more room for others. She stressed nimbleness and looking past single data points.
items.score_note: Fine-tuning near neutral, no lean on the next move. The Substack page is dated Jan 9, 2026; the SF Fed coverage post linking to it is stamped Jan 6, so the recording is from the first days of January.

items.speaker: J.P. Morgan economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated Friday Jan 9 after December jobs report, reported by Reuters Jan 12
items.quote: If the labor market weakens again in the coming months, or if inflation falls materially, the Fed could still ease later this year,
items.summary: J.P. Morgan withdrew its call for a January cut and now forecasts the next Fed move to be a 25bp hike in Q3 2027. It allows that easing later in 2026 is still possible if labor weakens or inflation falls materially, but expects the labor market to tighten by Q2 and disinflation to be gradual.
items.score_note: Base case removes all 2026 cuts and makes the next move a hike (2027); hike is distant, so +1 not +2.
items.call: no cuts in 2026; next move a 25bp hike in Q3 2027 (January cut call withdrawn)

items.speaker: Bill Ackman
items.occasion: X post to Trump, Bessent and FHFA's Pulte proposing prepayment penalties on new Fannie/Freddie mortgages to lower mortgage rates
items.quote: One of the unique features of U.S. conventional mortgages is that they are prepayable at any time without a penalty,
items.summary: Ackman argued that the free prepayment option forces MBS buyers to demand a wider spread, and that offering mortgages with prepayment penalties could cut mortgage rates by roughly 65 basis points. He asked the administration to have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac offer such loans.
items.score_note: Mortgage-spread structure proposal, not a view on the Fed policy-rate path.

items.speaker: Bill Ackman
items.occasion: Fireside chat with UBS's Iqbal Khan at UBS Asia Wealth Forum 2026, Singapore (morning of Jan 12 Singapore time = evening Jan 11 US Eastern)
items.quote: I think the Fed will abandon the goal of 2%.
items.summary: Ackman said a return to 2% inflation is fiction and the Fed will end up with a 2.5%-3% goal. He doubted the couple of further Fed cuts the market expects, saying tax cuts, deregulation and heavy AI investment are driving growth that is partly inflationary, and that the Fed is not heading back to meaningfully low rates.
items.score_note: Forecast of fewer cuts than the market expects and no return to low rates (+1). A higher tolerated inflation goal is itself dovish, so kept at +1 rather than +2; he did not call for hikes.

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated Sunday Jan 11, reported by Reuters Jan 12
items.quote: If the labor market stabilizes as we expect, the FOMC will likely shift from risk management mode to normalization mode,
items.summary: Goldman pushed its two 2026 cuts back to June and September from March and June after the December jobs report, and lowered its 12-month US recession probability to 20% from 30%.
items.score_note: Still forecasts two cuts in 2026 but later; cuts not imminent, so -1.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and September (previously March and June)

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Jan 11 edition)
items.quote: The core policy question is whether these trends remain consistent with Fed Chair Powell’s view that the central bank is "well-positioned" to remain patient on interest rates.
items.summary: Reviewing the latest labor data and looking ahead to inflation figures, El-Erian says US data show employment decoupling from strong growth. He frames the key question as whether inflation and labor trends still fit Powell's view that the Fed can stay patient on rates.
items.score_note: Frames the Fed as on a patient hold and poses an open question; no lean either way.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post reacting to a New York Times report on the Fed chair (evening of Jan 11 ET)
items.quote: This is the scenario I feared months ago when I suggested the Chair step down to protect the institution’s independence.
items.summary: Commenting on a New York Times report about the Fed chair, El-Erian warns the situation could expose deeper issues and further undermine the credibility of a Fed whose public standing is already fragile. He recalls having suggested months earlier that the Chair step down to protect independence and says the nominee to replace him must be committed to the reforms needed to restore the Fed's effectiveness.
items.score_note: About Fed independence, credibility and reform; no statement on the rate path.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: Video statement on DOJ grand jury subpoenas served on the Federal Reserve
items.quote: The threat of criminal charges is a consequence of the Federal Reserve setting interest rates based on our best assessment of what will serve the public
items.summary: Powell said the DOJ served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas threatening a criminal indictment over his June 2025 testimony on the building renovation, called the stated reasons pretexts, and framed it as pressure to set rates by presidential preference. He said he will keep doing the job. No statement on the rate path itself.
items.score_note: Political-pressure statement; nothing on the direction of rates.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle aboard Air Force One
items.quote: With no help from the Fed, because we have a total stiff at the Fed.
items.summary: Discussing the $200 billion mortgage bond purchases, Trump said interest rates are falling very rapidly 'with no help from the Fed' and called the Fed Chair 'a total stiff'.
items.score_note: Complains the Fed is not helping rates fall; no explicit cut demand in this exchange.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: NBC News phone interview after Powell disclosed the DOJ subpoenas (as reported by Reuters)
items.quote: I don’t know anything about it, but he’s certainly not very good at the Fed, and he’s not very good at building buildings
items.summary: After Powell disclosed that the Justice Department had threatened him with a criminal indictment, Trump told NBC News he had no knowledge of the action but that Powell is not very good at the Fed or at building buildings.
items.score_note: Reaction to the Powell probe; no statement on what rates should do.

items.speaker: BofA Global Research (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note after December jobs report, quoted in Reuters Jan 12
items.quote: Mix of data is consistent with our view that breakeven job growth might be falling (labor supply shock) even faster than the Fed will concede,
items.summary: BofA kept its forecast of cuts in June and July 2026 after the December jobs report, arguing breakeven job growth is falling because of a labor supply shock.
items.score_note: Maintains two cuts in mid-2026; not imminent.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and July (maintained)

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Project Syndicate op-ed on the 2026 outlook for the AI-led market rally, as quoted by Business Insider
items.quote: The animal spirits that drove indiscriminate, massive financing last year will increasingly be tamed by bubble fears that force investors to be more selective
items.summary: El-Erian argues the AI narrative will not be strong enough in 2026 to overshadow structural uncertainties such as a K-shaped economy and geopolitics. He says last year's indiscriminate, massive financing will be restrained by bubble fears. No view on the Fed rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; statement is about AI-related financing and bubble fears.
items.ai_quote: The animal spirits that drove indiscriminate, massive financing last year will increasingly be tamed by bubble fears that force investors to be more selective

items.speaker: Rick Rieder
items.role: Head of global fixed income, BlackRock (as described on page)
items.occasion: CNBC interview on Jan 12, quoted by Fortune (Jan 28)
items.quote: The Fed’s got to get the rate down to 3%
items.summary: Rieder, then a finalist for Fed chair, said the Fed has to get the policy rate down to 3% from 3.50-3.75%.
items.score_note: Explicitly says the Fed must cut by another 50bp or more; a should statement, not a forecast.
items.call: Fed should cut the funds rate to 3%

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Council on Foreign Relations, New York, 'A Few Words for the New Year'
items.quote: Monetary policy is now well positioned to support the stabilization of the labor market and the return of inflation to the FOMC’s longer-run goal of 2 percent.
items.summary: Williams said the 75 bp of cuts in 2025 moved a modestly restrictive stance closer to neutral and brought risks into better balance. He expects inflation to peak at about 2-3/4 to 3 percent in the first half of 2026 as tariffs pass through, then fall to 2 percent in 2027, with GDP growth of 2-1/2 to 2-3/4 percent. He gave no signal on timing of further moves and said he remains data dependent; reserve management purchases are not a change in stance. Speaking to reporters afterward, he warned that attacks on central bank independence often lead to bad outcomes including high inflation, and said he hoped the next chair would uphold the dual mandate.
items.score_note: Describes policy as well positioned after the 2025 cuts with no lean on the next move; balanced hold.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Remarks to the CFA Society Washington (Reuters via SRN News)
items.quote: Nobody wants inflation expectations to get embedded and nobody wants the labor market to deteriorate further,
items.summary: Barkin calls December CPI encouraging because it did not rebound, and describes a delicate balance: inflation above target but not accelerating, unemployment not rising out of control. He sees no urgency, saying rate moves work with a 12-month lag and no single meeting matters that much. He declines to discuss the Powell subpoenas but says independent central banks deliver better outcomes.
items.score_note: Two-sided, no urgency in either direction.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Media call after JPMorgan Q4 2025 results (reporters' call, not the analyst call)
items.quote: It will probably raise inflation expectations.
items.summary: Asked about the DOJ criminal inquiry into Fed Chair Powell, Dimon said he has enormous respect for Powell and that anything chipping away at Fed independence is not a good idea. He said it would have the reverse consequences of what the administration wants and probably raise inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Fed independence only; he states no view on the policy rate path, only that political pressure would backfire via inflation expectations.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: DoubleLine annual 'Just Markets' webcast ('Clue'); quotes via ETF Trends recap dated Jan 14
items.quote: You’re better off in cash than 30-year Treasuries,
items.summary: Gundlach said the 'weapon' hurting markets is the deficit-based economy and that the two-year Treasury will outperform the 30-year. The recap says he noted the two-year yield has stopped falling and that the Fed follows the two-year; he cited waning confidence in central bankers and inflationary policies behind gold's rise.
items.score_note: No direct quote on the policy path; the recap paraphrases that the two-year yield stopped falling and the Fed tracks it, which implies a hold. Scored 0 on that paraphrase (nearer 0 than +1).

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: MNI webcast, Q&A moderated by Pedro da Costa (video only on stlouisfed.org; quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: I see little reason for near-term further easing of policy.
items.summary: Musalem said the 3.50%-3.75% policy rate is roughly neutral and need not fall unless the resilient labor market starts to fail or inflation falls faster than expected. He said it is too early to call a higher-productivity regime and too early to "outsource" the job of returning inflation to 2%. In the same webcast he said he expects the next Fed chair to stay committed to the dual mandate.
items.score_note: Explicit pushback on near-term cuts while markets priced further easing; no hint of hikes.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post after December CPI release
items.quote: That means that Jerome “Too Late” Powell should cut interest rates, MEANINGFULLY!!!
items.summary: Reacting to the CPI print, Trump said the low inflation numbers mean Powell should cut rates meaningfully, or he will continue to be 'too late'. He also touted growth numbers and tariffs.
items.score_note: Explicit call for a meaningful rate cut now.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle before Marine One departure (after CPI release)
items.quote: that would give Too Late Powell the chance to give us a nice, beautiful big rate cut
items.summary: Leaving for Detroit after the CPI release, Trump said very low inflation gives Powell the chance to deliver a big rate cut, which would be great for the country.
items.score_note: Explicit call for a big rate cut.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Speech to the Detroit Economic Club
items.quote: our country becomes stronger and therefore interest rates should go down, not up.
items.summary: Trump said the Fed raises rates and kills every rally whenever good numbers are announced, and that he wants a Fed head under whom rates go down when the economy is strong. He called Powell 'a real stiff' and 'that jerk' who 'will be gone soon', and said mortgage rates are falling without the Fed's help.
items.score_note: Says rates should go down, not up, and attacks the Fed for hiking on good news.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks during Ford plant tour, Dearborn, Michigan
items.quote: he's bad because his interest rates were too high.
items.summary: Asked about Senator Tillis's objections to the Powell probe, Trump said 'we have a bad fed chairman' who is bad because his interest rates were too high, and cited that day's inflation and growth reports.
items.score_note: Criticism of rates being too high, phrased in the past tense; no explicit cut demand here.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: CBS News interview with Tony Dokoupil, Dearborn
items.quote: he's been too high on interest rates, and I call him too late.
items.summary: Asked about accusations of pressuring the Fed, Trump called Powell 'a lousy Fed chairman', said he has been too high on interest rates and 'should have reduced' by more, and criticised the Fed building renovation.
items.score_note: Says Powell should have cut more; criticism of past policy rather than an explicit new cut demand.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle after Air Force One arrival
items.quote: We should have lower rates.
items.summary: Asked about Jamie Dimon's warning against chipping away at Fed independence, Trump said Dimon is wrong, that what he is doing is fine, Powell has done a bad job and 'we should have lower rates'.
items.score_note: Explicit statement that rates should be lower, in defence of pressuring the Fed.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: NPR Morning Edition interview with A Martinez (transcript)
items.quote: So if that tariff inflation proves to be more lasting than we hope, that would be a serious issue that we'd have to think about.
items.summary: Goolsbee says the CPI report 'didn't get worse' and that showing inflation is on a path back to 2 percent is the challenge of the next couple of months. He hopes tariff price effects are one-and-done. He does not discuss the rate path directly. He says Fed independence is critical for long-run inflation and calls Powell a first-ballot Hall of Fame chair after the Justice Department subpoenas.
items.score_note: No direct rate guidance; inflation is the focus but he frames it as wait for evidence.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: New York Times interview with Colby Smith (held Jan 13, published Jan 14; Reuters report of the interview)
items.quote: I don’t see any impetus to cut in January
items.summary: Kashkari says he did not want the December cut, sees no impetus to cut in January and calls it 'way too soon' for another cut, though one could be possible later in 2026 if unemployment jumps, especially if inflation also eases. He calls inflation staying above 2 percent for another two or three years very concerning, and says the Trump administration's threats against the Fed are really about monetary policy.
items.score_note: Pushes back on near-term cut talk and stresses inflation, while leaving a later cut possible: +1.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Virtual town hall with the Wisconsin Bankers Association (Reuters report)
items.quote: we are really going to have to watch both sides of our dual mandate
items.summary: Kashkari expects pretty good growth and inflation heading down, though he does not know whether it reaches 2.5 percent by year-end. He gives no rate guidance, says both sides of the mandate need watching and that being too aggressive with rates could hurt the labor market. On the next chair: one vote, and the best argument wins.
items.score_note: Balanced, no lean on the rate path. Time converted from 11:00 a.m. CT on the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Speech 'Regulations, the Supply Side, and Monetary Policy', Delphi Economic Forum, Athens
items.quote: In recent quarters, policy has been tighter than it should have been to reflect significant deregulation lifting potential growth and reducing inflation.
items.summary: Miran argued that US deregulation is a large positive productivity shock that lifts potential output more than actual output and pushes prices down (roughly half a percentage point a year on the price level through 2030 by his estimate), so the correct response is to cut rates. He said ignoring this would make policy needlessly contractionary and that deregulation is one factor supporting further easing.
items.score_note: Says policy has been too tight and that the correct response is to cut rates.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia State of the Economy event, 'Economic Trends and Opportunities for Philadelphia'
items.quote: I view the current level of the federal funds rate as still a little restrictive.
items.summary: Paulson repeated her ASSA message: cautious optimism on inflation (December CPI did not change her view), the funds rate still a little restrictive, and trends that argue against tighter policy. Labor market risks have risen though claims are flat. If inflation moderates, the labor market stabilizes and growth is around 2 percent, some modest further adjustments to the funds rate would likely be appropriate later in the year.
items.score_note: Same easing lean as January 3: restrictive policy, labor risks, modest cuts later in the year conditional on the baseline.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Reuters interview in the Oval Office
items.quote: I made a lot of money with business, so I think I have a better understanding of it than Too Late Jerome Powell.
items.summary: Trump said he has no plan to fire Powell despite the DOJ investigation but that it is 'too early' to say, that 'the two Kevins' (Warsh, Hassett) are very good and he would announce a pick in the next couple of weeks, and that 'a president should have something to say' about Fed policy. He said 'I don't care' about criticism that he is eroding Fed independence.
items.score_note: Asserts a presidential say over Fed policy but states no rate direction in the quoted text.

items.speaker: Wells Fargo Research Team (Wells Fargo Economics)
items.occasion: Wells Fargo US Economic Outlook: January 2026, syndicated in full on FXStreet under the Wells Fargo Research Team byline
items.quote: We are sticking with our previous forecast of two 25 bps rate cuts in March and June, followed by a long pause at 3.00%-3.25% for the federal funds rate.
items.summary: Wells Fargo Economics kept its call for cuts in March and June, citing a labor market modestly on the wrong side of full employment and encouraging core inflation, but said the window for more cuts is closing and risks are skewed toward later and/or less easing.
items.score_note: Earliest cut call among the houses (March), but two meetings away and with risks flagged toward less easing; between -2 and -1, chose -1.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, March and June, then a long pause at 3.00%-3.25%

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Yahoo Finance interview (same day as his Wharton Future of Finance Forum stablecoin panel)
items.quote: A reasonable base case is that the labor market is continuing to stabilize, and that inflation will continue to come down to 2%
items.summary: Barr told Yahoo Finance that rates are at the right level, in the range of neutral, with risks on both sides of the mandate (low job creation versus possibly persistent inflation). He is taking a wait-and-see approach on further cuts and said shutdown-distorted data must be treated with caution into the spring. He called the DOJ probe of the Fed and the accusations against Cook an assault on Fed independence and said a new chair must persuade the committee with data.
items.score_note: Says rates are at the right level with two-sided risks and no lean; wait-and-see on further cuts.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: LinkedIn post (Reuters reprint on a radio-station syndication page; the LinkedIn original was not opened)
items.quote: We will need to be deliberate as we calibrate policy to achieve both price stability and full employment
items.summary: Daly wrote that incoming data look promising: growth projections are solid, the labor market is stabilizing and inflation is expected to improve over the year. She said policy is in a good place to respond to however the economy evolves and that calibration should be deliberate.
items.score_note: "Good place" and deliberate calibration ahead of the January hold; no lean.

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs Research (firm article citing David Mericle, chief US economist)
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs Insights article on the 2026 US outlook, dated Jan 15, 2026
items.quote: Goldman Sachs Research predicts that the Fed will deliver rate cuts of 25 basis points each in June and September
items.summary: Goldman Sachs Research forecast above-consensus growth and below-consensus inflation for 2026 and two 25bp cuts in June and September, ending the cycle at 3%-3.25%.
items.score_note: Two cuts in 2026, mid-year onward; firm-authored article text rather than a quotation of an individual.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and September, to a terminal 3%-3.25%

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: we have to have convincing evidence that we're on path back to 2% inflation.
items.summary: Goolsbee says the job market still has strength and the most important task is getting inflation back to 2 percent. Rates can still go down a fair amount, with cuts possible this year, but only with convincing evidence inflation is heading to target.
items.score_note: Baseline is a lower rate path this year, conditional on inflation evidence; not a call for near-term cuts. Torn between -1 and 0.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: US Chamber of Commerce event, conversation with David Rubenstein
items.quote: it will drive rates higher not lower
items.summary: Dimon ruled out ever being Fed chair and repeated that interfering with Fed independence would push rates up rather than down. He added that everyone he knows, including the president, says an independent Fed board is needed. Coverage of the same event also has him warning that US deficits are not sustainable.
items.score_note: Statement is about Fed independence and its effect on market rates, not about what the Fed should or will do with the policy rate.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CNN 'Erin Burnett OutFront' interview (recorded, aired 7 p.m. ET)
items.quote: And we need to continue doing our work to get inflation back down and hopefully keep the labor market strong at the same time.
items.summary: Mostly about Fed independence and Powell, whom he praises. On the economy he says inflation is still too high at close to 3 percent, a meaningful gap from 2 percent, and the job market is decent but cooling a little. No statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: Stresses the inflation gap but says nothing on rates and names both mandate sides; between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk on the Street' interview on BlackRock Q4 2025 results day (transcript posted by BlackRock on Jan 23)
items.quote: There’s good justification for lowering rates if you believe in the productivity power of AI and the deflationary impact of China’s $1 trillion trade surplus.
items.summary: Fink expected a steeper yield curve in 2026 and said there is good justification for lowering rates because AI and China's trade surplus are deflationary. He said the US is too focused on monetary policy and not enough on fiscal discipline, and that deficits could one day produce low inflation but elevated interest rates if foreign buyers hesitate. On AI infrastructure he said he does not see a bubble and fears under-investment.
items.score_note: Says lowering rates is justified (leans easier) but conditions it on the AI-deflation thesis and warns deficits can push long rates up, so -1 rather than -2. Business Insider's same-day report of his CNBC remarks adds a non-base-case scenario of the 10-year above 5%. The BlackRock page is dated Jan 23 (posting date); the interview was on results day, Jan 15.
items.ai_quote: But we’re working with hyperscalers who are giving us 15‑ to 20‑year leases.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Wall Street Journal interview (published January 15; highlights as relayed by investingLive)
items.quote: comfortable holding interest rates steady
items.summary: Paulson told the WSJ she is comfortable holding rates steady at the January 27-28 meeting and sees no hurry to cut again. She views the current range as slightly above neutral and wants to see January price data. She said labor market risks are a little bit higher than inflation risks and that the labor market could break quickly; she could favor modest cuts later in the year if inflation falls as she expects or the labor market weakens. The WSJ original is paywalled; only short quoted phrases are available in the open summary.
items.score_note: Supports a January hold, but sees policy above neutral, labor risks slightly higher than inflation risks, and modest cuts later in the year; easing lean without urgency.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy", Economic Club of Kansas City
items.quote: With inflation pressures still evident, my preference would be to keep monetary policy modestly restrictive.
items.summary: Schmid explained his dissents against the October and December 2025 cuts: inflation near 3% is too high, cuts would do little for a labor market cooled by structural forces, and policy is no longer very restrictive because the neutral rate has risen. He said he sees little reason to lower the policy rate further. Headline-level wire reports of the Q&A add that he sees little reason to cut and puts full employment at roughly 3.5%-4.5% unemployment.
items.score_note: Pushes back on further cuts and says policy is not very restrictive; does not call for a hike.

items.speaker: Ted Pick
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Q4 2025 earnings call (prepared remarks)
items.quote: 2026 starts with the tailwinds of constructive fiscal policy and easier monetary policy.
items.summary: Pick opens the call saying the US economy proved resilient in 2025 and that 2026 begins with constructive fiscal policy and easier monetary policy as tailwinds for capital markets, with geopolitics front and center.
items.score_note: Describes easier monetary policy as an existing tailwind; no statement on what the Fed will or should do next, so unscored.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Outlook 26: The New England Economic Forum, Foxborough: 'Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy'
items.quote: Absent a clear and sustained improvement in labor market conditions, we should remain ready to adjust policy to bring it closer to neutral.
items.summary: Sees policy as moderately restrictive, the labor market as increasingly fragile, and underlying inflation ex-tariffs close to 2 percent. Wants the Committee to keep focusing on employment risks, act preemptively, and avoid signaling a pause without evidence that conditions have changed.
items.score_note: Employment risks dominate and she argues against signaling a pause; she stops short of calling for a cut at the January meeting, so -1.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Introductory remarks at 'Outlook 26: The New England Economic Forum', Foxborough (official PDF text)
items.quote: While I won’t be addressing the economy or monetary policy in these brief comments
items.summary: Collins introduces Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman at a New England bankers' forum. She states she is not addressing the economy or monetary policy.
items.score_note: Official remarks with no monetary-policy content; listed for coverage.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: American Institute for Economic Research / Shadow Open Market Committee / Florida Atlantic University conference, Boca Raton: 'Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy Implementation'
items.quote: the current policy stance leaves us well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate
items.summary: Cautiously optimistic: labor market stabilizing, inflation somewhat elevated, risks to both sides of the mandate. Says 175bp of cuts brought the funds rate into a range consistent with neutral and declines to prejudge the January meeting. Second half explains that reserve management purchases begun in December 2025 are not QE and have no implications for the policy stance.
items.score_note: Hold-and-watch language with two-sided risks; no lean either way.

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Global Research web article on the Fed's next move (version dated January 16, 2026; archived Jan 22)
items.quote: The recent stabilization in the unemployment rate should finally bring some cohesion to the FOMC, and we now look for the Committee to be on hold at the January meeting.
items.summary: J.P. Morgan Global Research no longer sees a January cut, expects the Fed on hold through 2026 at 3.5-3.75%, and projects a 25bp hike in Q3 2027. Feroli added that easing later this year is possible if labor weakens or inflation falls materially.
items.score_note: Public restatement of the Jan 9 call: no 2026 cuts and next move a hike in 2027; hike is distant, so +1.
items.call: on hold through 2026; 25bp hike in Q3 2027

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post denying he offered Jamie Dimon the Fed Chair job
items.quote: This statement is totally untrue, there was never such an offer
items.summary: Trump denied a Wall Street Journal report that he had offered Jamie Dimon the Fed Chair job and said he would sue JPMorgan over debanking. No rate-path content.
items.score_note: Fed Chair selection only; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Jan 18 edition)
items.quote: This latter consensus has effectively erased expectations for near-term Fed action, with implied probabilities for the next few FOMC meetings now sitting at de minimis levels.
items.summary: El-Erian describes the DOJ subpoena of Powell and Powell's defiant video as an extraordinary escalation of the Trump-Fed feud, noting Treasury and dollar volatility stayed low. He says central bankers closed ranks around independence and Fed officials showed no urgency to cut, wiping out pricing of near-term moves.
items.score_note: Describes a hold for the next few FOMC meetings; no directional lean of his own.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview from Davos (Joe Kernen)
items.quote: my prediction is that inflation is going to drop substantially this year
items.summary: Bessent said Trump could decide on the next Fed Chair as soon as next week (four candidates left), called Powell's plan to attend the Supreme Court hearing on Lisa Cook a mistake, and said the Fed loses $100 billion a year from mistimed asset purchases. He argued the US is in a 1990s-style productivity boom, the Fed should keep an open mind and let the economy run, and inflation will drop substantially this year.
items.score_note: Argues against tightening on strong growth and forecasts lower inflation; no explicit call for an immediate cut in this transcript.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs Exchanges podcast, recorded January 20 (published January 23)
items.quote: And the expectations are still for a cut or two in 2026.
items.summary: Solomon said the macro setup is pretty good for risk assets because of a confluence of stimulative policy: fiscal stimulus, monetary easing (100 basis points of cuts last year with a cut or two still expected in 2026), deregulation and an AI infrastructure investment boom. He expected more stimulative actions ahead of the midterms and saw geopolitics as the main uncertainty.
items.score_note: He cites the expectation of one or two more cuts in 2026 as part of his constructive base case; it is a description of expected easing, not a call for cuts, so -1.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview at World Economic Forum, Davos
items.quote: When you have conflicts, international geopolitical conflicts, even allies do not want to hold each other's debt.
items.summary: Dalio warns trade wars can turn into capital wars in which foreign holders are less willing to buy US debt while the US keeps issuing large volumes. He says the monetary order is breaking down and central banks prefer hard currency (gold) to fiat debt.
items.score_note: No view on the policy-rate path; about Treasury supply-demand and reserve diversification.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Semafor interview at Davos
items.quote: You could easily imagine it could simply become unpopular to buy or hold US debt
items.summary: Dalio tells Semafor that US reliance on foreign buyers of its debt is an enormous vulnerability amid the Greenland dispute. He says it could become unpopular abroad to buy or hold US debt.
items.score_note: No policy-rate view; bond demand risk only.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: White House press briefing
items.quote: In the old days if you had good numbers, they'd lower interest rates or they wouldn't do anything.
items.summary: Trump said growth could be far higher if the Fed did not raise rates every time there are good numbers, said 'they shouldn't do it', and that the Fed tries to 'kill' success.
items.score_note: Opposes rate hikes in response to strong growth; no explicit cut demand in this passage.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks to reporters on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum, Davos
items.quote: I’m not concerned at all.
items.summary: Asked whether the Greenland dispute could trigger European selling of US Treasuries, Bessent said he was not concerned, called Denmark's Treasury holdings 'irrelevant' and said Treasury auctions have seen record foreign investment.
items.score_note: About foreign demand for Treasuries; no statement on Fed policy.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: World Economic Forum, Davos, on-stage interview
items.quote: I don't like the courts doing stuff like that.
items.summary: At Davos Dimon criticised the administration's probe of Fed Chair Powell, saying courts should be very thoughtful before picking up something like that. Yahoo Finance's video page of the same session says (journalist's paraphrase, not a direct quote) that he called the probe lawfare but also argued the Fed is not quite as independent as people think. He also called the proposed 10% credit card rate cap an economic disaster.
items.score_note: Fed independence and the Powell probe only; no view on the rate path. The 'not as independent as people think' line was found only as a journalist's paraphrase.

items.speaker: Jeremy Schwartz
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (Jan 16-21)
items.quote: we suspect the new leadership will likely manage to get another 50 basis points of rate cuts later in the year
items.summary: Schwartz said the economic outlook on its face argues for a hold and maybe even putting hikes on the table later, but Nomura expects the Fed on hold through the rest of Powell's term (May) and then 50bp of cuts later in 2026 under the new chair.
items.score_note: Base case is 50bp of cuts later in 2026, driven by new leadership rather than data; mentions hikes as what the data alone might suggest.
items.call: on hold through Powell's term (May); 50bp of cuts later in 2026 under new Fed leadership

items.speaker: Ken Griffin
items.occasion: Remarks at the World Economic Forum in Davos, reported by Reuters
items.quote: The easy money policies that Trump is trying to encourage the Fed to pursue increase the risk of inflation
items.summary: Griffin says Trump's tariffs raised US inflation and disrupted long-standing trade relationships, and that pushing the Fed toward easy money raises inflation risk and leaves Trump and his party politically exposed. Reuters notes he reiterated his concern about the administration's attacks on the Fed.
items.score_note: Pushes back on pressure for rate cuts on inflation grounds; does not call for hikes.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: World Economic Forum, Davos, panel discussion
items.quote: I think there will be big failures, but I don't think we are in a bubble,
items.summary: On a Davos panel Fink said the AI investment boom will produce big failures but is not a bubble, and that Western economies must scale spending to compete with China. He warned the build-out fails if the technology stays the domain of six hyperscalers. No comment on Fed policy.
items.score_note: AI capex view only; no rate-path content.
items.ai_quote: If technology is just the domain of the six hyperscalers, we will fail,

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Fortune interview at World Economic Forum, Davos (with Kamal Ahmed)
items.quote: Do you print money or do you let a debt crisis happen?
items.summary: Dalio says the debt problem is so large that the monetary order is breaking down and policymakers face a choice between printing money and allowing a debt crisis. Fortune pairs this with his earlier remark that the debt will be repaid in devalued dollars.
items.score_note: He frames a dilemma (print vs. debt crisis) without saying which way the Fed will or should go in this quote. Debt-crisis remarks concern government debt, not private or corporate credit, so credit_view is null.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Joe Kernen in Davos (aired on Closing Bell)
items.quote: He's always too late, except when it comes to politics for the other side, where he was actually too early.
items.summary: Trump said the Fed Chair shortlist was down to 'maybe one in my mind', praised Hassett, Rieder and the others, and said he wants a Greenspan-like chair who will not raise rates when growth numbers are strong. He said growth is not a big cause of inflation, called Powell always too late, and said Powell's life 'won't be very, very happy' if he stays on as governor.
items.score_note: Clear dovish pressure (Powell too late, do not hike on good numbers) but no explicit 'cut now' in this interview; scored nearer 0.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Special address at the World Economic Forum, Davos
items.quote: we should be paying a much lower interest rate than we are.
items.summary: Trump said he would announce a new Fed chairman 'in the not too distant future', complained that Fed chairs change once they get the job and raise rates, called Powell a terrible chairman who is always too late, and said the US should pay the lowest interest rate of any country.
items.score_note: Explicitly says US rates should be much lower, the lowest in the world.

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast, quarterly economics roundtable (recorded Thursday Jan 22, 10am New York)
items.quote: If that's the case, then we think the Fed can execute one or two more rate cuts.
items.summary: Gapen said tariff pass-through should last through Q1, after which inflation pressures diminish and the Fed can deliver one or two more cuts, which Morgan Stanley has in the second half of the year.
items.score_note: Expects one or two more cuts in 2026, conditional on inflation easing.
items.call: 2026: one or two more cuts, in the second half of the year, if inflation comes down

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post on mortgage rates hitting a three-year low
items.quote: The Fed has been hurt and discredited during Too Late’s reign!
items.summary: Trump said mortgage rates hit a three-year low despite Powell's 'never ending quest to keep Interest Rates high', and that the market is overtaking Powell's obstinance.
items.score_note: Attacks Powell for keeping rates high (implied wish for lower rates) without an explicit cut demand in this post.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle aboard Air Force One (return from Davos)
items.quote: Despite that, we have interest rates going down.
items.summary: Asked whether the DOJ investigation might make Powell stay longer at the Fed, Trump said he is not concerned, called Powell 'always too late', and said interest rates are going down despite him.
items.score_note: 'Too late' criticism without an explicit demand in this exchange.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Bloomberg interview at Goldman Sachs' annual Asia-Pacific conference
items.quote: I think the chance of a recession this year is low in the US
items.summary: Solomon put the base case for a US recession at one in seven and said he would not expect one without an exogenous event that changes sentiment. He expected a strong capital markets year with broader market participation, while noting the risk of a potential bubble in AI stocks and geopolitical speed bumps. No direct comment on the Fed in the reported remarks.
items.score_note: Growth and markets outlook only; the reference to the Fed's rate-cutting cycle in the article is the journalist's, not his.

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted by investingLive
items.quote: We have penciled in the next 25bp rate cut in June, followed by a final cut in September to 3-3.25%.
items.summary: Ahead of the January meeting Goldman expected an uneventful hold, saying the FOMC had just delivered three cuts and is well positioned while it assesses their impact; it kept its path of a June cut and a final September cut to 3-3.25%.
items.score_note: Two more cuts in 2026 but not before June.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and September, to a terminal 3-3.25%

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted by investingLive
items.quote: We expect the Fed to remain on hold at its January meeting, keeping the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.5-3.75%.
items.summary: Morgan Stanley expected a January hold with the easing-bias language retained, and expected Powell to deliver a dovish hold that still points to further rate cuts rather than a durable pause.
items.score_note: Expects the Fed to keep an explicit easing bias; no dates in the quoted passage.
items.call: hold in January; dovish hold with easing bias retained (no dated path in passage)

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle before Marine One departure (first day of January FOMC)
items.quote: I'd like to see interest rates go down, everything else is going down.
items.summary: Asked how far he would like mortgage rates to drop, Trump said he would like to see interest rates go down, as energy, gasoline and grocery prices are falling.
items.score_note: General wish for lower rates in answer to a mortgage-rate question; not a direct demand on the Fed.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Speech on the economy and energy, Clive, Iowa
items.quote: he wants to keep rates as high as possible.
items.summary: Trump called Powell a bad Fed chairman who is 'too late' and wants to keep rates as high as possible, and said mortgage rates were driven down to a three-year low despite him.
items.score_note: Attacks Powell for keeping rates high; implied wish for lower rates, no explicit cut demand.

items.speaker: Barclays economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: signal it is in no rush to cut rates further
items.summary: Barclays expected the FOMC to signal it is in no rush to cut again and to describe downside employment risks and upside inflation risks as more balanced; its path was 50bp of cuts in 2026, in June and December.
items.score_note: Two cuts in 2026, the first not before June, with a no-rush message.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, cuts in June and December

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk on the Street interview (Sara Eisen), FOMC decision day
items.quote: I do think that there are many members on the board who had a false narrative on inflation
items.summary: Asked whether a hold at that day's FOMC would be a mistake, Bessent said it is up to the Fed but that many board members had a false narrative on inflation and he hopes they keep an open mind over the next couple of months. He said inflation is moving back toward target and there are four great Fed Chair candidates.
items.score_note: Declines to call the hold a mistake but says the Fed's inflation narrative is wrong; leans easier.

items.speaker: BofA economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: The Fed is firmly on hold, and the balance of risk hasn't changed.
items.summary: BofA said politics may take center stage at the January meeting, the Fed is firmly on hold with the balance of risk unchanged, and market pricing creates risk of a dovish surprise from Powell; its path was 50bp of cuts in June and July.
items.score_note: Firmly on hold near term but two cuts forecast for mid-2026.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, cuts in June and July

items.speaker: Citi economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: the Fed will likely deliver more cuts than are priced
items.summary: Citi said a soft labor market and cooling inflation mean the Fed will likely deliver more cuts over 2026 than the market prices; its path was 75bp, in March, July and September.
items.score_note: Most dovish house in the set: three cuts starting in March, more than priced. March is two meetings away, so between -2 and -1; chose -1.
items.call: 2026: 75bp, cuts in March, July and September

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Scott Wapner after the FOMC press conference (quotes via Business Insider)
items.quote: If you slash interest rates, then you're not only running a weaker dollar policy, but you're running an inflationary policy,
items.summary: Gundlach said inflation is running near 3% and that cutting rates below inflation would stoke prices and weaken the dollar further. He recommended non-US stocks, short-maturity bonds and precious metals, and said he was bearish on long bonds.
items.score_note: Warns against rate cuts as inflationary; no call for hikes, so +1.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Dissent at the January 27-28 FOMC meeting (preferred a 25 bp cut; Waller dissented with him)
items.quote: who preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting
items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3.50-3.75%. Miran and Waller voted against, preferring a 25 bp cut. The quote is the Committee statement's wording of the dissent, not Miran's own words; no separate Miran dissent statement was found on the Board's site.
items.score_note: Formal dissent in favor of an immediate cut.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, January 27-28 meeting: opening statement
items.quote: we see the current stance of monetary policy as appropriate to promote progress toward both our maximum-employment and 2 percent inflation goals
items.summary: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% after 75 bp of cuts over the previous three meetings (Miran and Waller dissented for a 25 bp cut). Powell said the rate is within a range of plausible neutral estimates, the labor market shows signs of stabilizing, core PCE is 3.0% mostly because of tariffs on goods, and the Committee is well positioned to decide the extent and timing of further adjustments meeting by meeting.
items.score_note: Hold described as appropriate, two-sided risks, no lean on timing of the next move.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, January 27-28 meeting: Q&A on the next move (cut timing, possibility of a hike)
items.quote: it isn’t anybody’s base case right now—anybody’s base case—that the next move will be a rate hike
items.summary: Asked whether the next move is necessarily down, Powell said upside inflation risks and downside employment risks have both diminished and declined to say they are fully balanced. He said tariff inflation peaking and coming down would tell the Fed it can loosen, as would renewed labor weakness; a hike is not off the table but is nobody's base case. He also said it is hard to call policy significantly restrictive (loosely neutral or somewhat restrictive) and that a good piece of normalization is done.
items.score_note: Easing still the conditional direction but no timing commitment and policy described as near neutral; balanced, so 0 rather than -1.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, January 27-28 meeting: Q&A on Fed independence and political pressure
items.quote: monetary policy can be used through an election cycle to affect the economy in a way that will be politically worthwhile
items.summary: Powell declined to add to his January 11 statement, to say whether the Fed had responded to the subpoenas, or to say whether he will stay on as a Governor. He explained why he attended the Supreme Court hearing in the Lisa Cook case, defended central bank independence as standard practice in advanced democracies, and advised his successor to stay out of elected politics.
items.score_note: Independence and political pressure only; no rate-path content in this exchange.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, January 27-28 meeting: Q&A on the fiscal path and long-term rates
items.quote: The U.S. federal budget deficit is uncontroversially on an unsustainable path.
items.summary: Asked about Japan's bond-market turmoil, Powell said the US deficit path is unsustainable and is not being addressed, though he did not connect it to a near-term market event. He said 10-year yields are driven more by assessments of the fiscal path and risk than by the overnight rate, so there is no tight link between Fed cuts and long rates. He declined to comment on the dollar and said gold and silver moves carry little macro message.
items.score_note: Fiscal and term-premium commentary; no stance on the policy rate path.

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts note after the January FOMC: Fed Holds Steady and Signals Longer-Term Easing Bias
items.quote: We expect the Fed will remain on hold until later this year, when rate cuts are likely to resume.
items.summary: Wilding expects the Fed to stay on hold for now and resume rate cuts later in 2026 as inflation pressures recede with productivity gains, fading tariff effects and softer housing costs.
items.score_note: Cuts expected to resume later in 2026; not imminent.
items.call: on hold until later in 2026, then rate cuts resume

items.speaker: Wells Fargo economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: the higher the hurdle becomes to justify on economic grounds the need
items.summary: Wells Fargo kept 50bp of cuts in March and June but said the longer the FOMC waits, the higher the hurdle to justify further easing, and it did not expect Powell to hint at a March cut.
items.score_note: Keeps March and June cuts while conceding the hurdle is rising; chose -1 rather than -2.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, cuts in March and June

items.speaker: J.P. Morgan Wealth Management strategists (not named in quoted passage)
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Wealth Management web article after the January 28 FOMC
items.quote: Our strategists anticipate one more rate cut this year, in line with consensus.
items.summary: The wealth-management arm (distinct from Feroli's Global Research, which forecasts no cuts) said its strategists do not anticipate a cut until summer and expect one more cut in 2026.
items.score_note: One cut expected in 2026, not before summer. Not the investment-bank research call.
items.call: 2026: one more cut, not before summer

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Keynote speaker introduction (FDIC Chairman Travis Hill), SMU 'Payments of the Future' symposium, Dallas Fed
items.quote: As the Federal Reserve System explores emerging technologies such as tokenization and smart contracts, we remain focused on balancing innovation with safety.
items.summary: Short welcome and speaker introduction at a digital-payments symposium the day after the January FOMC. Covers payments innovation and stablecoin regulation only; nothing on the economy or the rate path.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; official speech kept for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post the morning after the January FOMC hold
items.quote: The Fed should substantially lower interest rates, NOW!
items.summary: Trump said Powell 'again refused to cut interest rates' with no reason to keep them high, is hurting the country and national security, and is costing hundreds of billions in interest expense. He said the US should pay the lowest interest rate of any country because of tariff revenue.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for substantially lower rates now.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Cabinet meeting at the White House (day after January FOMC hold)
items.quote: We should have the lowest interest rate anywhere in the world.
items.summary: Trump said the Fed's rates are 'unacceptably high', the US is paying far too much interest and should have the lowest rate in the world. He said he wants a system where good news leads to lower rather than higher rates, that 'if inflation comes, we'll take care of it when it comes', and that the right Fed choice would help get rates down.
items.score_note: Calls Fed rates unacceptably high and demands the lowest rate in the world.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle at a movie premiere, Washington
items.quote: you notice that the interest rates now are falling despite The Fed.
items.summary: Asked about the 10-2 FOMC vote to hold, Trump said there are 'political people' on the Fed who vote against him, that the Fed could have been much more helpful, and that he would announce his Fed Chair choice the next morning.
items.score_note: Says the Fed should have been more helpful and frames the hold as political; no explicit demand in this exchange.

items.speaker: Raphael Bostic
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (until 2026-02-28; non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview with Steve Liesman (one line quoted in a Reuters analysis via SRN News)
items.quote: When the economy grows the balance sheet needs to grow with it.
items.summary: On the day Warsh was nominated, Bostic said the size of the Fed's balance sheet is about right and must grow with the economy, pushing back on Warsh's call to shrink the Fed's market footprint. The Atlanta Fed's listing says the interview also covered independence, inflation and interest rates, but no rate-path quote could be opened.
items.score_note: Only a balance-sheet quote is available; no rate-path statement in an openable source.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: SW Graduate School of Banking at SMU Cox, 161st Assembly for Bank Directors, Oahu: 'Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy'
items.quote: I continue to see policy as moderately restrictive, and, looking ahead to 2026, my Summary of Economic Projections includes three cuts for this year.
items.summary: Explains her vote to hold in January: after 75bp of cuts the Fed can 'keep policy powder dry' for a little while, with two more jobs and inflation reports before March. Downside labor risks have not diminished; the Fed should be ready to move toward neutral and should not imply an extended hold.
items.score_note: Voted to hold but projects three 2026 cuts and warns against signaling an extended pause; leaning easier, not calling for an immediate cut.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, CNBC 'Money Movers' (CNBC excerpts of unofficial transcript)
items.quote: It's an economy that can, that can have lower rates because it can have a stronger labor market than it has now.
items.summary: Two days after dissenting, Miran said there is no inflation problem (market-based core ex housing at 2.2%), that the unemployment rate is about half a point too high, and that tariffs are not a significant driver of overall inflation. He praised Warsh's nomination and said the central bank should accommodate job reallocation caused by new technology.
items.score_note: Says the economy can and should have lower rates, right after a dissent for a cut.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "U.S. Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy" and moderated Q&A, Arkansas Business Forecast Luncheon, Rogers, Ark. (University of Arkansas CBER)
items.quote: With inflation above target and the risks to the outlook evenly balanced, I believe it would be unadvisable to lower the rate into accommodative territory at this time.
items.summary: Two days after the January hold, Musalem said he supported keeping the funds rate at 3.5%-3.75%, called that setting neutral, and said risks to the outlook are evenly balanced. He expects growth at or above trend and inflation to resume falling toward 2% as tariff effects fade, but said cutting into accommodative territory would be unadvisable.
items.score_note: Hold with balanced risks would be 0, but he explicitly pushes back on further cuts (unadvisable to lower the rate into accommodative territory) at a time markets priced cuts; scored +1 on the rubric line "pushes back on cut talk". Borderline with 0.

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Hard Lessons Ep.4 (녹화 2026-01-30, 공개 2026-02-27) · Iliana Bouzali
items.quote: My guess is the Fed is certainly not gonna hike and probably gonna cut.
items.summary: US economy already strong and getting stronger with fiscal stimulus; he guesses the Fed will not hike and will probably cut. Short bonds as a hedge: if the Fed cuts into a booming economy, inflation could take off.
items.summary_kr: 미국 경제는 이미 강하고 재정부양으로 더 강해질 것으로 봄. 연준은 인상은 확실히 안 하고 아마 인하할 것으로 추측함. 호황에 인하하면 인플레가 튈 수 있어 채권 숏을 헤지로 들고 있다고 밝힘.
items.score_note: 연준이 인하할 것이라는 전망(probably). 본인이 인하를 지지한 것은 아님.

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Hard Lessons Ep.4 (녹화 2026-01-30, 공개 2026-02-27) · Iliana Bouzali
items.quote: I couldn't think of anybody better prepared to be Fed Chair for what's ahead of us.
items.summary: On Warsh's nomination the same day: an extraordinary talent who has 'been training for this for 25 years'. Also most excited about the Fed and Treasury (Warsh and Bessent) working together.
items.summary_kr: Warsh 지명 당일 발언. 25년간 이 자리를 준비해 온 사람이라 평가하고, Warsh와 Bessent가 연준·재무부 공조를 해낼 것으로 낙관함. 금리 경로 언급은 없음.

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Hard Lessons Ep.4 (녹화 2026-01-30, 공개 2026-02-27) · Iliana Bouzali
items.quote: They're all preceded by asset bubbles.
items.summary: Asked which 2026 risk he fears most, he picks narrative-driven bubbles: every really bad economic outcome was preceded by an asset bubble. But he adds 'I don't think we're there.'
items.summary_kr: 2026년 가장 두려운 위험으로 내러티브 버블을 꼽음. 대공황·금융위기 같은 큰 사고는 전부 자산 버블 뒤에 왔다고 봄. 다만 아직 그 단계는 아니라고 말함.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social posts announcing the nomination of Kevin Warsh as Fed Chair
items.quote: I am pleased to announce that I am nominating Kevin Warsh to be the CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD OF GOVERNORS OF THE FEDERAL RESERVE SYSTEM.
items.summary: Trump announced Warsh's nomination, said he will 'go down as one of the GREAT Fed Chairmen' and is 'central casting'. In follow-up posts at 07:34 and 07:45 (statuses 36362, 36366) he said he kept Hassett at the White House and praised Waller and Rieder. No rate-path statement in these posts.
items.score_note: Personnel announcement; no policy-rate content in the post text.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Oval Office remarks at executive order signing (day of Warsh nomination)
items.quote: But he certainly wants to cut rates.
items.summary: Asked whether Warsh committed to cut rates, Trump said no, that asking would be inappropriate and he wants to keep it 'nice and pure', but that Warsh certainly wants to cut rates. He called Warsh the perfect candidate and 'central casting'.
items.score_note: Expresses expectation that his nominee will cut, while denying he asked for a commitment; scored -1 rather than -2 because no direct demand is made.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Statement explaining his dissent at the January 27-28 FOMC meeting (the vote on January 28 was a hold; he preferred a 25bp cut)
items.quote: monetary policy is still restricting economic activity, and economic data make it clear to me further easing is needed
items.summary: Explains his January 28 dissent in favor of a 25bp cut. Labor market is weak (2025 payroll growth likely revised to zero), tariff inflation should be looked through, underlying inflation is close to 2 percent, and the policy rate is 50 to 75bp above neutral.
items.score_note: Dissent in favor of an immediate cut and says further easing is needed.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Feb 1 edition)
items.quote: Warsh is a respected figure with deep expertise and experience, and a clear mandate to reform the central bank.
items.summary: After the January FOMC left rates unchanged and Trump nominated Kevin Warsh, El-Erian calls the Powell press conference uneventful and welcomes Warsh as a qualified reformer. He notes the confirmation timeline is uncertain because two senators are resisting until the DOJ probe of Powell is resolved.
items.score_note: Comments on the nominee and Fed reform, not on the direction of rates.

items.speaker: Raphael Bostic
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (until 2026-02-28; non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Moderated discussion with Dennis Lockhart, Rotary Club of Atlanta (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: So I think this is the time to be patient.
items.summary: Bostic says that with the economy strong and the labor market stabilized, cutting rates would make it very unlikely inflation returns to target; Reuters reports he believes the Fed should not cut at all this year. He says Warsh faces a tall task in persuading the Committee and must build trust.
items.score_note: Opposes any cut in 2026 on inflation grounds; pushes back on cut talk but does not ask for a hike.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Fireside chat with Ben Horowitz at an a16z founder event (held a few weeks before the a16z write-up of Feb 2)
items.quote: we’re in a rate cutting cycle
items.summary: In remarks quoted by a16z, Solomon listed fiscal stimulus, monetary stimulus, a rate cutting cycle and an AI capital investment supercycle as a cocktail of stimulus that makes it very hard to slow the economy down. He predicted 2026 could be the biggest M&A year in history.
items.score_note: Treats continued Fed easing as a given (rate cutting cycle); a forecast, not advocacy, so -1. The quote sits inside an ellipsized pull quote on the page; only the clause between the ellipses is used. Event date not stated; article date used.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Oval Office bill-signing remarks (Q&A on the Powell probe)
items.quote: No, she's going to take it to the end and see.
items.summary: Asked whether he would like US Attorney Jeanine Pirro to drop the investigation of Powell to ease Warsh's confirmation, Trump said no, that she will take it to the end, and that the Fed renovation shows gross incompetence or theft.
items.score_note: About the Powell investigation; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'U.S. Economy: The Road Ahead' (Richmond Fed posted text)
items.quote: But we know things change, and as they do, we remain ready to respond as appropriate.
items.summary: Barkin describes the 175 basis points of cuts as insurance to support the labor market while the Fed completes the last mile on inflation, and says 'so far, so good'. The Fed stands ready to respond as conditions change. He again flags that demand is concentrated in the AI ecosystem and wealthy consumers, so an AI pullback could hit investment, stocks and consumption.
items.score_note: Hold with readiness to respond in either direction; no lean stated. Time from the Richmond Fed media advisory.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
