items.occasion: Interview, Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria'
items.quote: I'm probably looking for a little bit more than a point of interest rate cuts over the course of the year
items.summary: Miran said the Fed is keeping rates too high mostly because of quirks in how inflation is measured rather than real price pressures, and that he will keep arguing for his view inside the Committee. He called Warsh a fantastic choice for Chair.
items.score_note: Explicit call for a little more than 100 bp of cuts in 2026.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: House Financial Services Committee hearing on the FSOC annual report (Q&A)
items.quote: I do believe that the Federal Reserve has to maintain credibility and be like Caesar’s wife, beyond reproach.
items.summary: In Q&A Bessent said he considers the Fed an independent agency but has no opinion on whether a president may fire Fed officials over policy disagreements. He said Fed independence rests on public trust that was lost when it let inflation 'ravage' incomes, that Trump has the right to voice views on rates, and that he was wrong to have called tariffs inflationary. The prepared statement (treasury.gov sb0387) has no monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Fed independence and credibility only; no statement on what rates should do.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Economic Club of Miami: 'Economic Outlook'
items.quote: At this time, I see risks as tilted toward higher inflation.
items.summary: Cook said inflation progress stalled in 2025 (core PCE about 3 percent) while the labor market stabilized at 4.4 percent unemployment. She supported the January hold and said her focus stays on inflation until she sees stronger evidence it is moving sustainably back to target, absent unexpected labor-market changes; weak sentiment does not signal slack that demand-side policy can fix. She stressed credibility after nearly five years of above-target inflation. In the Q&A (Reuters) she said policy is "mildly restrictive but ever so mildly restrictive" and that after last year's easing "this is the right time to sit back and wait to see what happens".
items.score_note: Explicit risk tilt toward inflation and a bar for further easing; no mention of hikes, so +1.

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Global Research web article on the Fed's next move (version dated February 04, 2026, after the January FOMC and Warsh nomination; archived Feb 19)
items.quote: We see the Fed holding the target range for the funds rate steady at 3.5-3.75% for the rest of the year.
items.summary: After the January hold and the Warsh nomination, J.P. Morgan Global Research continued to expect no change in 2026 and a 25bp hike in Q3 2027; Feroli thinks Warsh may not find it easy to persuade the committee to cut.
items.score_note: Unchanged call: hold all year, next move a 2027 hike.
items.call: on hold for the rest of 2026; 25bp hike in Q3 2027

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: NBC News interview with Tom Llamas
items.quote: He would not have gotten the job, no.
items.summary: Asked whether Warsh understands that he wants lower rates, Trump said 'I think he does. But I think he wants to anyway', and confirmed that if Warsh had said he wanted to raise rates he would not have gotten the job. He said US rates are 'way high', inflation is low, and all he has to do now is 'get down the interest rates'. He said the Fed is 'in theory' an independent body.
items.score_note: Makes lower rates a condition for the Fed Chair job and says rates must come down.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Senate Banking Committee hearing on the FSOC annual report (Q&A)
items.quote: That is up to the president
items.summary: Asked by Senator Warren to promise that Warsh would not be sued or investigated if he does not cut rates the way Trump wants, Bessent replied 'That is up to the president'. The prepared statement (treasury.gov sb0388) has no monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Declines to rule out legal pressure on the Fed nominee; no statement on the rate path itself.

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast on the January FOMC (recorded Thursday Feb 5, 8:30am New York)
items.quote: And in our view, it was more of a dovish hold.
items.summary: Gapen read the January meeting as a dovish hold: the Fed still has an easing bias and rates should generally move lower over time, likely when inflation comes down.
items.score_note: Sees an easing bias and lower rates over time; no dated path in the passage.
items.call: dovish hold; Fed keeps an easing bias and cuts later when inflation comes down (no dates in passage)

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Halftime Report interview (Scott Wapner), excerpts
items.quote: The President has great respect for the Fed, for the Fed’s independence, and Kevin Warsh is his choice.
items.summary: CNBC published excerpts only. Bessent said Trump respects Fed independence and that Warsh brings credibility and will be a fantastic leader on monetary policy and regulation. On the Powell probe he said 'no crime, but probably guilty of incompetence'. The page header misprints the year as 2025; the body and video link give Friday, February 6, 2026.
items.score_note: No rate-path content in the published excerpts.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview with Ann Saphir (Reuters exclusive, Yahoo Finance copy)
items.quote: I was supportive of that decision, but frankly, I thought you could make a case for going ahead and taking a little more off
items.summary: Daly said she supported the January hold but that a case could be made for another cut, and that she leans toward additional cuts in 2026, whether one or two being hard to say. She is a little more worried about the labor market than about inflation and called the job market precarious; cutting requires real confidence that tariff effects roll off and inflation is falling, or more worry about jobs than the data now show.
items.score_note: Leans toward one or two more cuts and puts labor-market risk first, but supported the hold and sets conditions; -1 rather than -2.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Brookings Institution, Washington: 'Economic Outlook and Supply-Side (Dis)Inflation Dynamics'
items.quote: The current policy stance is well positioned to address the risks to both sides of our dual mandate.
items.summary: Supported the January hold. Policy rate is broadly within the range of neutral estimates; further adjustments depend on data, outlook and balance of risks. Expects disinflation to resume once tariffs pass through; says AI-related demand could raise inflation temporarily but productivity gains leave more leeway without precautionary restraint. In the moderated Q&A (Brookings transcript PDF, https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/20260206_Transcript_unedited.pdf) he said the policy rate is supporting the labor market and he does not want to see any more weakening there, while inflation is still above target.
items.score_note: Explicitly balanced, meeting-by-meeting; the Q&A added nothing that tilts it.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Feb 7 edition)
items.quote: Second, what is the bond market’s appetite for funding this expansion, given widening spreads and some frisson in the leveraged loan market?
items.summary: El-Erian says softer labor data led markets to price a 60% chance of a June cut and that policy divergence among advanced-economy central banks could become a 2026 theme. On hyperscaler capex (Alphabet and Amazon alone guiding to about $400 billion) he asks whether the spending will pay off and whether the bond market will fund it given wider spreads and jitters in leveraged loans.
items.score_note: Reports market pricing of a June cut without endorsing it; main own view is the question about debt funding of AI capex.
items.ai_quote: Second, what is the bond market’s appetite for funding this expansion, given widening spreads and some frisson in the leveraged loan market?

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Fox News 'Sunday Morning Futures' interview
items.quote: I would think that they’ll probably sit back, take at least a year to decide what they want to do.
items.summary: Bessent said balance sheet decisions are up to the Fed, that he would not expect it to do anything quickly, and that an ample-reserves regime requires a larger balance sheet. He said Warsh will be a very independent Fed chief.
items.score_note: Forecast that the Fed will not shrink its balance sheet quickly; neutral for the rate path.

items.speaker: Marc Rowan
items.occasion: Apollo Q4 2025 earnings call (Q&A)
items.quote: And so I do think that there is going to be increased dispersion amongst managers.
items.summary: Rowan says the market's reaction to software is extreme, with some quality companies down 50% to 70%, but stresses that direct-lending exposure is first lien and that Apollo's own software exposure is minimal. He expects more dispersion among managers after a long easy period.
items.score_note: Credit-quality commentary only; no view on the Fed or the rate path.
items.ai_quote: Most of the investments that are made into these private BDCs are de-risking for the individual making the investment.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Conversation for WBUR podcast 'Is Business Broken?', WBUR CitySpace, Boston University
items.quote: to me indicates that housing inflation is going to normalize, I think, pretty quickly this year
items.summary: Miran argued that apparently elevated inflation reflects measurement problems, especially lagged housing costs, that tariffs are not a material driver of inflation, and that the Fed's job is stable prices rather than a lower price level. He said the Fed should stick to interest rate policy and not politicize itself. Earlier the same day at BU's Questrom School he argued that foreign exporters bear most of the tariff cost (Reuters).
items.score_note: Argues the inflation obstacle to easing is a measurement artifact, but the university write-up carries no direct call for a cut on this occasion.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Fox Business interview with Larry Kudlow
items.quote: We should be two points lower right now.
items.summary: Trump said rates should already have been cut and should be two points lower, that every point costs $600 billion and two points lower would eliminate the deficit, and that the US should have the lowest rates in the world. He said all the new Fed head has to do is lower interest rates and complained that the Fed stops growth by raising rates. Factba.se dates the interview February 9 (the URL slug carries a 2023 typo).
items.score_note: Explicit demand for rates two points lower.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: UBS Financial Services Conference, fireside chat
items.quote: There is uncertainty around inflation, and there's uncertainty on geopolitics.
items.summary: Solomon said 2026 could be a top-decile year for dealmaking, helped by deregulation and sponsors needing to return capital. He said the capital needed for the AI technology cycle will lift the overall capital-raising cycle and pointed to mega-cap tech firms raising debt for AI projects. He listed trade, inflation and geopolitics as uncertainties.
items.score_note: Mentions inflation only as an uncertainty; no view on the Fed rate path in the reported remarks.
items.ai_quote: The need for capital to continue on this technology cycle is going to have an impact on the overall capital-raising cycle

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech to the Ohio Bankers League, 'Recipe for a Thriving US Economy: Strong Banks, Patient Policy, and an Independent yet Accountable Central Bank'
items.quote: Based on my forecast, we could be on hold for quite some time.
items.summary: Hammack said she supported the January hold, that the funds rate is in the vicinity of neutral and not meaningfully restraining the economy, and that she prefers to err on the side of patience rather than fine tune. Inflation is still too high and has moved sideways for two years, with a risk it stays near 3 percent. She sees the risks of a higher or lower path for the funds rate as about balanced and defended Fed independence. In the banking half of the speech she listed nonbank growth, including private credit, among the well-known financial-stability risks.
items.score_note: Extended hold with explicitly balanced risks to the rate path; pushes back on near-term cuts but states no tightening lean. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.ai_quote: These services include private credit, whose speed, flexibility, limited disclosure, and customization often make it an appealing alternative to traditional bank loans.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Speech 'Outlook for the economy and monetary policy', FIA-SIFMA Asset Management Derivatives Forum, Austin (followed by moderated conversation)
items.quote: But right now, I am more worried about inflation remaining stubbornly high.
items.summary: Logan says she supported the January hold, that labor-market downside risks have meaningfully dissipated, and that policy may be very close to neutral and providing little restraint. If inflation falls and the labor market stays stable, no further rate cuts are needed; a cut could become appropriate only with material further labor cooling. On implementation she backs the end of runoff and reserve management purchases as technical, says purchases should not be mechanical and should track the TGCR-IORB spread, and calls for a centrally cleared standing repo option.
items.score_note: Pushes back on further cuts, sees policy near neutral and says inflation is the bigger worry, but is 'cautiously optimistic' the current stance works and does not raise hikes: +1, not +2.

items.speaker: David Einhorn
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Sara Eisen
items.quote: I think by the time we get to the end of the year, it's going to be substantially more than two cuts
items.summary: Einhorn says there will be substantially more than the two cuts markets price and that Kevin Warsh will persuade the committee to cut by arguing productivity, even if the economy is running hot, unless inflation reaches 4% or 5%. He calls betting on more cuts one of the best trades available and says US fiscal and monetary policies 'don't make any sense', a reason he owns gold.
items.score_note: Explicit forecast of substantially more than two cuts in 2026.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Moderated conversation with the Ohio State University community at WOSU Public Media, Columbus (as reported by The Lantern)
items.quote: I think we’re supposed to stay on hold right here
items.summary: At a mostly educational event about how the Fed works, Hammack said the labor market is stabilizing and that keeping rates where they are is the right course to bring inflation down; she does not want to fine-tune the economy. MNI separately reported that on February 11 she said the January jobs report showed a labor market finding a healthy balance while inflation is still too high.
items.score_note: Restates the hold from her February 10 speech with no new lean; student-newspaper report with a short direct quote.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Remarks after the January jobs report, as reported by Bloomberg (venue not stated in the visible text)
items.quote: a variety of reasons why I want to see lower interest rates
items.summary: Miran said the surprisingly strong January jobs data does not mean the Fed should hold off on further cuts, citing supply-side reforms such as deregulation and an expected slowdown in housing inflation. Only the opening paragraphs of the Bloomberg article are visible on this page.
items.score_note: Says he wants lower rates and that strong jobs data is no reason to delay cuts.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "Monetary Policy and the Economic Outlook", Economic Forum of Albuquerque, N.M.
items.quote: In my view, further rate cuts risk allowing high inflation to persist even longer.
items.summary: Schmid said demand is outpacing supply with inflation closer to 3% than 2%, so a somewhat restrictive stance is appropriate, and the funds rate is arguably no longer restraining activity much, if at all. He supported the January hold. On the balance sheet, he said the reserve-management bill purchases begun in December are not easing and that the Fed should keep shrinking its MBS holdings and shorten its Treasury duration.
items.score_note: Opposes further cuts on inflation grounds and doubts policy is restrictive; no call for a hike.

items.speaker: Stephen Juneau
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Feb 11)
items.quote: The Fed will cut twice this year under Warsh (but) it's not necessarily due to a clear economic argument,
items.summary: Juneau said BofA expects two cuts in 2026 under Warsh, but not because of a clear economic case; with more expansionary fiscal policy it "could be a recipe for overdoing it".
items.score_note: Forecast is two cuts in 2026 even though he sees weak economic justification.
items.call: 2026: two cuts under Warsh

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Conversation at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Global Perspectives event
items.quote: As long as I remain unconcerned about inflation, I think it makes sense to continue trying to underwrite the labor market with looser monetary policy
items.summary: Miran said the biggest risk to the economy is misjudging how tight policy is, that he has a hard time being concerned about inflation because very low shelter inflation offsets other components, and that supply is expanding faster than demand so the economy can grow without inflation.
items.score_note: Explicitly argues for looser policy now.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: X post on wealth vs. money and bubbles (as quoted by Benzinga/Yahoo)
items.quote: And when there's a lot of wealth relative to the amount of hard money available — like we're seeing today — bubbles are created.
items.summary: Dalio posts that wealth is worth nothing unless it can be converted into money, and that today's high ratio of financial wealth to money creates bubbles. The article notes he compares the ratio to 1929 and 2000 and sees forced selling (e.g. for wealth taxes) as a possible popper.
items.score_note: No policy-rate view; bubble mechanics only.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview (as reported by Reuters)
items.quote: anyone who cares about the integrity, the independence of the Fed is going to want to see continuity with Kevin Warsh
items.summary: Bessent said the Senate Banking Committee will proceed with Warsh hearings despite Senator Tillis's hold, that he proposed the committee run its own review of the Fed renovation, and that the DOJ probe's subpoenas need not mean charges. He said he expects inflation to be near the Fed's 2% target by mid-2026.
items.score_note: Mostly about the confirmation process; the inflation forecast is reported indirectly and no rate view is quoted.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Yahoo Finance interview with Jennifer Schonberger after January CPI
items.quote: I think rates can still keep going down a fair bit more, but we just need to see the progress on inflation,
items.summary: Goolsbee wants more progress on inflation and a steady job market before supporting another cut. He says services inflation is not tamed and tends to be persistent, and that he does not know how restrictive policy is; the Fed should see improvement rather than count on it before cutting.
items.score_note: Path is lower by 'a fair bit', conditional on inflation progress; doubts about restrictiveness temper it. Torn between -1 and 0.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: American Bankers Association 2026 Conference for Community Bankers, Orlando: 'Revitalizing Bank Mortgage Lending, One Step with Basel'
items.quote: These are legitimate concerns, and I want to be clear that holding MSRs is not the right choice for every bank.
items.summary: Bank capital treatment of mortgages and mortgage servicing rights. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: New York Association for Business Economics, New York: 'What Will Artificial Intelligence Mean for the Labor Market and the Economy?'
items.quote: I would like to see evidence that goods price inflation is sustainably retreating before considering reducing the policy rate further, provided labor market conditions remain stable.
items.summary: Barr said the labor market is stabilizing in a delicate balance while PCE inflation is stuck near 3 percent and the risk of persistent above-target inflation is significant. He said it will likely be appropriate to hold rates steady for some time and that the AI boom is unlikely to be a reason for lowering policy rates (higher r*, possible short-term inflation from data-center power demand). In an 'AI disappoints' scenario he said the balance of risks shifts from the labor market to the financial sector, citing estimates that AI investment needs $1 trillion of new debt over five years.
items.score_note: Hold for some time, sets a bar for further cuts, calls persistent-inflation risk significant and says AI is not a reason to lower rates; no talk of hikes, so +1 not +2.
items.ai_quote: One estimate is that AI investment will require the issuance of $1 trillion in new debt over the next five years, and other estimates are even higher.

items.speaker: Citi analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note written Tuesday Feb 17 ahead of January FOMC minutes, quoted by Reuters Feb 18
items.quote: The Fed is prepared to lower rates further this year if inflation cools
items.summary: Citi analysts wrote that the Fed is prepared to cut further in 2026 if inflation cools and that this should show up in the January FOMC minutes.
items.score_note: Expects further cuts this year conditional on cooler inflation; no timing on the page.
items.call: further cuts in 2026 if inflation cools (timing not stated on page)

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Keynote "The AI Moment? Possibilities, Productivity, and Policy" and conversation with Ed Ludlow, Silicon Valley Leadership Group / San Jose State University (official Q&A transcript)
items.quote: So right now we’re modestly restrictive, slightly restrictive, depending on who you talk to.
items.summary: In the prepared speech Daly drew on the 1990s, when the Greenspan FOMC stayed patient as productivity rose, and said policy must be forward-looking but evidence-based on AI. In the Q&A she said policy is modestly or slightly restrictive, with roughly 75 basis points to go to a neutral rate near 3%, but that inflation needs to come down first.
items.score_note: Describes policy as slightly restrictive with room to go to neutral (a mild easing bias) but conditions it on inflation falling; no call for a near-term move, so 0 rather than -1.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: I still think there's several more rate cuts that can happen in 2026,
items.summary: Goolsbee says several more cuts are possible in 2026 if data show inflation is on a path to 2 percent, 'but we've got to see it'. He discounts the cool January CPI because services inflation is not tamed and says inflation has stalled around 3 percent. He treats roughly 3 percent as a loose neutral target.
items.score_note: Expects several cuts this year toward about 3 percent, but conditional on inflation progress not yet seen.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta 2026 Banking Outlook Conference (pre-recorded video): Opening Remarks
items.quote: Last October, and for the first time, the Federal Reserve published supervisory operating principles.
items.summary: Opening remarks on the supervisory agenda, with a farewell to Atlanta Fed President Bostic. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: In Conversation: Mary C. Daly with Rob Kaplan (Harvard Business School audience, SF Fed; official transcript)
items.quote: But our dual mandate goals that are price stability and full employment, both seem to be in a good place.
items.summary: Daly said the 75 basis points of cuts in late 2025 put the labor market in a better place, inflation keeps coming down outside tariff-affected goods, and policy is in a good place. She said the Fed should neither constrain an economy that may get a productivity lift from AI nor forget inflation is above target.
items.score_note: Policy "in a good place", both mandates in a good place, no lean on the next move.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Q&A with Jim Ryan, Midwest Economic Outlook Summit, Fargo-Moorhead-West Fargo Chamber, Fargo ND (MPR News report)
items.quote: Ultimately, we need to see where does inflation go?
items.summary: Kashkari says future rate decisions depend on whether inflation comes all the way back to 2 percent and whether unemployment keeps rising, levels off or falls. He calls Kevin Hassett's demand to discipline New York Fed researchers another step to compromise Fed independence and says the Fed will keep deciding on data and analysis. In a separate MPR interview that week he described cautious optimism and called Warsh a well qualified pick.
items.score_note: Purely data dependent, no lean. Time converted from 8:05 a.m. CT on the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview with The Peg (The Blind Spot), conducted February 18 and published February 19
items.quote: if I had to put down the dot today, I probably would have moved it back to where it was in September
items.summary: Miran said that with data in hand he would move his end-2026 dot back to its September level (100 bp of cuts rather than the 150 bp he wrote in December) because the labor market came in a little better and goods inflation firmed. He still argued measured inflation is biased up by portfolio-management fees and lagged shelter, said AI on balance argues for looser policy but cannot be quantified, and said he prefers lowering reserve demand through regulatory changes and then shrinking the balance sheet without returning to scarce reserves, holding more bills and less duration.
items.score_note: A less accommodative path than his December dot, but still well below the Committee median; a revision toward tighter from a dovish position, so -1.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on Blue Owl restricting withdrawals from a retail private-credit fund
items.quote: Is this a “canary-in-the-coalmine” moment, similar to August 2007?
items.summary: Reacting to Blue Owl permanently halting redemptions at a retail private-debt fund, El-Erian compares the episode to BNP Paribas freezing funds in August 2007. He says systemic risks are nowhere near 2008 scale but a significant valuation hit is looming for specific assets and private-market investing may have gone too far.
items.score_note: Credit-stress warning only; no statement on the Fed rate path.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks before the Economic Club of Dallas: Economic Security First
items.quote: Economic security is the foundation that allows a country to fulfill its most basic obligation of safeguarding its people.
items.summary: Speech on economic security, supply chains and industrial policy. No Fed, interest-rate or Treasury-market content in the published text.
items.score_note: Official text with no statement on the Fed's policy rate; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Raphael Bostic
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (until 2026-02-28; non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Moderated conversation, Birmingham Business Journal event, Birmingham, Alabama (Reuters via SRN News)
items.quote: What that means is that we have to worry about the implications for prices on a strong economy,
items.summary: Bostic says 2.2 percent full-year growth is a pretty strong number, above his 1.8 percent estimate of potential, and he expects 2.4 percent this year. With inflation around 3 percent, a long way from target, strong growth is a reason to worry about prices; Reuters characterizes this as an argument for not cutting rates. He also flags disruption from the Supreme Court tariff ruling.
items.score_note: Above-potential growth plus 3 percent inflation used as a case against cuts; no hike call.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Moderated conversation, 10th Annual Bank Regulation Research Conference, Columbia University, New York (Reuters report)
items.quote: I'm not fully convinced that we're on a pathway to our 2% target
items.summary: Logan says policy is well positioned for the risks and she is cautiously optimistic inflation is on a path back toward target, but she is not fully convinced it will get to 2 percent because tariffs are still working through prices. She adds that the Supreme Court tariff ruling adds new uncertainty.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate, but the only risk she stresses is inflation not returning to 2 percent; consistent with her Feb 10 'no further cuts needed' line. Mild +1.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Fox Business interview with Edward Lawrence, 'The Claman Countdown', live from the St. Louis Fed Economy Museum (video page)
items.quote: well positioned
items.summary: Video-only interview. Fox Business's page title quotes Musalem as saying policy is 'well positioned' amid rate-cut speculation; the page says he discussed the Supreme Court tariff ruling, Warsh's nomination, monetary policy and data. A Reuters reprint of the same interview (https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-02-20/feds-musalem-tariff-ruling-could-mean-uncertainty) quotes him only on tariffs: one-for-one replacement tariffs would leave his forecast unchanged but the transition could bring a period of uncertainty for companies.
items.score_note: Only a two-word quotation in the outlet headline is available as text; "well positioned" signals comfort with holding. Thin evidence, scored 0 rather than inferring a lean from the video.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post on shutdowns and interest rates
items.quote: Also, LOWER INTEREST RATES.
items.summary: Trump blamed the earlier shutdown for costing two points of GDP, said no shutdowns, demanded lower interest rates and called Powell 'the WORST'.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for lower rates.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press conference on the Supreme Court tariff decision
items.quote: Interest rates should come down very substantially.
items.summary: Trump said the US has 'a very incompetent fed chairman who likes high interest rates' for political reasons, that rates should come down very substantially, and that the US should pay the lowest rates on the planet.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for substantially lower rates.

items.speaker: Michael Burry
items.role: Investor, founder of Scion Asset Management
items.occasion: X post addressed to Oracle, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia and others, as embedded by Benzinga
items.quote: It is consuming all your cash flow, you are borrowing, you are financing in ways you never have
items.summary: Burry asks the hyperscalers when spending on the AI data-center buildout actually ends, saying it consumes all their cash flow and forces borrowing and unfamiliar financing. He accuses them of accounting tricks that hide expense by stretching depreciation and says asset quality matters in the long run.
items.score_note: AI capex financing and accounting critique; no monetary-policy content.
items.ai_quote: It is consuming all your cash flow, you are borrowing, you are financing in ways you never have

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Feb 22 edition)
items.quote: this does not appear to be a systemic risk on par with what led to the Global Financial Crisis
items.summary: El-Erian notes core PCE came in hot at 3.0% and that the Fed minutes showed a widening range of views, with several participants wanting language that keeps rate hikes possible. On private credit he says investing has reached excessive levels and 'market-for-lemons' effects should be expected, but he does not see GFC-scale systemic risk.
items.score_note: Reports the two-sided tone of the Fed minutes without taking a rate view; main message is that private-credit stress is real but not systemic.
items.ai_quote: private credit investing has reached excessive levels in advanced economies

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Comments to journalists ahead of NABE address (Reuters via Kitco, published Feb 24)
items.quote: I'm a little concerned about front loading that too much if there's not yet evidence that inflation is headed back to 2%
items.summary: Goolsbee is optimistic several more cuts will be appropriate by end-2026 but says there is not yet evidence inflation is heading to 2 percent. He rejects cutting on the basis of expected productivity gains, saying the Greenspan analogy does not fit and policy could overheat the economy. He describes AI data-center demand overloading scarce labor in places like Cedar Rapids.
items.score_note: Easing baseline for year-end offset by an explicit warning against cutting now and against the productivity argument; torn between -1 and 0, chose 0.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: JPMorgan Chase 2026 Company Update (investor day), Q&A
items.quote: I think that the balance sheet of the Fed is too big.
items.summary: Dimon says the Fed's balance sheet is too big, that it has lost $1 trillion and took its eye off interest-rate exposure, and that it cannot shrink the balance sheet without changing LCR and liquidity rules; he expects Warsh's review to take about a year and not to be done too quickly. On credit he says today's competition resembles 2005 to 2007, with a rising tide lifting all boats and 'a couple of people doing some dumb things', and that the credit cycle will turn with surprises.
items.score_note: View is on the size of the Fed balance sheet and bank liquidity rules, not on the policy-rate path; left unscored.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: 42nd Annual NABE Economic Policy Conference, Washington: 'Labor Market Data: Signal or Noise?'
items.quote: As things stand today, I rate these two possible outcomes as close to a coin flip.
items.summary: After the strong January jobs report he says a March hold may be appropriate if February data confirm it, but if the good news is revised away a 25bp cut should be made in March; he rates the two outcomes a coin flip. Underlying inflation near 2 percent; the Supreme Court tariff ruling does not change his policy view. In Q&A (AP) he called solid growth with zero job growth something he had never seen.
items.score_note: Choice is only between holding and cutting, and he restates his January case for a cut; conditional rather than an outright call, so -1 not -2.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Virtual panel with Susan Collins, moderated by Neil Irwin, Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference (Boston Fed write-up, posted Feb 25)
items.quote: Until you actually bring the inflation rate down, you’re going to see individual companies feeling like they need to push further.
items.summary: Barkin says inflation is above target, consumers are pushing back on prices, and published inflation is a reference number in every pricing decision, so firms keep pushing until it comes down. He attributes the productivity pickup to automation investment and low turnover rather than AI. Reuters reports he called monetary policy well positioned for the risks.
items.score_note: Inflation concern without any stated lean on rates; Reuters has him calling policy well positioned.

items.speaker: Raphael Bostic
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (until 2026-02-28; non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters exit interview (Reuters story carried by Business Recorder)
items.quote: if we are having structural change, then we really need to lean into that truth,
items.summary: Bostic says AI may be raising structural unemployment, which the Fed cannot offset with lower rates; trying to do so risks both mandate measures moving the wrong way. Reuters presents this as his parting case that rates need not fall much further, if at all, and that the Fed should keep pressing on inflation about a point above target. He says last year's cuts were motivated by weakness in labor-market niches.
items.score_note: Argues against cutting to offset structural joblessness and for continued focus on inflation; no hike call.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Welcoming remarks, 2026 Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference, Boston (official PDF text)
items.quote: Governor Chris Waller serves on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
items.summary: Collins opens a Boston Fed conference on finance and payments technology and introduces Governor Waller. The remarks contain no statement on the policy rate or the outlook.
items.score_note: Official remarks with no monetary-policy content; listed for coverage.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Panel discussion (with Tom Barkin) at the Boston Fed Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: I think that it's quite likely that it'll be appropriate to hold in the current range for some time,
items.summary: Collins says policy is mildly restrictive or close to neutral and that holding the current range for some time is quite likely appropriate, with a patient, deliberate approach. To cut again she wants more confidence that disinflation resumes, which her default outlook places later this year. Barkin, on the same panel, called policy well positioned.
items.score_note: Extended hold with a conditional easing path later in the year; no lean for the near term.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: 42nd Annual NABE Economic Policy Conference, Washington: opening remarks for the 'AI and Productivity across the Economy' panel
items.quote: With investment contributing to strong aggregate demand, it is possible that the current neutral rate is higher than before the pandemic.
items.summary: Cook discussed AI and monetary policy in structural terms. An AI-driven rise in unemployment may not signal slack, so demand-side policy might not offset it without raising inflation pressure. Soaring AI investment in data centers and chips may mean the current neutral rate is higher than before the pandemic, though this could reverse later. She gave no near-term rate guidance.
items.score_note: Structural remarks with no near-term rate call. The higher-neutral-rate point leans hawkish, but torn between 0 and +1 so scored 0.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Remarks at the 42nd Annual NABE Economic Policy Conference, Washington DC (Chicago Fed posted text)
items.quote: Before we cut rates more to stimulate the economy, let’s be sure inflation is heading back to 2%.
items.summary: Goolsbee says progress on inflation stalled in 2025 at about 3 percent and that it is not obvious policy is even restrictive at that inflation rate. He remains optimistic there can be more rate cuts this year, but only after actual progress on inflation; front-loading too many cuts is not prudent. Services inflation running at 3.3 percent is hard to call transitory. He also argues AI data-center investment has been a smaller driver of GDP growth than portrayed.
items.score_note: Pushes back on near-term cuts and doubts policy is restrictive (+1), yet keeps a baseline of more cuts this year (-1); torn, chose 0.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: State of the Union address
items.quote: And low interest rates will solve the Biden created housing problem
items.summary: In the State of the Union, Trump said mortgage rates are the lowest in four years and falling fast and that low interest rates will solve the housing problem. No direct statement about the Fed or Powell was found in the transcript search.
items.score_note: Mentions low rates as a housing fix but makes no statement about what the Fed should do; scored null.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston 2026 Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference (via webcast): 'Operationalizing AI at the Federal Reserve'
items.quote: AI is one clear example of how the Federal Reserve can execute boldly, at scale, when we take a System-first approach.
items.summary: Speech on how the Federal Reserve System deploys AI tools internally. No statement on the rate path in the prepared text.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content in the prepared text.

items.speaker: Raphael Bostic
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (until 2026-02-28; non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Farewell essay 'Farewell to the Best Job I've Ever Had' (Atlanta Fed, message from the president)
items.quote: Safeguarding our special status includes protecting the Fed's independence.
items.summary: In his final essay Bostic reviews his tenure and warns that legal and rhetorical battles around the Fed are making people doubt its independence. He says outcomes are better with an independent central bank: lower inflation and more robust performance. No statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: Independence and farewell message; no rate-path content. Listed because it is the bank's official essay series and was wire-reported.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Moderated Q&A "Role of the Federal Reserve in the St. Louis Region", Missouri Athletic Club Speaker Series, St. Louis (video only on stlouisfed.org; quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: these two risks in my assessment are roughly balanced right now
items.summary: Musalem said the current policy rate appropriately balances risks. His baseline has inflation heading back toward 2% later in the year and the labor market stabilizing; more layoffs with low job creation could worsen the labor market (not his base case), and inflation could stay higher for longer.
items.score_note: Hold with explicitly balanced two-sided risks.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Appearance before the Economic Club of Colorado (Reuters reprint)
items.quote: I think we have work to do on the inflation side of things
items.summary: Schmid said the Fed has work to do on inflation while employment is in a pretty good place; Reuters noted he did not say how policy should respond. On the balance sheet he said the debate is about the right level of reserves, that the Fed's MBS holdings keep mortgage rates probably 75 to 100 basis points lower than otherwise, and (per a later Reuters story) that the long duration of the portfolio creates a distortion.
items.score_note: Inflation named as the unfinished side of the mandate with employment fine; no explicit rate call, so a mild +1.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Testimony on Supervision and Regulation, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (prepared text)
items.quote: Therefore, I support efforts by Congress to reduce burden on community banks.
items.summary: Prepared testimony covers bank conditions, capital, supervision and community-bank relief. No statement on the rate path in the prepared text; the hearing Q&A was not reviewed.
items.score_note: Regulation only in the prepared text.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Fox News 'America Reports' interview (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: I have some confidence rates can come down several more times this year in 2026,
items.summary: Goolsbee says his forecast of several cuts later this year makes him one of the more optimistic policymakers, but he does not want to front-load cuts before there is evidence inflation is heading back to 2 percent.
items.score_note: Forecasts several cuts in 2026 but not soon; conditional on inflation evidence. Torn between -1 and 0.

items.speaker: Howard Marks
items.occasion: Oaktree memo 'AI Hurtles Ahead'
items.quote: no one should go all-in without acknowledging that they face the risk of ruin if things go badly
items.summary: Follow-up to his December 'Is It a Bubble?' memo. Marks says AI is real and its potential more likely underestimated, but infrastructure booms always cause capital to be malinvested, some AI revenue is circular, and none of that says AI assets are fairly priced. He advises a moderate, selective position. No comment on Fed policy.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content; AI-investment bubble discussion only. credit_view bubble_warning is a mild one (he advises neither all-in nor all-out).
items.ai_quote: Claude’s answer doesn’t necessarily preclude the possibility that demand growth could slow or infrastructure building could run ahead of it.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria'
items.quote: I definitely think the labor market can be supported by the Federal Reserve further
items.summary: Miran said strong January job growth was a really good thing but it is way too early to sound an all clear on the labor market, and that the Fed should still cut a full percentage point this year through four quarter-point moves because inflation is no longer a problem.
items.score_note: Explicit call for four cuts this year.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Project Syndicate op-ed 'What Will the Fed’s “Warsh Era” Bring?'
items.quote: To focus solely on rate cuts is to misunderstand the Fed’s situation and the scale of the challenge awaiting its next leader.
items.summary: El-Erian argues that speculation about how hard Warsh will push for rate cuts misses the point. He says the next chair inherits a Fed that is fractured internally and lacks credibility externally, and that Warsh should strengthen its analytical framework and establish a balance-sheet theory.
items.score_note: Explicitly sets the rate question aside in favor of institutional and balance-sheet reform.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on the drivers of market risk aversion
items.quote: Additional red flags in the private credit markets in advanced countries, including news about loose underwriting standards, write-downs, and fraud.
items.summary: El-Erian lists reasons for the risk aversion that pushed stocks down and the 10-year Treasury yield below 4%: geopolitical tensions, unemployment worries after Block said it would cut 40% of its workforce, and more red flags in private credit such as loose underwriting, write-downs and fraud.
items.score_note: Market and credit commentary; no view on the Fed rate path.
items.ai_quote: Additional red flags in the private credit markets in advanced countries, including news about loose underwriting standards, write-downs, and fraud.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Speech on energy, Corpus Christi, Texas
items.quote: He's too late in reducing mortgage interest rates or interest rates.
items.summary: Trump called Powell 'a lousy guy in the fed', 'too late' in reducing interest rates, and said he will fortunately be 'out of there soon'.
items.score_note: 'Too late' criticism implying rates should have been cut; no explicit new demand.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Mar 1 edition, after the US-Israel strikes on Iran)
items.quote: Also, as energy costs rise and growth faces more headwinds, the path for central banks becomes even trickier.
items.summary: Writing after the weekend US-Israel military action against Iran, El-Erian says the cumulative disruptions raise the prospect of a fresh bout of stagflation in a so-far resilient global economy. He says higher energy costs and weaker growth make the central-bank path trickier.
items.score_note: Stagflation framing with two-sided risks for central banks; no directional call.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at JPMorgan's leveraged finance conference, Miami Beach
items.quote: It’s been coming down, but it seems to maybe have leveled off around 3%.
items.summary: Two days after the US and Israel struck Iran, Dimon called inflation the skunk at the party and said it seems to have leveled off around 3%. He said the conflict would add only a teeny bit to inflation and would not be a major inflationary hit unless prolonged. He also said asset prices are high and there is more exuberance than there should be.
items.score_note: No explicit Fed call. Inflation is his main risk (stuck near 3%) but he played down the Iran shock unless prolonged; torn between 0 and +1, chose the level nearer 0.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks 'A Reset on Liquidity Regulation' (prepared by Bessent, delivered by Under Secretary McKernan)
items.quote: After March 2023, almost everyone now agrees that operational readiness and discount window stigma need a better solution.
items.summary: Prepared by Bessent and delivered by Under Secretary Jonathan McKernan. Argues bank liquidity rules force excessive self-insurance, entrench discount-window stigma and reduce lending, and calls for counting lender-of-last-resort capacity. No policy-rate content.
items.score_note: Bank liquidity regulation and discount window design; no policy-rate content. AI tag because the text links liquidity rules to less bank lending for AI hyperscalers.
items.ai_quote: that necessarily means less lending for mortgages, small businesses, AI hyperscalers, and critical infrastructure.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Roundtable on Liquidity and Lender of Last Resort, Committee on Capital Markets Regulation, Washington: 'Liquidity Resiliency, Financial Stability, and the Role of the Federal Reserve'
items.quote: Some see tension between monetary policy implementation tools and regulatory objectives.
items.summary: Discount window stigma and modernization and liquidity regulation. Touches the interaction of implementation tools with liquidity rules but says nothing on the rate path.
items.score_note: Liquidity regulation and discount window design only.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Australian Financial Review Business Summit, Sydney (Tuesday March 3 local time)
items.quote: I think the market reaction has been more benign, given the magnitude of this, than you might think.
items.summary: Days into the Iran war Solomon said he was surprised by how benign the market reaction had been and that markets would need a couple of weeks to digest it. He said the things to watch are whether it becomes prolonged, filters into energy supply chains and affects consumer sentiment. Bloomberg reported he also said he is watching private credit portfolios for frothiness (not verified, paywalled).
items.score_note: Energy-shock and market commentary only; no statement on what the Fed should or will do.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Bloomberg Invest conference, 'Monetary Policy First-Hand' conversation with Michael McKee, New York (Reuters report)
items.quote: I felt like policy was in a pretty good place and we have the luxury of just letting it gradually glide back to neutral
items.summary: Days after the US-Israel attack on Iran, Kashkari says he had a lot of confidence in the outlook until then: he came into 2026 expecting easing inflation to allow a single rate cut. Now the Fed needs to see how long and how big the new shock is, and whether it looks like Russia-Ukraine or like the Hamas attack. He warns that headline inflation staying elevated after five years of high inflation is a scenario to watch closely for expectations.
items.score_note: His prior of one cut (-1 flavour) is now suspended by the oil shock and an explicit inflation-expectations worry (+1 flavour); net wait-and-see. Time from the Minneapolis Fed event page.

items.speaker: Marc Rowan
items.occasion: Interview at Bloomberg Invest, New York, as reported by Investing.com
items.quote: This will be a shakeout — I don't think it is going to be short term
items.summary: Rowan warns that a shakeout is coming for private-credit firms amid concerns about defaults on loans to software companies and redemptions at business development companies. He calls it foreseeable and says all a manager can do is to have been a good underwriter and risk manager.
items.score_note: Private-credit stress view only; nothing on the rate path.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: All-In Podcast interview with David Friedberg (published Mar 3; transcript copy)
items.quote: But you can’t make interest rates severely artificially low because one man’s debts are another man’s assets.
items.summary: Dalio says the Fed faces a hard balancing act: rates too low hurt creditors and fuel a bubble, rates too high squeeze debtors, and a K-shaped economy makes one rate fit badly. He thinks re-expansion of the Fed balance sheet is likely down the road, calls Warsh a practical man with a tough job, and says AI is eating everything and might eat itself by not producing adequate profits.
items.score_note: On rates he argues for balance (not artificially low, not too high) = 0; separately he forecasts Fed Treasury buying is 'likely down the road', which leans -1 on the balance sheet.
items.ai_quote: Right now it looks to me like AI basically is eating everything and it might eat itself.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy", Metro Denver Executive Club, Denver, Colo.
items.quote: Overall, with inflation still running hot, it appears that demand is outpacing supply across much of the economy.
items.summary: Schmid said the labor market looks in balance while inflation remains closer to 3% than 2% and the Fed cannot be complacent after nearly five years above target. He argued that demand-led growth, including aging-related health care spending, is not disinflationary and that AI-led supply gains are not here yet.
items.score_note: Inflation is the dominant concern and the framing argues against easing, but the text gives no explicit rate-path statement; +1 is the mild hawkish lean.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at America's Credit Unions Governmental Affairs Conference, Washington DC, 'Two Sides of a Coin'
items.quote: further reductions in the federal funds rate will eventually be warranted to prevent monetary policy from inadvertently becoming more restrictive
items.summary: Williams said policy is well positioned, tariff effects on prices look one-off with no second-round effects, and inflation should fall to about 2-1/2 percent in 2026 and 2 percent in 2027. If inflation follows that path, further rate reductions will eventually be warranted so that policy does not passively tighten. He expects GDP growth of about 2-1/2 percent and unemployment edging down. The prepared text did not mention the Iran war; in comments the same day reported by MNI he said it was early days, that higher energy prices affect the near-term inflation outlook, and that the shock can hit both mandate goals in opposing ways.
items.score_note: No urgency (policy 'well positioned' now), but he explicitly states an easing bias: further cuts eventually warranted if inflation falls as he expects.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: New York Times interview (published March 4; quotes as relayed by Reuters)
items.quote: It’s important to make sure that we’re maintaining policy at a level where we can drive inflation back down to target while balancing any potential softness in the labor market
items.summary: Hammack said it is too early to gauge the economic impact of the Iran war and backed holding rates steady for quite some time. With inflation too high and the labor market relatively steady, the Fed should stay focused on price pressures. She laid out both directions: more accommodation if the labor market weakens further, more restriction if inflation does not move toward target as she expects.
items.score_note: Extended hold with both a cut and a hike scenario spelled out; emphasis on inflation but no lean on the next move.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, Bloomberg Television
items.quote: I believe it's appropriate to continue acting
items.summary: Miran said it is still appropriate to keep cutting rates and that the Middle East conflict has not changed his forecasts for the labor market or inflation. Reuters' account of the same interview adds that he sees limited evidence that oil feeds into core inflation and wants four quarter-point cuts this year to reach roughly neutral.
items.score_note: Explicit call to keep cutting despite the oil shock.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: That certainly puts pause to any conclusion that we're done fighting this,
items.summary: Barkin says last year's cuts rested on labor-market risks rising and inflation risks falling, and that data over the past couple of months suggest the balance has moved in the other direction. A couple of months of relatively high PCE inflation argue against concluding the inflation fight is over.
items.score_note: Says the risk balance has shifted toward inflation and away from the labor market, undercutting further cuts; no hike talk.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Remarks accepting the Foreign Policy Association Medal, FPA Financial Services Dinner, New York (edited transcript on Chicago Fed site)
items.quote: The world has learned the hard way over the last 113 years how important central bank independence is for keeping inflation under control.
items.summary: Goolsbee defends the regional Reserve Bank structure and central bank independence, noting Reserve Bank presidents are not political appointees. There is no statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: Official remarks on independence and the Fed's structure; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Fox Business interview on the day of the February jobs report (payrolls -92,000)
items.quote: This confirms to me that the labor market continues to be weak, and it could use some support from our policy rate.
items.summary: Says she was fine with the January hold, but the weak February jobs report suggests January strength may have been an anomaly and the labor market could use support from the policy rate. Bloomberg headlined it 'Labor Market May Need More Support'. Last remarks before the March blackout. The source page is dated March 7 and relays Bloomberg's report of the March 6 interview.
items.score_note: Clear easing lean on labor weakness; only one secondary page with the quote was readable (Bloomberg original is paywalled), so I kept -1 rather than -2.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech 'Observations on the Economic Outlook, and Small Business', Springfield Regional Chamber Outlook 2026 (official PDF text)
items.quote: in my view argues for maintaining policy rates at their current, mildly restrictive levels for some time
items.summary: Collins sees a patient, deliberate approach as appropriate. Her baseline has a still-uncertain inflation picture with continued upside risks and a relatively stable labor market, which argues for holding rates at mildly restrictive levels for some time. Policy is well positioned to adjust as conditions evolve.
items.score_note: Extended hold; upside inflation risks mentioned but stance described as patient and adjustable; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Panel discussion presentation on the value of private-sector data (official transcript)
items.quote: And this just reminds us that monetary policy is a contextual decision that takes a lot of evidence, a lot of science, a lot of practice, but also some judgment
items.summary: Daly discussed how the FOMC has used private-sector data (ADP, Zillow rents, PriceStats) alongside official statistics, with examples from the 1990s, 2020 and 2025. No statement on the current rate path.
items.score_note: Official panel remarks about data sources; no usable stance on the rate path.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' interview with Steve Liesman after the February jobs report (quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: But we also have inflation printing above target and oil prices rising.
items.summary: After a weak February jobs report, Daly said hopes that the labor market was steadying may have been too much, but inflation is above target and oil prices are rising, so both goals are at risk and the Fed must keep its eye on both.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided: labor weaker, inflation and oil higher; no stated lean on rates.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview after the February jobs report (Reuters via SRN News)
items.quote: As we get more uncertainties, I kind of think that time at which it makes sense to act keeps getting pushed back.
items.summary: On the day of a weak February jobs report, Goolsbee says he still hopes and expects inflation progress will let the Fed resume moving rates down toward a settling point below the current level by the end of the year, but mounting uncertainties keep pushing back the time to act. Chicago Fed's media list shows he also spoke to the NYT and WSJ that day about stagflation risks.
items.score_note: Keeps an eventual easing path but pushes its timing back; balanced on the day.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Panel remarks at the 2026 US Monetary Policy Forum (Chicago Booth, New York), 'On the Safe-Haven Status of the Dollar'
items.quote: Under my base case, I think policy should be on hold for quite some time as we see evidence that inflation is coming down and the labor market stabilizes further.
items.summary: In remarks mostly about the dollar's reserve role, Hammack said policy is in a good position with the funds rate around neutral. Her base case is an extended hold while inflation comes down and the labor market stabilizes, and she sees two-sided risks to rates. She also flagged the unsustainable path of US fiscal debt as a risk to demand for dollar assets and stressed Fed independence.
items.score_note: Extended hold with two-sided risks to rates; no lean.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Reuters interview (New York, same day as her US Monetary Policy Forum remarks)
items.quote: that might be a reason why we might need to be more restrictive from policy perspective
items.summary: On the day February payrolls fell by 92,000 and markets added to rate-cut bets, Hammack said rates should be on hold for quite some time and that she still expects decent progress on inflation this year. If inflation is not making progress in the second half, the Fed might need to be more restrictive. She said it is too early to judge the oil shock, which depends on its magnitude and persistence, and that the jobs data show signs of stabilizing.
items.score_note: Base case is hold, but the only conditional she raised was tightening and she played down the weak jobs report; open to hiking. Her same-day prepared remarks (scored 0) cite two-sided risks, so this is a mild +1.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, CNBC 'Money Movers', after the February jobs report
items.quote: I think that the labor market can use more accommodation from monetary policy.
items.summary: After payrolls fell by 92,000 in February, Miran said the Fed does not have an inflation problem, that a modestly restrictive stance is not appropriate and policy should be close to neutral, and that higher oil prices are a one-off shock to headline inflation. Asked whether he would dissent again he said he hoped the Committee would vote to cut.
items.score_note: Explicitly wants a cut at the next meeting.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Discussant remarks at the 2026 US Monetary Policy Forum on 'Private Canaries: The Value of Private-Sector Data for U.S. Monetary Policy Making'
items.quote: Private data and public data are complements.
items.summary: Paulson discussed how the FOMC assembles a picture of the economy from public and private data and how data use may explain gaps between policymaker and market rate expectations. She suggested communication could be improved by being systematic about which data matter and why. She gave no view on the current stance or rate path.
items.score_note: Discussion of data and communication; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note on Wednesday Mar 11, reported by Reuters (copy published Mar 12 HKT)
items.quote: By September, we expect both some further labour market softening and progress on underlying inflation to contribute to the case for a cut,
items.summary: Goldman pushed its two 2026 cuts to September and December from June and September, citing inflation risks from the Middle East conflict; it said earlier cuts remain possible if the labor market weakens sooner, and that oil-driven inflation worries would not stop the Fed easing in that case.
items.score_note: Still two cuts in 2026 but delayed by a quarter; explicitly keeps the door open to earlier cuts. (Page is a Hong Kong reprint of Reuters with British spelling.)
items.call: 2026: two cuts, September and December (previously June and September)

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Cato Institute Policy Forum on Basel III and Bank Capital Rules, Washington: 'Capital Rules for the Real Economy'
items.quote: Changes to the G-SIB surcharge based on underlying risk are appropriate but increases driven mainly by real economic growth and inflation do not reflect increases in systemic risk.
items.summary: Bank capital proposals (Basel III endgame, G-SIB surcharge, stress capital). No monetary-policy content. Delivered during the pre-FOMC blackout.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Jeremy Schwartz
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Mar 12)
items.quote: He can probably get one or two cuts this year.
items.summary: Schwartz said forecasts must factor in what Warsh has told the president he will try to do, but it depends on committee dynamics and data; Warsh can probably get one or two cuts in 2026.
items.score_note: Still expects one or two cuts in 2026 despite war-driven inflation risk.
items.call: 2026: one or two cuts under Warsh

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on a Bloomberg headline about private-credit funds capping withdrawals
items.quote: It’s a classic contagion phenomenon: "If you can’t sell what you want, you sell what you can."
items.summary: Reacting to a Bloomberg headline on private credit (Business Insider identifies it as Morgan Stanley and Cliffwater capping fund withdrawals), El-Erian warns of an 'ATM' scenario in which investors liquidate healthy funds because they are the available source of cash. He says the line between liquidity and solvency can blur under extreme conditions, adding 'we are not at that point' but it is worth watching.
items.score_note: Contagion warning on private-credit liquidity; no rate-path view.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post demanding an inter-meeting cut
items.quote: He should be dropping Interest Rates, IMMEDIATELY, not waiting for the next meeting!
items.summary: Trump asked where Powell was and said he should cut rates immediately rather than wait for the March 17-18 meeting.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for an immediate, inter-meeting cut.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: BlackRock 2026 Infrastructure Summit, panel discussion (held the week of the article)
items.quote: They may in the short run overinvest, but the long-term demand will catch up,
items.summary: Fink said one or two bankruptcies among AI players are inevitable and that this is capitalism. He wants more, not less, AI infrastructure investment and said hyperscalers may overinvest in the short run but demand will catch up. He was not worried about their debt-funded spending, noting their return on equity is still better than BlackRock's.
items.score_note: AI capex and hyperscaler financing only; no rate-path content.
items.ai_quote: Their return on equity is still better than mine and I have a pretty good return on equity,

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Fortune commentary by Dalio on the Big Cycle
items.quote: What is now happening in the markets and with the monetary system is consistent with that template.
items.summary: Dalio writes that in past pre-war periods creditors feared the reserve-currency debtor would devalue or default, so they and central banks moved from bonds to gold. He says current markets and the monetary system fit that template and he is not optimistic.
items.score_note: No policy-rate view; debasement and bond-demand theme.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Mar 15 edition, ahead of the March FOMC)
items.quote: Some of these have been evident for some time, such as persistent inflation in the US and private credit excesses in advanced economies.
items.summary: El-Erian says core PCE stayed sticky at 3.1%, the sixth straight year above target, and that the more the war escalates the greater the risk of broader inflation, lower growth, higher unemployment and systemic financial instability. He notes markets quickly priced 2026 rate hikes for the single-mandate ECB and Bank of England, and that JPMorgan led banks in lowering facilities for some private-credit funds.
items.score_note: Flags persistent US inflation and private-credit excesses, but gives no explicit view of what the Fed will or should do at the coming meeting.
items.ai_quote: Some of these have been evident for some time, such as persistent inflation in the US and private credit excesses in advanced economies.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post attacking Judge Boasberg over the Powell investigation
items.quote: What Boasberg has done on the “Too Late” Powell case, and many others, has little to do with the Law, and everything to do with Politics.
items.summary: Trump attacked Judge James Boasberg for blocking the investigation of Powell and the Fed building renovation, calling Powell an 'absolutely terrible' Fed Chairman guilty of 'gross incompetence, total dishonesty, or both'. No rate-path content.
items.score_note: About the Powell investigation and renovation costs; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Deutsche Bank research (morning note citing its economists; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Deutsche Bank note ahead of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted by FXStreet Insights Team (Mar 16, 07:38 GMT)
items.quote: Starting with the Fed, our economists expect them to keep rates unchanged this week and think they’ll emphasise elevated geopolitical uncertainty.
items.summary: Deutsche Bank economists expected a hold in March with emphasis on geopolitical uncertainty and oil-driven inflation risk, and a dot plot still signalling one 2026 cut, though it would not take much to shift the median dot.
items.score_note: Hold call with inflation risk emphasized; no change to the rate path stated. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.call: hold in March; dot plot still expected to show one 2026 cut

items.speaker: Matthew Luzzetti
items.role: Chief U.S. economist, Deutsche Bank Securities
items.occasion: Research note written the week of Mar 9, quoted by Reuters Mar 16
items.quote: A question that was almost unthinkable two weeks ago is now being more heavily debated: Could the Fed raise rates in 2026?
items.summary: Luzzetti raised the question of a 2026 rate hike after the oil shock; per Reuters he concluded that increases were still unlikely absent a clear jump in inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Raises hike risk but concludes hikes unlikely; between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.call: 2026 hikes debated but still unlikely absent a clear jump in inflation expectations

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks to reporters at a Kennedy Center board lunch (day before March FOMC)
items.quote: He should cut them right now.
items.summary: Trump said Powell is always too late and should cut interest rates right now, that the Fed should hold a special meeting, and that 'a third-grade student would know' it is the time to cut. He also attacked the Fed building renovation.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for an immediate cut and a special meeting.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Interview with Business Insider on recession odds
items.quote: Phase one is higher inflation that eats away at people's purchasing power, that increases costs for businesses.
items.summary: El-Erian raises his US recession odds from about 25% to 35% because of the oil shock from the Iran war. He describes a two-phase bear case of higher inflation followed by lower growth and higher unemployment, and warns that hotter inflation could interact with fragilities such as private-credit redemptions and trigger a financial accident that tightens credit.
items.score_note: Stagflation and financial-accident risk; he does not say what the Fed will or should do.

items.speaker: BofA economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: We don't think the Fed needs to cut any further, but the majority of the committee is still holding on to a low neutral rate
items.summary: BofA said it does not think the Fed needs to cut further, but the committee majority holds a low neutral-rate view, which opens the door to more cuts on any blip in the data, especially with Warsh advocating cuts; its forecast was 25bp cuts in June and July.
items.score_note: Forecast basis: two cuts in June and July, even though BofA itself sees no need for them.
items.call: 2026: 25bp cuts in June and July (hold in March)

items.speaker: Citi economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: We see risks tilted dovish at the FOMC meeting.
items.summary: Citi expected Fed officials to treat the oil jump as a temporary supply shock they can look through, with near-zero job growth and slower spending raising concern about employment; it expected an 8-2 hold and 25bp cuts to follow in April, July and September.
items.score_note: Three cuts still forecast, the first at the next meeting after March; most dovish house. Between -2 and -1, chose -1 because the March decision itself was a hold call.
items.call: 2026: 25bp cuts in April, July and September (hold in March)

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: For the Fed, the war increases both the risk that earlier rate cuts will be needed to address labour market
items.summary: Goldman expected a 7-3 hold with the statement acknowledging war-related uncertainty, and said the war raises both the risk of earlier cuts to address labor softening and the risk that higher inflation delays cuts; its path was 25bp cuts in September and December.
items.score_note: Two cuts later in 2026 with two-sided risk around timing.
items.call: 2026: 25bp cuts in September and December

items.speaker: J.P. Morgan economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: We look for the median dot to continue to look for one cut this year, though
items.summary: J.P. Morgan expected the median dot to keep one 2026 cut, with a little under even odds that it moves to no cut, and said any endorsement of looking through energy inflation would be conditional on stable inflation expectations; its own forecast is no rate change through 2026.
