items.score_note: This page states only no change through 2026. The +1 keeps the firm consistent with its own published call (jpmorgan.com versions dated Feb 20 and Apr 17 both give the next move as a Q3 2027 hike); on this page alone it would be 0.
items.call: no rate changes through the whole of 2026

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Dissent at the March 17-18 FOMC meeting (preferred a 25 bp cut; sole dissenter)
items.quote: Voting against this action was Stephen I. Miran, who preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.
items.summary: The FOMC held at 3.50-3.75%. Miran was the only dissenter and preferred a 25 bp cut. The quote is the Committee statement's wording, not Miran's own words.
items.score_note: Formal dissent in favor of an immediate cut.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, March 17-18 meeting: opening statement
items.quote: In the near term, higher energy prices will push up overall inflation, but it is too soon to know the scope and duration of the potential effects on the economy.
items.summary: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% (Miran dissented for a 25 bp cut). Powell said the current stance is appropriate, the implications of the Middle East conflict are uncertain, and near-term inflation expectations have risen with oil. The SEP median funds rate was unchanged from December at 3.4% for end-2026 and 3.1% for end-2027; median 2026 PCE inflation 2.7% and GDP growth 2.4%.
items.score_note: Hold, attentive to both sides, median still shows one cut in 2026; no lean expressed.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, March 17-18 meeting: Q&A on the next move (hike discussed, cuts conditional)
items.quote: The vast majority of participants don’t see that as their base case, and, of course, we don’t take things off the table.
items.summary: Powell confirmed that the possibility that the next move is an increase came up at the meeting, as in January, but said the vast majority do not see it as the base case. He said four or five participants moved from two cuts to one, that the rate forecast is conditional on tariff disinflation showing up mid-year (no progress, no cut), and that policy sits on the borderline between restrictive and not, which he called the right place. He added that the AI data-center buildout is probably pushing inflation up at the margin and raising the neutral rate in the near term.
items.score_note: Explicitly balances downside labor risk against upside inflation risk and says neither clearly dominates; hike talk acknowledged but not endorsed. Torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, March 17-18 meeting: Q&A on looking through the oil shock
items.quote: we are very strongly committed to doing what it takes to keep inflation expectations anchored at 2 percent
items.summary: Powell said the standard practice of looking through energy shocks depends on anchored expectations and, now, on the context of five years of above-target inflation, so it would not be approached lightly; the question does not arise until tariff disinflation is visible. He said repeated shocks (pandemic, tariffs, energy) are the kind of thing that can cause trouble for expectations. He declined to say what oil price would prompt a hike, and said the net effect of the oil shock is downward pressure on spending and employment and upward pressure on inflation.
items.score_note: Vigilant on expectations but no commitment to tighten and he notes the growth hit too; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, March 17-18 meeting: Q&A on his own future and the DOJ investigation
items.quote: I have no intention of leaving the Board until the investigation is well and truly over, with transparency and finality
items.summary: Powell said that if his successor is not confirmed by the end of his term as Chair he would serve as Chair pro tem, that he will not leave the Board while the investigation is ongoing, and that he has not decided whether to stay on as a Governor afterwards. He said independence is what allows the Fed to do what is needed for price stability.
items.score_note: Personnel and independence; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post on the morning of the March FOMC decision
items.quote: When is “Too Late” Powell lowering INTEREST RATES?
items.summary: One-line post on FOMC decision day asking when Powell will lower interest rates.
items.score_note: Explicit pressure for a rate cut on decision day.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Fox Business Network interview (day after March FOMC)
items.quote: The meetings are going very well.
items.summary: Bessent declined to comment on whether the DOJ investigation of Powell would be dropped, said Warsh's meetings with senators are going very well and there will be a hearing, and that only the vote would be held up.
items.score_note: Confirmation process only; no rate-path content in the Reuters report.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Interview with Business Insider on how a private-credit crisis could unfold
items.quote: It starts with one fund, Blue Owl, and the next thing we know, other funds start putting up gates.
items.summary: El-Erian lays out a chain of events in which liquidity fears in private credit snowball, banks pull back on lending and a credit crunch causes a demand shock. He says it is very important to interrupt the process before it gathers steam.
items.score_note: Calls for the contagion process to be interrupted but does not specify a Fed rate action.

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley strategists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note the morning after the March 18 FOMC, reported by Reuters
items.quote: The primary risk to our view remains that rate cuts come later or not at all,
items.summary: Morgan Stanley pushed its next cut to September from June and now expects quarter-point cuts in September and December 2026, joining Goldman Sachs and Barclays. It flags the risk that cuts come later or not at all, while a second-round oil surge could weaken activity and prompt cuts.
items.score_note: Still two cuts in 2026 but delayed three months, with risk skewed to later/none.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, September and December (previously June and September)

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding and Graeme Westwood
items.role: Economist, PIMCO (Wilding); co-author Westwood (title not on page)
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts note after the March FOMC: Caution Takes Center Stage at the March Fed Meeting
items.quote: we still expect to see the Fed remain on hold through most of 2026, before resuming their easing cycle toward a neutral rate just above 3%
items.summary: PIMCO said the Fed signaled continued patience on the timing of cuts; it still expects a hold through most of 2026 before easing resumes toward a neutral rate just above 3%, and sees labor market vulnerabilities as the more material risk.
items.score_note: Easing still expected to resume late in 2026; labor risk emphasized over inflation.
items.call: on hold through most of 2026, then easing resumes toward neutral just above 3%

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Oval Office remarks with Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi (day after March FOMC hold)
items.quote: Today, certainly you should be lowering interest rates.
items.summary: Trump called Powell grossly incompetent and stubborn, said he has 'Trump Derangement Syndrome', and said that today the Fed certainly should be lowering interest rates.
items.score_note: Explicit statement that the Fed should be cutting now, the day after it held.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria' interview, two days after the March FOMC
items.quote: I've written three cuts in for before the end of 2026 to hopefully support the labor market.
items.summary: Still concerned about the job market and has three cuts in her 2026 projection, against a Committee median of one. Says it is too early to tell what longer-term imprint the Iran war will leave on activity and on rate decisions; expects strong growth supported by supply-side policies.
items.score_note: Projects three cuts this year to support jobs but had just voted to hold and names no timing; torn between -1 and -2, chose -1.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs 2025 annual report, letter to shareholders
items.quote: fiscal stimulus in developed economies, monetary easing, AI capital investment, and a more balanced regulatory regime in the US
items.summary: Solomon wrote that, although the economic effects of the US-Israel military action against Iran are hard to predict, he still sees potential for a constructive environment built on fiscal stimulus, monetary easing, AI capital investment and lighter regulation. He warned that recent concerns about private credit, including underwriting quality and exposure to software companies hurt by AI, are a reminder that the credit cycle has not been repealed, and that greater capital deployment into AI requires diligent risk management.
items.score_note: Lists monetary easing as a tailwind but gives no forecast of further cuts and flags the Iran war as a wildcard; torn between -1 and 0, chose the level nearer 0.
items.ai_quote: the credit cycle has not been repealed

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' interview, two days after the March FOMC
items.quote: if things go reasonably well and the labor market continues to be weak, I would start advocating again for cutting the policy rate later this year
items.summary: Says caution is warranted after the Iran war and oil spike and that he voted to hold in March, but this does not mean staying put all year. Would resume advocating cuts later in 2026 if the labor market stays weak; also wants to see whether tariff effects roll off and what happens to inflation. Reuters reports he said he had planned to dissent for a cut after the February payroll loss until the Strait of Hormuz closure raised inflation risk.
items.score_note: Holds for now but the only direction he discusses is resuming cuts; torn between 0 and -1, kept -1 because the stated lean is explicitly toward easing later this year.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: Acceptance remarks, Paul A. Volcker Public Integrity Award, American Society for Public Administration (pre-recorded video)
items.quote: we need independence to do what is right, and we need integrity to use that independence wisely
items.summary: Short award remarks praising Volcker for holding firm against political pressure to bring inflation down in the early 1980s. No comment on current policy.
items.score_note: Official speech with no current monetary-policy content; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Mar 22 edition, after the March FOMC)
items.quote: Yield curves bear-flattened as traders pushed Federal Reserve rate-cut expectations into 2027, while simultaneously pricing in 2026 rate hikes for both the BoE and ECB.
items.summary: El-Erian says energy prices rose for a fourth week, pushing borrowing costs up and reigniting inflation fears. He calls the March Fed statement and forecasts 'meh', overshadowed by Powell saying he will not leave the Board until the DOJ investigation is over, and flags supply-chain and financial contagion as themes to watch.
items.score_note: Reports market repricing (Fed cuts pushed into 2027) rather than giving his own rate call.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: LinkedIn post (Reuters reprint; the LinkedIn original was not opened)
items.quote: in a good place, we need to remain flexible
items.summary: Daly wrote that unless the Iran conflict resolves quickly and the Fed can look through a temporary oil price rise, there is "no single most-likely path" for rates: a protracted conflict raises the risk of both higher inflation and a weaker labor market. Full sentence in the reprint: "With policy in a good place, we need to remain flexible, able to respond to rapidly evolving risks."
items.score_note: No directional lean; two-sided risks and flexibility. The quote is a fragment because the reprint embeds invisible characters elsewhere in the sentence.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview with Steve Liesman (CNBC article)
items.quote: I remain fairly optimistic that by the end of '26 rates could go down, but I wanted to see proof that we're back on an inflation headed to 2%.
items.summary: Goolsbee says he is more worried about inflation than unemployment and warns against repeating the 'team transitory' mistake. He agreed with the January and March holds. He is still fairly optimistic rates could fall by end-2026 but says the war throws a wrench into the plans and progress on inflation is needed. Reuters quotes him saying inflation has to be a little ahead of employment as a priority; Bloomberg's headline says he could see circumstances for a hike.
items.score_note: Inflation named as the greater risk (+1) while he keeps an end-2026 easing hope (-1); torn, chose 0.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: CNBC Closing Bell interview
items.quote: A little bit like 2006, where everything is overvalued, cracks are starting to form.
items.summary: Gundlach compared the environment to 2006, with overvalued assets and cracks being dismissed as contained. He said private credit funds were deluged with redemption requests above the 5% gates and that retail investors will ask for much more at the next liquidity window. DoubleLine's recap adds that he challenged the narrative of imminent rate cuts.
items.score_note: The CNBC article quotes only his credit remarks; the rate view comes from DoubleLine's own recap of this interview (titled 'The Case for Rate Cuts Is Falling Apart', https://doubleline.com/markets-insights/jeffrey-gundlach-the-case-for-rate-cuts-is-falling-apart-cnbc/), a paraphrase: he challenges imminent-cut expectations citing persistent inflation and a two-year yield above fed funds. No hike call there, so +1.
items.ai_quote: We all know that the private credit industry was deluged with redemption requests

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: 2026 annual chairman's letter to investors
items.quote: And when the Magnificent 7 companies build out data centers or power infrastructure, even they turn to the capital markets.
items.summary: Fink's letter argues that capital markets, not banks or governments carrying record debt, now fund growth, including the data-center and power build-out of the largest technology companies, and that more people should own a share of that growth. It promotes infrastructure and private credit as growth areas for BlackRock. It says nothing about the Fed or the rate path.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content. The letter page carries no date; March 23, 2026 is taken from the Reuters report of its release (finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/blackrock-ceo-fink-backs-staying-115903674.html).
items.ai_quote: And when the Magnificent 7 companies build out data centers or power infrastructure, even they turn to the capital markets.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, Bloomberg Television
items.quote: We should wait for all the information to come in before really changing our outlook
items.summary: Miran said it is premature to judge how the jump in oil prices will look twelve months out, that an oil shock is traditionally looked through so his outlook for gradual rate cuts is unchanged, and that both inflation and unemployment risks have become more concerning because the oil shock is also a negative demand shock. He confirmed he trimmed his 2026 projection from six cuts to four at the March meeting.
items.score_note: Keeps his call for gradual cuts five days after dissenting; path trimmed to four cuts but direction unchanged.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: 2026 National Community Investment Conference, Phoenix: 'Developing Communities through Public-private Partnerships'
items.quote: I supported this decision, and it is my view that we may need to keep rates steady for some time as we assess economic conditions.
items.summary: In a short policy passage inside a community-development speech, Barr said he supported the March hold and that rates may need to stay steady for some time. Inflation is notably above 2 percent; he wants evidence that goods and services inflation is sustainably retreating before considering further cuts, provided the labor market stays stable, and said the Middle East conflict adds risks through oil and gasoline prices.
items.score_note: Same message as Feb 17: extended hold with a bar for further cuts and inflation named as the problem; the only move contemplated is still a cut, so +1 rather than higher.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: PBS NewsHour interview with Geoff Bennett (transcript)
items.quote: For it to be realistic that rates would come down further this year, we have got to see progress in inflation, I think
items.summary: Asked whether one cut this year is still realistic, Goolsbee says he does not know and it depends how long the conflict lasts. Stagflationary shocks are the worst case for a central bank because there is no obvious playbook. If inflation, already above target for five years, starts trending up again, the Fed will have to think through its options.
items.score_note: Cuts made conditional on inflation progress, stagflation framed as two-sided; no explicit tightening lean.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: BBC interview
items.quote: We have two very extreme outcomes,
items.summary: Fink told the BBC that a year from now oil could be at $40 or above $150, with nothing in the middle, depending on how the Iran war ends. In the bad case he said there would be a global recession and broad supply-chain disruption. In the same interview (Times of India report) he rejected the idea of an AI bubble.
items.score_note: Energy and growth scenarios only; he gives no view on what the Fed should or will do.
items.ai_quote: I do not believe we have a bubble at all.

items.speaker: Lindsay Rosner
items.role: Head of Multi-Sector Investing, Goldman Sachs Asset Management
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs The Markets podcast (recorded March 25, 2026), transcript PDF
items.quote: that they will cut two times this year
items.summary: Rosner (GSAM, the asset-management arm, not GS Research) said the modal case is still two Fed cuts in 2026, out of consensus with a market that had priced a hold, because the Fed looks at core PCE and still weighs the labor market; she does not expect lasting effects that force a hike.
items.score_note: Two cuts in 2026 as the modal case and pushback on hike pricing. Asset-management view.
items.call: 2026: two cuts (modal case); Fed not on hold all year

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Conversation at the Digital Asset Summit 2026, New York
items.quote: I boosted my policy rate by half a percent, not due to oil and Iran, but due to the inflation data that we received
items.summary: Miran said he raised his end-2026 rate projection by half a point at the March meeting because of disappointing inflation data since December, not because of oil, which puts his projection at about neutral. Bloomberg's video summary says he does not think policy needs to be 'slamming on the gas' but should not hold the economy back.
items.score_note: A hawkish revision of his own path driven by inflation data, while still wanting policy at neutral (below the current rate). Revision toward tighter from a dovish position, so -1.

items.speaker: Ted Pick
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley 2026 annual letter to shareholders (signed March 25, 2026)
items.quote: We expect the mix of tailwinds and headwinds that we saw in 2025 to continue in 2026 and are prepared to execute in this environment.
items.summary: Pick's letter is mostly a review of 2025: he says the US economy was resilient, fiscal conditions were constructive, monetary policy eased and inflation moderated. Looking ahead he only says the 2025 mix of tailwinds and headwinds should continue in 2026, noting that geopolitical complexity remains and asset prices reflect several years of strong gains. No view on the Fed rate path, credit stress or AI financing risk.
items.score_note: Official text with no forward-looking monetary-policy content; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Brookings Institution, Washington: 'Brief Remarks on the Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy' (opening remarks before a moderated conversation)
items.quote: Our current policy stance puts us in a good place to hold steady while we evaluate incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks.
items.summary: Barr said he supported the March hold. After five years of elevated inflation and a rise in near-term expectations, he is particularly concerned that the Middle East energy shock could lift longer-term inflation expectations and said the Fed needs to be especially vigilant; core inflation was likely 3 percent in February. He also noted near-zero job creation leaves the labor market vulnerable, and closed by criticizing recent bank capital, leverage, stress-test and supervision changes as reducing resilience.
items.score_note: Calls the inflation trajectory 'a key concern right now' and stresses expectations risk from a new price shock, while still describing a hold; labor vulnerability noted but secondary.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Yale Program on Financial Stability, New Haven: 'Reflections on Financial Stability'
items.quote: While I take comfort in the very high levels of resilience of the U.S. G-SIBs, vigilance in ensuring their continued resilience is critical.
items.summary: Cook, chair of the Board's Committee on Financial Stability, described how the committee, the Financial Stability Report and scenario analysis work. She said recent committee topics include hedge fund trading strategies, the rise of private credit and bank links to nonbanks (bank commitments to nonbank financials growing about 9 percent a year, three times C&I lending), and used 'What if AI disappoints?' as an example scenario. No comment on the policy rate. Yale's write-up says the Q&A touched on the Iran war's effect on inflation risk, but no direct quote is available.
items.score_note: Financial-stability speech with no statement on the rate path.
items.ai_quote: Recently, among the issues we have discussed are hedge fund trading strategies, the rise of private credit arrangements, and the connections between banks and a range of nonbank financial entities.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Global Perspectives Speaker Series, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas: 'Economic Outlook and Energy Effects'
items.quote: I am confident that our current policy stance is well positioned to respond to a range of outcomes.
items.summary: Supported the March hold. Sees downside risk to the labor market and upside risk to inflation, with the energy price jump from the Middle East conflict and tariff uncertainty complicating both sides. Rate is broadly neutral; still speaks of 'additional adjustments' depending on data.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks named explicitly, stance described as well positioned; no lean.

items.speaker: Jonathan Millar
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Mar 26)
items.quote: entirely plausible the Fed waits out the oil price for longer and delays cuts into next year.
items.summary: Millar said the Fed will not gain confidence on inflation until September, and that it is plausible cuts get delayed into 2027; he does not think markets (pricing hikes) lead the Fed.
items.score_note: Base case still a first cut in September 2026; flags delay risk and rejects hike pricing.
items.call: first cut September 2026; plausible cuts are delayed into 2027

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast on the March FOMC (recorded Thursday Mar 26, 8:30am New York)
items.quote: We've slid those back to September and December.
items.summary: Gapen said the answer to higher macro uncertainty is caution and later cuts: Morgan Stanley moved its cuts from June and September to September and December because higher oil prices mean it takes the Fed longer to conclude disinflation is occurring. He still thinks second-half cuts are reasonable.
items.score_note: Two cuts still forecast for 2026, delayed; same call as the Mar 19 note, restated in public.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, September and December (previously June and September)

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Speech 'Prospects for Shrinking the Fed's Balance Sheet', Economic Club of Miami
items.quote: It is therefore likely that a resumption of balance sheet reduction warrants additional reductions in the federal funds rate relative to baseline projections.
items.summary: Miran said he would like the balance sheet to shrink further, by roughly $1 trillion to $2 trillion, without returning to scarce reserves, by first lowering reserve demand (easing liquidity rules, destigmatizing the standing repo facility and discount window, and similar steps from a co-authored working paper). He said the preparatory steps would take well over a year, runoff should be slow and through maturities rather than sales, and because runoff is contractionary it would warrant a lower funds rate.
items.score_note: Wants a smaller balance sheet (tightening) but explicitly paired with a lower funds rate; no call for an immediate cut in this text, so -1 rather than -2.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Cabinet meeting at the White House
items.quote: Who wouldn't be lowering interest rates right now?
items.summary: In a long passage on the Fed building renovation and the DOJ suit, Trump said Powell's interest rates are too high, called him 'a moron at the fed', and asked who would not be lowering interest rates right now. He joked Warsh may never get an office in the Fed building.
items.score_note: Explicit view that rates should be cut now.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'Driving Through Economic Fog (Still)' (Richmond Fed posted text)
items.quote: it felt prudent to hold rates and await more clarity on how we should be leaning to best support the economy going forward
items.summary: Barkin says the funds rate sits at the higher end of the range of neutral and that holding in March was prudent given risks to both the labor market and inflation and a foggy outlook. Recent PCE data suggest progress on inflation may be at risk of stalling, and that was before the oil price spike; he will watch the shock's effect on inflation and inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Explicit two-sided risks and hold; inflation worry noted but no lean on direction. Time from the Richmond Fed media advisory.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Macroeconomics and Monetary Policy Conference (San Francisco Fed), 'Monetary Policy and Productivity'
items.quote: But if inflation is above 2 percent and has been for some time, I would be more cautious.
items.summary: Paulson laid out low, medium and high productivity scenarios for AI and their implications for the long-run funds rate. She said the 1990s Greenspan-style patience relied on credibility earned with inflation at 2 percent, whereas inflation has now been above target for six years, is 2.8 percent, and the Middle East conflict adds risks to inflation and growth. Faced with a growth surge she would weight the possibility of overheating more heavily; she sees no sign the labor market is adding to inflation. In the Q&A (Reuters, MNI) she said she is worried that repeated supply shocks pass more quickly and durably into inflation expectations, while calling the labor market fragile and stressing risks to both inflation and growth.
items.score_note: Conditional, hypothetical lean toward caution on inflation but no statement on the next move; between 0 and +1, chose 0. Earlier 'cuts later this year' language is absent.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Mar 29 edition)
items.quote: This hawkish shift is consistent with recent central bank commentary expressing deep concern over the war’s inflationary effects.
items.summary: El-Erian says markets reacted to the 'real and present danger of higher inflation' by pricing rate hikes for the ECB and Bank of England and, briefly, even the Fed. He notes more private-credit funds, including Apollo and Ares vehicles, limited withdrawals during the week.
items.score_note: Treats higher inflation as a real and present danger and the hawkish repricing as justified; stops short of predicting a Fed hike, hence +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks at Long Island Business Roundtable
items.quote: President Trump’s economic agenda is focused on three pillars: trade, tax, and deregulation.
items.summary: Remarks on tax cuts, refunds and small business. No Fed or interest-rate content in the published text.
items.score_note: Official text with no statement on the Fed's policy rate; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Chicago magazine Q&A with Mark Bazer (May 2026 issue, posted March 30; interview date not stated)
items.quote: I’ve been uncomfortable with front-loading too many cuts and counting on inflation going back to 2 percent on its own
items.summary: Goolsbee says inflation above 2 percent for nearly five years is not something to trifle with and weighs on rate decisions. He remains pretty optimistic rates could keep going down by the end of the year but is uncomfortable front-loading cuts. He warns that an administration ordering the central bank to cut regardless of conditions 'ends in tears', and says he respects Warsh.
items.score_note: Magazine lead time: text does not mention the Iran war, so it likely predates it. Easing hope and caution offset; torn between -1 and 0, chose 0.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Interview, CNBC 'Squawk on the Street'
items.quote: we could be about a point easier, gradually done over the course of a year
items.summary: Miran said policymakers should disregard the energy price spike unless a wage-price spiral or rising inflation expectations appear, of which he sees no evidence, and that changing the policy rate now would not affect inflation over the next couple of months. He still thinks rates could be about a point lower over a year.
items.score_note: Explicitly backs about 100 bp of easing over the year and looking through the oil shock.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Project Syndicate op-ed 'America Should Beware of Economic Hubris'
items.quote: Already, higher energy and borrowing costs are exacerbating the affordability pressures many Americans face, creating downside risks for jobs, consumption, and growth.
items.summary: El-Erian argues that even if the US keeps outperforming its peers it is not insulated from the Iran war's spillovers. He says higher energy and borrowing costs are worsening affordability and creating downside risks for jobs, consumption and growth.
items.score_note: Growth and affordability risks from the war; no statement on the Fed rate path.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: Moderated discussion, Harvard University Principles of Economics class (Ec 10b), Cambridge
items.quote: We feel like our policy's in a good place for us to wait and see how that turns out
items.summary: Powell told a Harvard class that policy is in a good place to wait and see how the Iran-war energy shock plays out, that there is tension between downside labor-market risk and upside inflation risk, and that longer-term inflation expectations appear well anchored. He said supply shocks are usually looked through but expectations must be monitored carefully because a series of shocks can raise them. Harvard's own write-ups add that he called the deficit path unsustainable and said the Fed is watching private credit closely without seeing a systemic threat.
items.score_note: Explicit wait-and-see with both risks named; no lean.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Staten Island Economic Development Corporation, 'Ferrying Through the Crosscurrents'
items.quote: But the current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to balance the risks to our maximum employment and price stability goals.
items.summary: Williams said the Middle East conflict has pushed up energy prices and could become a large supply shock that raises inflation and dampens activity, on top of tariffs; PCE inflation is around 3 percent. Longer-term expectations remain anchored and there are no second-round tariff effects. He called the stance well positioned to balance risks, raised his 2026 inflation forecast to about 2-3/4 percent, and dropped the earlier language about eventual further reductions. He told reporters that uncertainties and risks to both goals have increased and that he is using energy market pricing as his guide while watching for other scenarios.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks and 'well positioned'; no easing-bias sentence this time and no tightening lean.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Federalist Society, Washington: 'Brief Remarks on Stablecoins' (The GENIUS Act in Practice)
items.quote: A second key area of concern is financial stability.
items.summary: Remarks on stablecoin regulation under the GENIUS Act: run risk, reserve-asset quality, money laundering and the importance of regulatory implementation. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content (stablecoin regulation only).

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: CBA LIVE 26, Consumer Bankers Association, San Diego: 'Supporting Small Businesses'
items.quote: Small businesses create and maintain the largest share of these new jobs.
items.summary: Small-business credit and the regulatory agenda. Mentions the dual mandate only in passing; no rate-path content.
items.score_note: Regulation and small-business lending only.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: El País interview (conducted in Madrid the week before publication)
items.quote: But if you look at the default rates in private credit, they’re at normal levels.
items.summary: Asked whether private credit is the biggest risk to financial stability, Fink said no and called it an artificial debate fuelled by the press. He acknowledged short-term tension in retail funds that gate redemptions but said default rates are normal and some losses are just capitalism. The headline of the interview is his view that the global economy enters recession if the Iran war lasts more than a year.
items.score_note: Credit and growth views only; no statement on the Fed rate path found in the interview.
items.ai_quote: So, is there short-term tension in the private credit market?

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: CNBC interview on markets and the Iran war, as quoted by Business Insider
items.quote: You start with an energy shock, interest rate shock, broader inflation shock, demand shock.
items.summary: El-Erian says he has moved to maximum risk-off and would not buy the index, because a demand shock is the next tipping point for the global economy. He lays out a sequence from energy, interest-rate and inflation shocks to a demand shock and, if it continues, financial instability.
items.score_note: Describes a shock sequence ending in possible financial instability; no explicit Fed call.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy", Rotary Club of Oklahoma City, Okla.
items.quote: With inflation already running hot, now is not the time to assume that the inflation from higher oil prices will be transitory.
items.summary: After the Iran-related oil price jump, Schmid said he is more focused on inflation risks than on growth: inflation was near 3% before the shock, progress has stalled, and higher energy prices will raise core as well as headline inflation. He said the Fed must follow through with policy actions that validate stable inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Inflation risk explicitly dominates and he rejects looking through the oil shock; stops short of calling for a hike.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post on the Fed building renovation
items.quote: by an incompetent and possibly corrupt Fed Chairman.
items.summary: In a post about lawsuits over his own building projects, Trump said the Fed building has been 'decimated and destroyed' by an 'incompetent and possibly corrupt Fed Chairman' and is billions over budget. No rate-path content.
items.score_note: Personal attack on Powell over the renovation; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Reuters interview (conducted Tuesday March 31, published April 1; via SRN News)
items.quote: The hike case would be around inflation expectations starting to finally move,
items.summary: Barkin says households and firms still view the oil shock through a short-term lens; spending outside gasoline looks healthy. Scenarios could push the Fed in any direction: a hike would hinge on inflation expectations moving, which he does not see yet, while cuts would need inflation heading quickly to 2 percent or a weakening job market. Goods sellers have little pricing power left, services more.
items.score_note: Lays out both hike and cut cases and says expectations have not broken out; no lean.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "The Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy" and moderated Q&A, American Enterprise Institute, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: Policy is well positioned to address risks to both dual mandate objectives, and I expect the current setting of the policy rate will remain appropriate for some time.
items.summary: Musalem said he supported the January and March holds; the real policy rate is in the lower part of the neutral range and the current rate will likely stay appropriate for some time. Risks tilt both to a weaker labor market and to more persistent above-target inflation after the Middle East energy shock. He laid out both directions: he could support easing if labor weakens with inflation expectations contained, and could support raising the rate if core inflation or longer-term expectations move persistently higher; easing on the mere prospect of AI productivity would be risky.
items.score_note: Explicit extended hold with two-sided risks and symmetric conditions for a cut or a hike. Warnings about looking through supply shocks lean slightly hawkish, but the stated stance is balanced.
items.ai_quote: For now, recent stress in private credit markets appears mostly due to liquidity issues and some marking down of net asset values, rather than widespread credit quality problems.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Speech 'The banking system and the demand for reserves', Eleventh District Banking Conference, Dallas (prepared remarks; companion essay with Sam Schulhofer-Wohl 'Options for reducing the size of the Fed's balance sheet')
items.quote: So, I favor an approach that reduces banks’ need for reserves and shifts the demand curve inward.
items.summary: Balance-sheet speech: the Fed holds $6.7 trillion in assets (21 percent of GDP) with about $3 trillion of reserves. Logan argues against returning to scarce reserves or reserve quotas and prefers shrinking the balance sheet by reducing banks' reserve demand, through more efficient liquidity rules and easier access to the discount window, intraday credit and standing repo; any change should be gradual. The prepared text says nothing on the rate path (she deferred that to the fireside chat that followed).
items.score_note: Prepared remarks are about balance-sheet size and reserve demand only; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Fireside chat with Robert Hulsey after her balance-sheet speech, Eleventh District Banking Conference, Dallas Fed (Reuters report)
items.quote: it's incredibly important to restore price stability, to get inflation back to 2% because stable inflation is just the bedrock for a strong economy.
items.summary: In the Q&A after her prepared remarks Logan says the Iran war raises risks on both sides of the mandate and that policy is positioned to adjust to the data as it comes in. She says she was not convinced inflation was heading all the way to 2 percent even before the conflict, and that US oil producers will not raise output much in the short run, so energy prices stay a near-term problem. A quick resolution would mean a moderate impact; a longer war would pull the two mandates in opposite directions.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided and wait-and-see ('positioned to adjust'); inflation is her chief concern but she gives no directional lean on rates here. Torn between 0 and +1, chose 0. Separate item from the prepared speech because the rate-relevant remarks came only in the Q&A.

items.speaker: Manuel Abecasis
items.role: Analyst, Goldman Sachs (as described on page)
items.occasion: Research note arguing market pricing of 2026 hikes is too high, reported by Investing.com (reprint dated Apr 2)
items.quote: Our probability-weighted Fed forecast remains meaningfully more dovish than market pricing,
items.summary: Abecasis argued the roughly 45% market-implied chance of a 2026 hike overstates the risk: the oil shock is smaller and narrower than past ones, the labor market is softening, the funds rate is already 50-75bp above neutral, and oil shocks have not historically led to Fed tightening.
items.score_note: Pushes back on hike pricing and calls its own forecast more dovish than the market.
items.call: hikes in 2026 unlikely; probability-weighted forecast more dovish than market pricing

items.speaker: Citigroup economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated April 3 after March jobs report, reported by Reuters Apr 6
items.quote: But the timing of upcoming data suggests a later start to rate cuts than we had previously been expecting,
items.summary: Citi pushed back its timeline: 75bp of cuts now in September, October and December 2026 instead of June, July and September, citing persistent inflation risks and strong March job gains; it still expects a weakening labor market to bring cuts later in the year.
items.score_note: Keeps 75bp of 2026 cuts but delays the start by three months.
items.call: 2026: three cuts (75bp), September, October and December (previously June, July and September)

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: SF Fed Blog essay "Monetary Policy in a Slow (to No) Growth Labor Market"
items.quote: And with inflation already printing above target, policymakers will have to be very clear about how movement towards our mandated goals will be achieved.
items.summary: Daly wrote that with labor force growth near zero, zero or negative monthly job growth can be consistent with full employment, so ratios such as the unemployment rate are better gauges than payroll counts. Uncertainty about potential growth raises the risk of holding policy too loose or too tight, and communication gets harder with inflation above target.
items.score_note: Structural essay with no stated lean on the rate path; the point that weak payrolls need not signal slack mildly argues against reacting with cuts, but risks are framed as two-sided.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: CBS News interview with Aimee Picchi
items.quote: to me that starts pushing these decisions off to 2027 at the earliest,
items.summary: Goolsbee says that before the war he believed rates could come down multiple times in 2026, but the energy shock complicates that: with no improvement in inflation, cut decisions get pushed to 2027 at the earliest. He worries sticker shock could weigh on consumers, the backbone of growth, and that uncertainty keeps the labor market in low-hire, low-fire mode.
items.score_note: Withdraws his own 2026 cut baseline because of inflation; pushback on cuts rather than a hike call.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Apr 5 edition)
items.quote: a policy stance that stands in stark contrast to the analytical and intellectual agility recently shown by the other two systemically important central banks
items.summary: El-Erian contrasts the IMF, Bank of England and ECB, which updated their analysis of the war's impact, with senior Fed officials who kept repeating that policy is 'well-positioned'. He also notes Blue Owl capped withdrawals at 5% for two funds facing redemption requests of 22% and 41%.
items.score_note: Criticizes the Fed's wait-and-see 'well-positioned' stance as lacking agility but does not state which direction rates should move.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: NPR 'The Indicator from Planet Money' joint interview with Beth Hammack (transcript; Reuters says taped April 1)
items.quote: I was optimistic that we would get back to this path to 2% inflation, but yikes, it's going from orange to red lately.
items.summary: Asked to color-code the economy, Goolsbee rates inflation at least orange and heading to red: tariff price increases did not fade and another stagflationary shock has landed on top. He rates the labor market yellow, low-hiring and low-firing but mostly stable, and is a little anxious about frothy asset prices. No direct rate guidance.
items.score_note: Inflation risk clearly dominates his assessment; no explicit rate statement, so only +1.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Associated Press interview
items.quote: Or I could see where we might need to raise rates if inflation stays persistently above our target.
items.summary: Hammack told the AP her preference is to keep rates unchanged for quite some time, but she can foresee cutting if the labor market deteriorates significantly or raising rates if inflation stays persistently above target. Cleveland Fed estimates show inflation could reach 3.5 percent in April, which she described as moving in the wrong direction. Gas prices are the top concern she hears in her district, and the war has already lasted longer than she expected at the March meeting.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided (cut and hike scenarios) around an extended hold. Between 0 and +1 given the stress on inflation; chose 0.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: NPR 'The Indicator from Planet Money' podcast, joint interview with Austan Goolsbee (taped April 1, reported April 6)
items.quote: We've been trading closer to 3% than our objective of 2%.
items.summary: Asked to rate the economy by color, Hammack put inflation at a bright orange: above target for about five years and basically moving sideways for the past two. She rated the labor market yellow-green, with unemployment right around her estimate of maximum employment though in a fragile low-hiring, low-firing balance. She called financial stability generally green, naming private credit as a pocket she is watching and noting that financial conditions tightened over the past month. The transcript has no explicit rate-path comment; Reuters characterized both officials as seeing inflation as a far bigger problem than employment.
items.score_note: No rate-path statement; inflation risk clearly dominates labor in her own assessment, which is the +1 definition. Weak evidence, so treat as a soft +1. Taped before the March jobs report.
items.ai_quote: Private credit is certainly one of them.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Annual letter to shareholders (2025 annual report)
items.quote: which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect
items.summary: Dimon warns that oil and commodity shocks from the Iran war plus reshaped supply chains may bring stickier inflation and higher rates than markets expect; the 'skunk at the party' in 2026 would be inflation slowly going up, which alone could lift rates and hit asset prices. He lists fiscal stimulus, Fed purchases of $40 billion a month and $725 billion of hyperscaler AI capex as short-run inflationary supports. On credit he says private credit is probably not systemic, but losses in the next credit cycle will be higher than expected because standards have weakened.
items.score_note: Risk warning that rates end up higher than markets price; not an explicit call for hikes, so +1 rather than +2.
items.ai_quote: Overall, the investment in AI is not a speculative bubble; rather, it will deliver significant benefits.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: X post on private credit (reported by Business Insider on Apr 6; exact post date not stated)

items.ai_quote: It's 2007 for Private Credit.

items.speaker: Wells Fargo Investment Institute strategists (not named on page)

items.score_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); no hike call.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Moderated Q&A, Detroit Economic Club (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: I'm cautious - slash nervous - about it in the moment.
items.summary: Goolsbee says the oil spike from the Iran war hit before tariff inflation had faded, leaving the Fed in a very uncomfortable spot with no obvious cookbook on whether to heat things up or cool things down. The worst outcome would be a stagflationary recession if consumers lose confidence. The job market is stable but not great.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided: says it is not obvious which way policy should move.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: NPR Morning Edition interview with Steve Inskeep (the day after his shareholder letter)
items.quote: I just think it increases the odds of bad economic outcomes.
items.summary: Dimon said the wars add to a long list of uncertainties and could cause some form of recession, though he was not predicting one. He said people should be clear-eyed that the odds of bad economic outcomes have risen. The interview has no comment on Fed policy, inflation or interest rates.
items.score_note: Growth-risk comment only; no rate-path content in the transcript.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: College of Business Administration, University of Detroit Mercy: 'Economic Outlook and the Labor Market'
items.quote: I continue, however, to see our current policy stance as appropriately positioned to allow us to assess how the economy evolves.
items.summary: Repeats the March message: labor market roughly in balance but vulnerable, inflation above target, downside risk to jobs and upside risk to inflation. Supported the March hold; rate is broadly neutral and the stance allows time to assess energy-price and conflict effects.
items.score_note: Hold with two-sided risks; no lean.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview
items.quote: I expect headline inflation to actually be elevated, you know, in the middle of this year
items.summary: Williams said the Middle East energy shock will feed directly into headline inflation, which he expects to be elevated mid-year and about 2.75 percent for 2026, while reiterating that monetary policy is in the right place. Per MNI's transcript of the same interview he called policy 'really well positioned' to wait and see, kept his core inflation view near 2.5 percent, and trimmed his growth forecast to 2 to 2.5 percent. He also said FOMC leadership continuity is not in question if Warsh's confirmation is delayed.
items.score_note: Wait-and-see hold; acknowledges higher headline inflation but no change in his view of underlying inflation and no lean on the next move.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Keynote "Regionalism at the Federal Reserve: Many Voices, One Purpose" and conversation with Chip Childs, St. George Area Chamber of Commerce, Utah (official transcript of the conversation)
items.quote: So from my vantage point today, I see the underlying fundamentals of the economy as really in a good place.
items.summary: The prepared speech (https://www.frbsf.org/news-and-media/speeches/mary-c-daly/2026/04/many-voices-one-purpose/) is about the Fed's regional structure and independence. In the conversation Daly said the economy's fundamentals are solid, it is too early to judge the effect of the war and oil prices on inflation, and longer-run inflation expectations are well behaved. No statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: Official speech on Fed structure; outlook comments only, nothing usable on the policy rate path.

items.speaker: Wells Fargo economists (not named on page)
items.occasion: Wells Fargo research note quoted by FXStreet Insights Team (Apr 8)
items.quote: we have pushed out the start of easing but still expect 50 bps of total cuts this year
items.summary: Wells Fargo economists pushed back the start of easing because of higher oil prices and stickier inflation, but still expect 50bp of cuts in 2026, now at the September and December meetings; they see the next move as more likely a cut than a hike, with risks skewed to later and/or less easing.
items.score_note: Keeps two cuts in 2026, delayed to September and December; says a cut is more likely than a hike. Differs from Wells Fargo Investment Institute, which dropped 2026 cuts on Apr 6.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, 25bp cuts in September and December (start of easing pushed out)

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview given the day before the March CPI release (Reuters exclusive published April 10; quotes read in a same-day Reuters story)
items.quote: We had work to do before we had the oil price shock; with the oil price shock, the work just takes longer
items.summary: Daly said a higher CPI number would surprise no one and need not change the plan to hold or perhaps cut: if the ceasefire holds and oil falls, the Fed could eventually lower rates; if oil and inflation are sticky it can hold and wait. She thought a surge that forces the Fed to chase inflation with hikes is less likely, and said the Fed could just be holding steady until it knows the job is getting done. The SF Fed summary of the interview says she called policy in a "good place".
items.score_note: Holding pattern; she ranks a cut above a hike among the alternatives, a mild dovish tilt, but the stated stance is wait.

items.speaker: Howard Marks
items.occasion: Oaktree memo 'What's Going on in Private Credit?'
items.quote: Ultimately, high yield was fine (even great), and direct lending will be as well, but it may have to go through a credit cycle to get to a better place.
items.summary: Marks traces the direct-lending boom and the February 2026 scare over software loans exposed to AI disruption, which triggered redemption requests and gating at semi-liquid funds. He says the disruption so far is largely sentiment- and flow-driven rather than credit deterioration, but standards slipped in the good times and the 2022 rate rise 'threw sand in the gears' of private equity. No view on what the Fed should do.
items.score_note: Credit-stress commentary only; rates discussed historically (sea change), no stance on the policy path.
items.ai_quote: The implications of AI for the software industry, limitations on liquidity in private assets, and uncertainty regarding the accuracy of direct lending funds’ pricing have been there for years.

items.speaker: UBS Global Wealth Management analysts (not named on page)
items.occasion: UBS GWM comment ahead of March CPI, quoted in Reuters stock-market report (Apr 10)
items.quote: we continue to believe that the central bank remains on track to cut rates later this year,
items.summary: UBS Global Wealth Management said that although Fed officials expect higher oil prices to delay disinflation, it still believes the Fed is on track to cut later in 2026, expecting sequential core inflation to cool as tariff effects fade and labor demand falls.
items.score_note: Maintains cuts later in 2026 after the oil shock; a month later it pushed the first cut to December.
items.call: Fed on track to cut later in 2026 (timing not stated on page)

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (Apr 12 edition)
items.quote: The minutes suggest that, on balance, central bankers remain slightly more sensitive to labor market weakness than inflation—at least as of last month.
items.summary: El-Erian reads the March FOMC minutes as showing both sides of the dual mandate under pressure, with officials slightly more sensitive to labor weakness than to inflation. He notes the Warsh hearing was delayed and that the Fed asked banks to detail their private-credit exposure to assess stress and spillover risk.
items.score_note: Reads the Fed's reaction function as tilting slightly toward labor weakness, but hedged ('at least as of last month'); torn between 0 and -1, so 0.
items.ai_quote: At the end of the week, it emerged that the Federal Reserve had instructed banks to detail their exposure to private credit.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Semafor World Economy, Treasury Secretary Dinner interview with Ben Smith, Washington
items.quote: I think the Fed is doing the right thing by sitting and watching.
items.summary: Bessent said rates should be lowered 'eventually' but 'now ... we have to wait and see' how the Iran war affects the economy. He called the energy price shock a 'Team Transitory' case that will not get embedded in inflation expectations, said core inflation is coming down, and that he would be shocked if the ECB hiked. He said Warsh will have an open mind and will look hard at how the reserve banks are managed.
items.score_note: Endorses the Fed holding and watching for now while expecting cuts eventually; between 0 and -1, scored nearer 0.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs Q1 2026 earnings call
items.quote: Whenever you have a meaningful slowdown in the economy or a recession, there are higher loss levels in diversified credit portfolios.
items.summary: Solomon says media headlines have driven a lot of negative sentiment on private credit and that the market has to be put in perspective, but concedes it has been a very long credit cycle in which spreads tightened and lenders grew more aggressive, so a real slowdown would bring higher losses. He says spreads are turning more lender-friendly and the underlying economy remains relatively robust, while the effect of higher energy prices on inflation and growth is yet to be determined.
items.score_note: Credit-cycle commentary; inflation mentioned only as an open question, no rate-path view.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Conversation at the Symposium on Building the Financial System of the 21st Century, Washington
items.quote: There's thus far no evidence that inflation expectations are higher
items.summary: Miran said the Iran-war energy shock has not affected longer-run inflation expectations, that a wage-price spiral is very unlikely with the labor market cooling gradually, and that he expects inflation to be back near target in a year. Only the opening paragraphs of the Bloomberg article are visible; the text says 'Tuesday' although the page is timestamped Monday April 13, the date on the Fed calendar.
items.score_note: Argues for looking through the energy shock; no direct call for a cut in the visible text.

items.speaker: Michael Barr

items.quote: Given rapidly changing circumstances, it is too early to know the path for prices as events in the Middle East unfold.
items.summary: Community-development speech on rural economies. Mentions tariff disruption to farm exports, the fertilizer and diesel price jump from the Middle East conflict, and AI-driven data centers locating in rural areas (energy and water strain), but gives no view on the policy rate.
items.score_note: No statement about the policy rate path; price remarks are about farm input costs only.

The only direct quotation in the report is about wanting Warsh in place quickly. Bessent spoke at an IIF event and at WSJ Opinion Live that day; the report does not name the venue.
items.score_note: Reuters paraphrase: repeats call for cuts but accepts a pause; -1.

items.summary: Goolsbee says he had expected multiple cuts in 2026, but the longer inflation stays up the more that gets pushed out of 2026. Rates could go up in some circumstances; if the oil shock proves temporary and inflation heads back to 2 percent, decreases are on the table too.
items.score_note: Pushes cuts out to 2027 and acknowledges hikes are possible; still two-sided, so torn between 0 and +1, chose +1 because the shift is away from his earlier cut baseline and inflation is the stated reason.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Yahoo Finance interview with Brian Sozzi at the Semafor World Economy conference (video page transcript, auto-generated)

items.summary: Goolsbee loosely agrees with the market view that the Fed will not hike into an oil supply shock, but warns to watch second-round effects and inflation expectations, which could unanchor if gasoline stays near $5 for months. He says the 2 percent target must stay, that the longer the shock lasts the more it pushes cuts off, and that in stagflation neither raising, cutting nor holding solves the problem.
items.score_note: Not inclined to tighten into a supply shock, but cuts deferred; explicitly two-sided.

items.occasion: JPMorgan Chase Q1 2026 earnings call

items.summary: Asked whether a default cycle in private credit would be systemic, Dimon says no given its size, but repeats that when a credit cycle comes losses will be worse than people expect because underwriting has weakened. He says JPMorgan must be prepared for recession or stagflation, and that higher-for-longer rates with wider spreads would strain leveraged borrowers as they refinance, while stressing he is not forecasting.

The key question is how high energy prices stay and for how long. She cautioned that successive supply shocks on top of already elevated inflation may not be something the Fed can look through, and said it is a good time to stay patient.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem

items.summary: Musalem said policy is in a good place and should probably stay at this level for some time. The original Reuters headline (reuters.com, not readable here) says the oil shock is likely to keep core inflation near 3%.
