items.quote: Interest rates should be much lower than they are right now.
items.summary: Trump called Powell a disaster and a bad chairman who should be lowering rates, said he was not planning to drop the DOJ probe, and said that if Powell does not leave on time 'I'll have to fire him ... he will be fired'. He said Warsh will be great and rates should be much lower.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for much lower rates, with a threat to fire Powell.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Conversation at the Washington Economic Festival: Global Macro Sessions
items.quote: But given the risks to both sides, I said, OK, let's just go to neutral instead.
items.summary: Miran said the composition of inflation had become less favorable even before the war, that he now sees three or four cuts this year rather than four, and that he moved from wanting rates slightly below neutral to wanting them at neutral, which he puts a full point below the current 3.50-3.75%. He said the energy shock raises the risk of higher inflation further out if it persists, but he still expects inflation near target in a year and still favors cutting now.
items.score_note: Still advocates cutting toward neutral now (about 100 bp lower), though he has trimmed his path and concedes higher inflation risk; the stance on the day remains an explicit call for cuts.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Press gaggle before Marine One departure
items.quote: I think we should have lower interest rates.
items.summary: Asked whether he agrees with the view voiced the day before that the Fed should wait and see on the Iran war before lowering rates, Trump said 'No, I don't agree' and that rates should be lower.
items.score_note: Rejects wait-and-see and says rates should be lower now.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York 2026 Member Symposium, 'The Cosmos'
items.quote: This is an unusual set of circumstances, but the current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to balance the risks to our maximum employment and price stability goals.
items.summary: Williams repeated that the stance is well positioned as the Middle East conflict raises energy prices and risks a broader supply shock. He expects 2026 inflation of 2-3/4 to 3 percent, GDP growth of 2 to 2-1/2 percent and unemployment in a 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent range, with inflation back at 2 percent in 2027. Short-term inflation expectations have risen but medium and longer-term ones remain anchored. He also described the ample reserves framework as working well. He told reporters inflation will be well above 3 percent over the next few months, that it is not a time for strong forward guidance, and that it will be appropriate to bring rates down if inflation moderates back to 2 percent, 'but that's not where we are today'.
items.score_note: Balanced hold; flags both inflation and activity risks from the energy shock without a lean.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Conversation with Alex Mehran Sr., UC Berkeley Fisher Center for Real Estate & Urban Economics (official transcript)
items.quote: right now, policy’s in a very good place, slightly restrictive, not constraining the economy so much that the labor market’s faltering
items.summary: Daly said that before the oil shock she expected one or two more cuts toward a neutral rate around 3%; now, with oil lifting inflation, policy is slightly restrictive and in a very good place for wait-and-see. Scenarios: hold all year; raise if inflation really took off (not her modal outlook); or cut as in the March SEP (one cut) if the labor market falters or the conflict ends quickly. She would not be surprised by market pricing of zero cuts this year.
items.score_note: Explicit wait-and-see hold with a hike and a cut scenario both described; her earlier easing bias is suspended, not reversed.

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Global Research web article on the Fed's next move (version dated April 17, 2026; archived Apr 30)
items.quote: It should make the late April FOMC meeting an easy call for the Committee to stay on hold.
items.summary: J.P. Morgan Global Research expects a hold on April 28-29 and for the rest of 2026, then a 25bp hike in Q3 2027; it says the Fed could cut if the labor market weakens significantly or the energy fallout becomes more severe. Feroli calls the Fed's patience a key cushion for financial conditions.
items.score_note: Unchanged call through the oil shock: hold in 2026, next move a 2027 hike; cut risk acknowledged.
items.call: hold on April 28-29 and for the rest of 2026; 25bp hike in Q3 2027

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: David Kaserman Memorial Lecture, Auburn University: 'One Transitory Shock After Another'
items.quote: leaving me cautious about rate cuts now and more inclined toward cuts to support the labor market later this year when the outlook is more steady
items.summary: Two scenarios. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens he can look through energy prices: cautious on cuts now, inclined to cut later this year. If energy stays elevated, inflation may become embedded and holding the rate at the current range may be needed if inflation risks outweigh labor risks. Warns that a sequence of shocks requires more vigilance on expectations.
items.score_note: Hold now with a conditional cut lean in one scenario and an inflation-driven hold in the other; torn between -1 and 0, chose 0.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview, day of Warsh's Senate confirmation hearing
items.quote: we should have the lowest interest rate in the world.
items.summary: Asked whether he would be disappointed if Warsh did not cut rates right away, Trump answered 'I would.' He called Powell 'always too late', said Warsh is 'central casting', said he has been in favor of rate rises to stop inflation when needed, but that the US should have the lowest interest rate in the world. He did not commit to dropping the DOJ probe of Powell.
items.score_note: Says he would be disappointed without an immediate cut from the new chair and wants the lowest rate in the world.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Brookings Institution, Washington: 'Modernizing Federal Reserve Operations in the 21st Century'
items.quote: Each Bank president still has an independent voice at the FOMC on the appropriate course of monetary policy and that should continue.
items.summary: Speech on consolidating Reserve Bank back-office operations while keeping regional voices on the FOMC. No statement on the rate path. Delivered during the pre-FOMC blackout period.
items.score_note: Operations and governance only; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing: opening statement
items.quote: I'm committed to ensuring that the conduct of monetary policy remains strictly independent.
items.summary: In his opening statement Warsh called monetary policy independence essential, said it is not threatened when elected officials state views on rates, and said 'Inflation is the Fed's choice'. He said the Fed must stay in its lane, promised a reform-oriented Fed, and said US growth potential is rising. Source is CNN's rush transcript of the live hearing; the prepared text on banking.senate.gov could not be opened (bot protection).
items.score_note: Opening statement sets out independence and reform themes without a signal on the rate path or balance sheet; those answers are scored in separate items.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing: Q&A on the rate path and forward guidance
items.quote: I don't believe that I should be previewing for you what a future decision might be.
items.summary: Asked whether cutting rates toward 1% would raise prices, Warsh refused to preview decisions and said he does not believe in forward guidance. He argued the supply side is changing dramatically and potential growth is rising quickly, which makes the coming policy choice difficult; he also said the Fed has a short window to bring inflation back down, that AI could over time make the inflation job easier, and that policy works with long and variable lags. He rejected Senator Kennedy's summary that AI means rates can be cut now.
items.score_note: Declines to signal direction; pairs a supply-side argument (room for lower rates) with a stated need to bring inflation down. No lean either way.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing: Q&A on shrinking the balance sheet
items.quote: I think interest rates could be lower, inflation could be better, and the economy could be stronger
items.summary: Warsh said the large balance sheet has been unhelpful and is part of why the Fed is in the business of politics, and that he would work with the Treasury Secretary to make it smaller, slowly and deliberately and with clear communication. He said that with smaller holdings interest rates could be lower. In the hearing (CNN transcript) he also said the rate tool is fairer than the balance sheet, which disproportionately helps holders of financial assets, and called for a regime change in the conduct of policy, a new inflation framework and new communications.
items.score_note: Links a smaller balance sheet to a lower policy rate: balance-sheet tightening paired with a lower funds rate. No timing given, so -1 rather than -2.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing: Q&A on commitments to the President
items.quote: The president never once asked me to commit to any particular interest rate decision, period, and nor would I ever agree to do so if he had.
items.summary: Under questioning from Senators Reed and Kennedy, Warsh said he made no commitment to cut rates, would be an independent actor and 'absolutely not' the President's sock puppet. He said the President's views on rates sound like those of every other president, and that humble central bankers should listen and then make their own decisions.
items.score_note: Independence and political pressure; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Senate Appropriations subcommittee budget hearing (Q&A)
items.quote: swap lines, whether it’s from the Federal Reserve or the Treasury, are to maintain order in the dollar funding markets
items.summary: Bessent said several Gulf and Asian allies have requested dollar swap lines to cope with the energy shock, and that swap lines from the Fed or the Treasury exist to keep dollar funding markets orderly and prevent disorderly sales of US assets. The prepared statement (treasury.gov sb0466) has no monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Financial-stability backstops (swap lines); no statement on the policy rate.

items.speaker: Brett Ryan
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Apr 22), after Warsh confirmation hearing
items.quote: they really need to be careful of inflation expectations
items.summary: Ryan said Warsh is one voice and would need time to earn the committee's trust before cutting quickly, and that after five years of missing the target the Fed must guard against unanchored inflation expectations.
items.score_note: No dated rate path on the page; stresses inflation-expectations risk and no quick cuts. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.call: no quick cuts under Warsh (no dated path on page)

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (Apr 2026, published Apr 22)
items.quote: tariff inflation is transitory and oil puts upward pressure on headline inflation but doesn't translate into faster core inflation
items.summary: Gapen said tariff inflation is transitory and oil lifts headline but not core inflation, so the Fed can ease later in 2026; the main risk is inflation does not behave and the Fed just stays on hold.
items.score_note: Still forecasts easing later in 2026 one week before dropping the call.
items.call: Fed eases later in 2026; risk is the Fed just stays on hold

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks at a health care affordability event
items.quote: he's been terrible on interest rates because he should have lowered interest rates.
items.summary: Asked about the Pirro investigation of the Fed, Trump again attacked the cost of the Fed building and said Powell has been terrible on interest rates because he should have lowered them.
items.score_note: Past-tense criticism (should have lowered); no explicit new demand.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Oval Office remarks on Israel-Lebanon ceasefire extension
items.quote: he should have been lowering interest rates a long time ago.
items.summary: Asked whether someone other than the Justice Department could look into the Fed renovation, Trump said he has a real problem with Powell because he should have been lowering rates long ago, and that the economy is strong despite that.
items.score_note: Past-tense criticism; no explicit new demand.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: CNBC Money Movers interview
items.quote: Certainly, you would not cut interest rates now,
items.summary: Dalio says the US is certainly in a stagflationary period with inflation further from target. He says Kevin Warsh should not cut rates now because the Fed would lose credibility, and notes other central banks are not cutting.
items.score_note: Explicitly pushes back on cuts because of inflation and credibility; he does not call for hikes, so +1.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Norges Bank Investment Management investment conference (on-stage interview)
items.quote: We haven't had a credit recession in so long, so when we have one, it would be worse than people think
items.summary: Dimon said that on the current path of government debt there will be some kind of bond crisis that then has to be dealt with. He said private credit is not big enough to be systemic, but losses on all leveraged lending will be higher than expected when the credit cycle turns. Fortune's report of the same event quotes him saying inflation may tick up and catch many people off guard.
items.score_note: No explicit Fed call; he lists many inflationary forces (war, deficits, rearmament) and says inflation may tick up and surprise people, which leans tighter. Not +2 because no call for hikes.
items.ai_quote: I do believe that when we have a credit cycle, which will happen one day, losses on all leveraged lending in general will be higher than expected

items.speaker: Paul Tudor Jones
items.role: Founder and CIO, Tudor Investment Corp
items.occasion: 'Invest Like the Best' podcast with Patrick O'Shaughnessy (released Apr 28; quotes via CoinDesk)
items.quote: So you can see the budget deficit blowing up.
items.summary: Jones said US stocks are extremely overvalued relative to GDP and that a large equity drop would wipe out capital-gains tax revenue, blow up the deficit and hit the bond market. He called bitcoin the best inflation hedge, ahead of gold, because central-bank interventions make inflation trades take off.
items.score_note: No statement on the policy-rate path; fiscal and inflation-hedge remarks only.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: FOMC statement, April 28-29 meeting: dissent against retaining the easing bias (with Kashkari and Logan)
items.quote: who supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time
items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3.50-3.75 percent by an 8-4 vote. Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissented: they supported the hold but opposed keeping the 'additional adjustments' easing-bias language in the statement. Miran dissented in favor of a 25 bp cut. The quote is the statement's vote line, not Hammack's own words.
items.score_note: Hawkish dissent on forward guidance (remove easing bias) while supporting the hold; not a vote for a hike, so +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: CNBC Closing Bell interview with Scott Wapner after Powell's final FOMC press conference (quotes via DoubleLine's own recap page)
items.quote: the odds of a hike between now and year end are better than the odds of a cut.
items.summary: Gundlach called the press conference notably hawkish and the bond sell-off justified, and said headline CPI is heading to a 4 handle, making cuts essentially impossible; a hike is more likely than a cut by year end. He praised Powell's defense of Fed independence and warned of a wave of private-credit interval-fund redemption requests around June 23 ('Ides of June').
items.score_note: Forecast that a hike is more likely than a cut and cuts are essentially impossible; not a statement that the Fed will or must hike soon, so +1 rather than +2. Source is the firm's recap with direct quotes, not a transcript.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: FOMC meeting April 28-29, 2026: dissent against the easing-bias language (8-4 vote to hold at 3.50-3.75%; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan against the guidance, Miran for a cut)
items.quote: who supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time
items.summary: The FOMC statement records Kashkari (with Hammack and Logan) voting against the action: he supported holding the funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent but did not support keeping an easing bias in the statement. The quote is the Committee's wording of his position; his own essay followed on May 1.
items.score_note: Dissent against cut-leaning guidance while supporting the hold, not a dissent for a hike: +1. Quote is from the FOMC statement (Committee's description of the dissent).

items.speaker: Kay Haigh
items.role: Global co-head of fixed income and liquidity solutions, Goldman Sachs Asset Management
items.occasion: Emailed comment after the April 29 FOMC decision (Reuters instant view)
items.quote: This balance could see rates being brought back down to neutral later this year
items.summary: Haigh (GSAM, the asset-management arm, not GS Research) said the Fed is in a stable place, upside inflation risks have increased, and rates could still be brought back to neutral later in 2026 unless Iran re-escalates and energy prices rise.
items.score_note: Still sees room for cuts later in 2026, conditional; asset-management view, not the GS Research house call.
items.call: rates could be brought down to neutral later in 2026; restrictive for longer if Iran re-escalates

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: FOMC meeting April 28-29, 2026: dissent against the easing-bias language (8-4 vote to hold at 3.50-3.75%; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan against the guidance, Miran for a cut)
items.quote: who supported maintaining the target range for the federal funds rate but did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time
items.summary: The FOMC statement records Logan (with Hammack and Kashkari) voting against the action: she supported holding the funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent but did not support keeping an easing bias in the statement. The quote is the Committee's wording of her position, not her own words; her own explanation followed on May 1.
items.score_note: Dissent against cut-leaning guidance while supporting the hold, not a dissent for a hike: +1. Quote is from the FOMC statement (Committee's description of the dissent).

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Dissent at the April 28-29 FOMC meeting (preferred a 25 bp cut)
items.quote: Voting against this action were Stephen I. Miran, who preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting
items.summary: The FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% by 8-4. Miran again preferred a 25 bp cut, while Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissented in the other direction over the statement's easing bias. The quote is the Committee statement's wording, not Miran's own words.
items.score_note: Formal dissent in favor of an immediate cut, his third of the year.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: X post on the morning of the April FOMC decision (x.com/elerianm/status/2049448535242965284)
items.quote: The most interesting aspect of today’s Federal Reserve (FOMC) meeting—where interest rates will be left as is—will be the Chair’s press conference.
items.summary: Ahead of the April decision El-Erian says rates will be left unchanged and that the main interest is Powell's press conference, likely his last as Chair with the Senate Banking Committee expected to approve Kevin Warsh.
items.score_note: Expects a hold at the meeting; no lean on the subsequent path.

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note on Wednesday Apr 29 after the April FOMC, reported by Reuters Apr 30
items.quote: to continued strength in growth and labor markets, reducing the urgency for further policy easing
items.summary: Morgan Stanley dropped its forecast of two quarter-point cuts in 2026 and now expects no cuts this year, saying inflation above target and continued strength in growth and labor markets reduce the urgency for further easing.
items.score_note: Moves from two 2026 cuts to none; a hold forecast, not a hike call.
items.call: no cuts in 2026 (previously two quarter-point cuts)

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, April 28-29 meeting: opening statement (last as Chair)
items.quote: Inflation has moved up and is elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices.
items.summary: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% by 8-4: Miran dissented for a 25 bp cut; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan agreed with the hold but opposed keeping an easing bias in the statement. Powell said headline PCE inflation was 3.5% and core 3.2% in March, the stance is appropriate, and the Committee is attentive to both sides. He announced he will stay on as a Governor for a period to be determined after his term as Chair ends May 15 and will keep a low profile.
items.score_note: Statement text itself: hold is appropriate, both-sided risks; the tighter lean comes in the Q&A (separate item).

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, April 28-29 meeting: Q&A on the next move (bar for cuts, hikes)
items.quote: I think we’d want to see the back side of that and progress on tariffs before we even thought about, about reducing rates.
items.summary: Powell said the energy shock has not peaked and the Fed would want to see it fade and tariff inflation recede before even thinking about cuts. He said nobody is calling for a hike now, but if a hike is needed the Fed will signal it and do it. He put policy at the high end of neutral or mildly restrictive, said there is no case that it is meaningfully restrictive, and called that the right place to be while inflation is misbehaving and the labor market is stabilizing.
items.score_note: Pushes back on cuts, puts hikes on the table conditionally, inflation is the stated problem; no call to hike, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, April 28-29 meeting: Q&A on the easing bias in the statement
items.quote: the center is moving toward a more neutral place
items.summary: Powell said the number of participants who could support changing the guidance to a neutral stance (hike as likely as cut) rose over the intermeeting period and it is now a much closer call than in March. A majority, including him, saw no need to rush because the next 30 to 60 days could change the picture, but he said the change could come as soon as the next meeting and that the Fed would move to a neutral bias before any hiking bias.
items.score_note: He personally kept the easing-bias language and argued for waiting, while acknowledging the drift to neutral; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Jerome Powell
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, April 28-29 meeting: Q&A on Fed independence and his decision to stay on the Board
items.quote: I worry that these attacks are battering the institution
items.summary: Powell said the Administration's legal actions against the Fed are unprecedented, that independence is at risk, and that this is why he is staying on the Board; he noted the US Attorney closed the criminal investigation the previous Friday. He said he will not act as a shadow chair, took Warsh at his word on resisting political pressure, and said removing Reserve Bank presidents over policy views would be the beginning of the end of independent monetary policy. He said markets still price in Fed credibility on 2% inflation.
items.score_note: Independence and personnel; no rate-path content in these exchanges.

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts note after the April FOMC: Holding Pattern Continues Amid Competing Risks
items.quote: Our view remains that the next move will be a rate cut, but the timing is far from clear.
items.summary: Wilding read the three dissents against the easing bias as a hawkish lean but still expects the next move to be a cut, sees a high bar for hikes, and says a more persistent energy shock would delay cuts.
items.score_note: Next move still a cut but with no timing and no longer tied to 2026; high bar for hikes. Between -1 and 0, chose 0.
items.call: next move a cut, timing unclear; high bar for a hike

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post after Powell said he would stay on the Board (April FOMC day)
items.quote: Jerome “Too Late” Powell wants to stay at the Fed because he can’t get a job anywhere else
items.summary: Posted on the day of the April FOMC decision: Trump mocked Powell for wanting to stay at the Fed, saying nobody else wants him. No rate-path content.
items.score_note: Personal attack on Powell staying as governor; no policy-rate content.

items.speaker: Barclays economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note after the April 29 FOMC, quoted in Reuters round-up Apr 30
items.quote: skewed toward delayed rate cuts
items.summary: Barclays kept a baseline of one 25bp cut in September 2026 but said risks are skewed toward delayed rate cuts.
items.score_note: Baseline still one cut in 2026, with risk of delay; four days later it dropped the cut.
items.call: 2026: one 25bp cut in September; risks skewed toward delayed cuts

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks before the EXIM Annual Conference
items.quote: Economic security is national security, and thanks to President Trump’s leadership, the United States has never been more secure.
items.summary: Speech on export finance and economic security. No Fed or interest-rate content in the published text.
items.score_note: Official text with no statement on the Fed's policy rate; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Citi analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note after the April 29 FOMC, quoted by Reuters Apr 30
items.quote: cuts can be rapidly priced back in by markets if oil prices fall.
items.summary: Citi continued to project that cooler inflation and renewed loosening in labor markets will lead to rate reductions starting in September, and said cuts can be quickly priced back in if oil falls.
items.score_note: Keeps cuts from September 2026 after the hawkish April meeting.
items.call: cuts beginning September 2026 (maintained)

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Oval Office remarks at retirement accounts executive order signing (day after April FOMC)
items.quote: I think he's a negative force.
items.summary: Asked for his reaction to Powell staying on the Board of Governors, Trump said he does not care, that he predicted it because 'who's going to hire him', and that Powell is a negative force. He said the building cost angered him more than interest rates and praised Warsh.
items.score_note: Reaction to Powell staying as governor; no statement on what rates should do.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: FSOC Artificial Intelligence Series Roundtable on Cybersecurity and Risk Management, Washington: 'Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System'
items.quote: AI will become a force multiplier for the financial system, and in the broader U.S. economy.
items.summary: AI use in banks, supervisory approach and cyber risk. No monetary-policy or AI-financing content.
items.score_note: Supervision only.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Statement regarding her vote at the April 28-29 FOMC meeting
items.quote: I see this clear easing bias as no longer appropriate given the outlook.
items.summary: Hammack explained that she supported holding the funds rate steady but dissented because the statement's 'additional adjustments' language signals a pause in an easing cycle. She said inflation pressures are broad based, rising oil prices add to them, and unemployment has been near her estimate of full employment since last summer. She sees upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth and employment.
items.score_note: Wants the easing bias removed because of inflation risks; supports hold and does not call for a hike.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Minneapolis Fed essay 'Why I Dissented' (April 28-29 FOMC)
items.quote: the FOMC should offer a policy outlook that signals that the next rate change could be either a cut or a hike, depending on how the economy evolves.
items.summary: Kashkari says he backed the hold but dissented because the 'additional adjustments' phrase is forward guidance pointing to a cut. Before the Iran conflict he saw policy as mildly restrictive and pencilled in one more cut in 2026 (December and March SEP). Now he sees two scenarios: a quick reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, where the right response is an extended hold and then gradual easing; or an extended closure, where rate increases, potentially a series, could be warranted to defend inflation expectations even at a cost to jobs. Signalling two-way risk could tighten financial conditions somewhat today.
items.score_note: Drops his own cut bias and says a series of hikes could be warranted in the adverse scenario, but his benign-scenario path is still hold then ease: +1, not +2.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Statement from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on FOMC dissent (April 28-29 meeting)
items.quote: In light of the two-sided risks to monetary policy, I believed the FOMC should not give forward guidance implying a bias toward rate cuts at this time.
items.summary: Logan explains she backed the hold but dissented from the 'additional adjustments' language because it implies the next move is most likely a cut. She is increasingly concerned about how long inflation will take to return to 2 percent: underlying measures were running meaningfully above 2 percent even before the energy and commodity price increases, and the Middle East conflict could add further pressure, while the labor market is stable. She says the next rate change could plausibly be either an increase or a cut.
items.score_note: Explicitly removes the cut bias and puts a hike on the table as equally plausible, but does not call for a hike: +1.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Interview with Business Insider on American exceptionalism in markets
items.quote: Both the economy and markets carry significant 'baggage' from a period of relatively free and abundant money, driven by overly loose fiscal and monetary policies.
items.summary: El-Erian questions whether buy-the-dip behavior can continue at current valuations. He says the economy and markets carry baggage from an era of free and abundant money created by overly loose fiscal and monetary policy.
items.score_note: Backward-looking criticism of past loose policy; no statement on the current rate path.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Speech at The Villages, Florida
items.quote: He's too late with interest reductions.
items.summary: Trump said the administration brought mortgage rates down despite 'a hostile fed guy' who is too late with rate reductions, that rates would have been even lower otherwise, and that Warsh will be a fantastic Fed Chair.
items.score_note: 'Too late' criticism implying rates should be lower; no explicit demand.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Fox News 'The Journal Editorial Report' interview (Reuters via Yahoo Finance)
items.quote: We have got to get some assurance that we are going back to the 2% inflation target,
items.summary: Goolsbee calls the March PCE reading of 3.5 percent bad news and says the Fed must be cautious about cuts until inflation recedes. The composition of inflation does not look good, with services rising too. He says the split April decision shows the complications of forward guidance, and welcomes both Powell staying as governor and Warsh's arrival.

items.summary: Kashkari says everyone should be open-minded about where rates go: the longer the Strait of Hormuz is closed, the bigger the hit to US inflation, and in worse scenarios the Fed might have to go the other direction. The energy shock is by some measures already as big as after Russia invaded Ukraine; a CEO told him supply chains need six months to normalise even if the strait reopened today. The labor market is moving sideways at about 4.3 percent unemployment. He welcomes Warsh re-examining the dot plot and balance sheet, and calls the debt path unsustainable though not an immediate crisis.
items.score_note: Refuses to signal cuts and raises the possibility of hikes in worse scenarios, without calling for one. Time converted from the 9:40 a.m. CT slot in the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Cynosure Group Spring Symposium, New York, 'There Is No Try'
items.quote: Right now, the future is difficult to see, and the risks to both sides of our mandate have increased.
items.summary: Williams said PCE inflation rose to 3-1/2 percent in March, with tariffs and energy adding about a percentage point, and that he expects about 3 percent for 2026 before a return to 2 percent in 2027. He said the stance is well positioned to balance the risks and noted last week's FOMC hold at 3.50-3.75 percent. Risks to both sides of the mandate have increased and several plausible Middle East scenarios involve more severe supply dislocations. He told reporters he cannot give strong guidance for the next several meetings, sees nothing in the data that calls for a hike in the near term, fully supports the statement's language, and still expects cuts at some point once inflation falls, with the date pushed back.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate with risks higher on both sides; no directional lean.

He says the US faces several more years of above-target inflation even without the latest geopolitical shock.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem

He put the real funds rate at about 0.5% or lower, below the 1% long-run neutral, so policy is neutral or slightly accommodative. He sees plausible scenarios for holding for some time, for cutting, and for higher rates.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg News interview at the Boston Fed (Bloomberg story carried by The Boston Globe)
items.quote: I do think that there are scenarios in which it would be important to strongly consider a hike,
items.summary: Collins says she strongly supported the April hold but agreed with the dissenters that the statement should not presume the next move is a cut; she favors a more agnostic stance. Rates likely stay at mildly restrictive levels for longer with easing further down the road, yet a hike should be strongly considered in some scenarios, which is not her baseline. Her focus is the persistence of inflation; she sees it peaking slightly above 3.5 percent before easing to near 3 percent by year-end.
items.score_note: Sides with removing the easing bias and names hike scenarios; baseline is still a long hold.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview with Michael McKee (auto-generated transcript published with the Bloomberg Talks podcast clip, https://omny.fm/shows/bloomberg-talks/san-francisco-fed-president-mary-daly-talks-fed)
items.quote: the inflation expectations being well anchored is an important component of our ability to be patient
items.summary: Daly said the real signal from the April meeting is that everyone agreed to hold, and that the statement wording matters less than the FOMC's actions. It is too early to say the cutting cycle is over: if the conflict ends and oil falls, slightly restrictive policy keeps pushing inflation down. She does not see medium- or long-run inflation expectations drifting, sees little pass-through beyond energy surcharges, and said overreacting can damage the economy as much as underreacting.
items.score_note: Patient hold; plays down the easing-bias dissents and still leaves cuts possible, but gives no lean for the next move. Transcript is machine-generated; the Bloomberg text story (https://news.bgov.com/banking-law/feds-daly-says-statement-language-is-less-important-than-action) confirms the date and the statement-language quote.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)

items.quote: I think our statement should have a pretty neutral stance about whether the next move is down or up or just on hold for a really long period of time
items.summary: Hammack said her outlook is that rates will be on hold for quite some time and explained her April dissent: the statement should be neutral about whether the next move is down, up, or a long hold. She played down the discord implied by the 8-4 vote. Inflation has missed 2 percent for five years and the Iran conflict could make price pressures more persistent, while the job market is stable and inflation expectations are largely anchored.
items.score_note: Repeats the case for dropping the easing bias because inflation may be more persistent; her own desired stance is 'neutral', so this is +1 only in the sense of pushing back on cut guidance (consistent with the May 1 statement).

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Prepared remarks and panel, Hoover Institution Monetary Policy Conference 2026, Stanford (Chicago Fed posted text)
items.quote: The bigger the share of a productivity boom that is still on the way, the more likely rates will need to rise now.
items.summary: Goolsbee argues the rate implication of a productivity boom depends on whether it is expected. An unexpected surge lowers inflation and justifies lower rates, as in the 1990s; an anticipated AI-driven surge pulls spending forward through wealth effects and data-center investment, raising the natural rate and pushing the ideal policy rate higher. Waiting for actual overheating before acting makes the problem worse.
items.score_note: Analytical case that expected AI productivity gains point to higher, not lower, rates; no explicit call for a hike at a given meeting.

She hopes normalization can resume later this year, but can envision a scenario requiring some tightening, although that is not her most likely outlook. Policy is well positioned for now.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Money Marketeers of New York University, New York: 'Efficient and Effective Central Banking: Beyond the Balance Sheet'
items.quote: In sum, shrinking the Fed's balance sheet is the wrong goal, and reducing the resilience of the banking system is the wrong means.

He defended the ample-reserves regime and the current gradual bill purchases. The prepared text says nothing about the policy rate path. Reuters reported (paraphrase, no direct quote) that after the speech he said he had not decided what he wants the Fed to do at the next policy meeting.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview (Joe Kernen), morning after Warsh's Senate confirmation
items.quote: I firmly believe that nothing is more transient than a supply shock.
items.summary: After hot CPI and PPI prints, Bessent said the energy shock is transient, the Fed can look through it, and core inflation was falling before the Iran conflict. He said Warsh, confirmed the night before, will bring an open mind and that after one or two more hot inflation numbers there will be substantial disinflation.
items.score_note: Argues for looking through the energy shock (against hikes) and forecasts disinflation; does not call for an immediate cut.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City 2026 Future of Banking Conference (pre-recorded video): Opening Remarks
items.quote: Since the global financial crisis, the regulatory and supervisory approaches designed for large institutions have often been pushed down to community banks.
items.summary: Opening remarks on community banking and supervision. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Resignation letter to the President (released by the Board)
items.quote: it will run unemployment higher than it has to, fighting fake rather than real inflation
items.summary: Miran resigned effective upon or shortly before Kevin Warsh's swearing-in. He restated his case that lower immigration-driven population growth and deregulation are disinflationary and point to lower rates, that policy must be forward-looking, and that measurement biases (portfolio management fees, software quality adjustment) overstate inflation, which in effect lowers the Fed's inflation target. Only the first page of the scanned letter is machine-readable.
items.score_note: Restates the argument for lower rates in general terms; no explicit call for a cut at a specific meeting in the letter, so -1.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Speech "Leveraging Modern Payments Infrastructure in Community Banking", Future of Banking Conference, Kansas City, Mo.
items.quote: However, I see continued inflation as the most pressing risk to the economy.
items.summary: Mostly a payments and FedNow speech. In a short outlook passage Schmid said the economy is resilient and the labor market is functioning, but inflation is still too high and is the most pressing risk.
items.score_note: Only a brief outlook passage; inflation named as the dominant risk, no rate-path statement.

items.speaker: Seth Carpenter
items.role: Global Chief Economist and Head of Macro Research, Morgan Stanley
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast, mid-year global economic outlook (recorded Thursday May 14, 10am New York)
items.quote: We expect the Fed to now stay on hold all the way through 2026
items.summary: Carpenter said central banks have become less accommodative as inflation risks rose; Morgan Stanley expects the Fed on hold through 2026 and, if inflation does come down, two cuts in the first half of 2027.
items.score_note: Hold through 2026; next move still a cut in 2027.
items.call: on hold through 2026; two cuts in the first half of 2027 if inflation comes down

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at a Conference of Business Economists event, New York
items.quote: I don’t see there’s any reason at all to raise rates right now or lower rates right now
items.summary: Williams said monetary policy is in a good place and he sees no reason to raise or lower rates now, despite the Middle East energy shock and a jump in April CPI. Short-term inflation expectations have risen but longer-term ones are stable, the labor market is not adding to price pressures, and he sees no unusual second-round effects so far. He said the strong stock market reflects optimism about AI-related productivity growth.
items.score_note: Explicitly rules out both a hike and a cut for now; balanced hold on a day when markets were adding hike bets.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Statement with Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman on the Board vote naming Powell chair pro tempore
items.quote: Given that we do not support an unlimited timeframe for temporary chair designation, we cannot support this action.
items.summary: Bowman and Miran said they support Powell serving temporarily as chair until Warsh is sworn in but opposed an open-ended designation, arguing it should be limited to a week (up to a month) and then be subject to another Board vote or presidential action.
items.score_note: Board governance dispute; no monetary-policy content.

items.speaker: Stephen Miran
items.occasion: Exit interview with CNBC (published the day after his resignation)
items.quote: I still think it's important to frontload those cuts, because I still don't think that we should be exerting restraints in the labor market.
items.summary: Miran said that if he wrote a dot today he might have one fewer cut than in the March SEP, that is 75 bp rather than 100 bp of cuts this year, because of cuts already made and because the data has made him a little more concerned about inflation. He still wants those cuts front-loaded, says deregulation is disinflationary, and argues monetary policy cannot offset one-time price changes from tariffs or oil.
items.score_note: Still wants cuts and wants them front-loaded, although he trimmed the amount and acknowledged more inflation concern.

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.role: Chief Economic Adviser, Allianz; former PIMCO CEO
items.occasion: Weekly LinkedIn newsletter 'The Weekly Look at the Global Economy and Markets' (May 16 edition, after the Senate confirmed Warsh)
items.quote: He takes over a central bank that has allowed inflation to run above its 2% target for over five years
items.summary: El-Erian says Warsh inherits one of the hardest starts of any incoming chair: a new surge in inflation, risks to growth, a Fed with key policy errors behind it, political attack and an urgent need for operational reform. He expects Fed minutes and speeches to be parsed for recognition of growing policy dilemmas and escalating risks to financial stability.
items.score_note: Stresses a two-sided dilemma (inflation surge versus growth and financial-stability risks); criticism of past inflation overshoot is backward-looking.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: Fox News Sunday Morning Futures interview
items.quote: It’s just not possible, in my view, to cut interest rates when the two-year Treasury is almost 50 basis points higher than the Fed funds rate.
items.summary: Gundlach said the Fed cannot cut with the two-year yield almost 50bp above fed funds and that DoubleLine's models point to the next headline CPI starting with a four. He said stocks rally when the Fed does nothing about inflation, and that private credit always seems to need new investors.
items.score_note: Rules out cuts and says the Fed is not addressing inflation; no explicit hike call in the quoted text, so +1.
items.ai_quote: There’s something about the private credit market that seems that always needs new investors,

items.speaker: Aditya Bhave
items.role: Head of U.S. economics, Bank of America
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (May 14-19)
items.quote: It feels like if they are going to have their next move as a cut, it's more likely to be next year than this year,
items.summary: Bhave said both hikes and cuts are feasible, the base case is a hold and it is a close call between the other two; if the next move is a cut it is more likely in 2027 than 2026.
items.score_note: Base case hold with two-sided risk; explicitly says hikes are feasible but not the base case.
items.call: base case hold; hikes and cuts both feasible; a cut more likely in 2027 than 2026

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Atlanta Fed 2026 Financial Markets Conference, 'Navigating Uncertainty: Inflation, Labor Markets, and the Stance of Monetary Policy'
items.quote: Assuming the labor market remains in balance, rate cuts would only become appropriate once we have seen sustained progress on inflation.
items.summary: Paulson said inflation is too high (headline PCE 3.5 percent, core 3.2 percent in March) because of tariffs and the Middle East energy shock, but policy is mildly restrictive and appropriately positioned. Keeping rates steady lets the Fed assess risks; cuts need sustained inflation progress. She called it healthy that markets now price scenarios of an extended hold or further tightening, and said tightening might be needed if inflation expectations slip. She cited solid growth bolstered by AI infrastructure investment. In post-speech comments reported by MNI she said she did not join the April dissents because she saw no communication problem to solve, as markets had already priced out cuts.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate; rules out near-term cuts and accepts tightening scenarios, but describes policy as already mildly restrictive and well positioned. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks to reporters (as quoted by Axios; venue not stated)
items.quote: going to let him do what he wants to do
items.summary: Told that markets now see a rate hike this year as more likely than a cut and asked whether Warsh will deliver lower rates, Trump said he would let Warsh do what he wants, that he is very talented and will do a good job. Axios dates the exchange to Tuesday, May 19.
items.score_note: Declines to demand cuts or oppose a hike when asked directly; scored 0. A clear change from his earlier demands.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: EMERGE Financial Health 2026, Atlanta: 'Measuring Financial Health'
items.quote: Financial health begins with access, but it does not end there.
items.summary: Speech on measuring household financial health and the use of data and AI in consumer finance. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at JPMorgan's China summit, Shanghai (aired May 21 Shanghai time, late May 20 US Eastern)
items.quote: They could be much higher than they are today,
items.summary: Dimon told Bloomberg Television that interest rates could be much higher than today and that the world may have moved from a saving glut to not enough savings. The remark came as long Treasury yields hit multi-year highs and markets priced Fed hikes.
items.score_note: Forecast that rates can go much higher (savings shortage, deficits, inflation). It is about the level of rates broadly, not an explicit call for Fed hikes, so +1 rather than +2. Date: the interview video was posted about 23:18 ET on May 20; articles are dated May 21.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'Navigating Supply Shocks' (Richmond Fed posted text)
items.quote: it’s worth asking whether the cumulative impact of so many waves risks loosening the anchor
items.summary: Barkin explains the conventional case for looking through supply shocks but asks whether the Fed still has that luxury if shocks become more frequent. With inflation above 2 percent for over five years, he questions how secure the inflation expectations anchor is, while noting long-term measures remain anchored. The April hold made sense to buy time; rough seas could pressure either side of the mandate and the Fed is well positioned to respond.
items.score_note: Raises doubt about looking through supply shocks (hawkish tilt) but ends two-sided with no call to move; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0. Told Reuters he was not leaning toward one side of the mandate. Time from the Richmond Fed media advisory.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: WBEZ Chicago radio interview (quoted in a Reuters story via SRN News)
items.quote: we have a pretty significant inflation problem developing, but the job market has been mostly stable
items.summary: Goolsbee says a pretty significant inflation problem is developing while the job market is mostly stable, and that he is most attuned to the inflation side because progress stopped.
items.score_note: Inflation side singled out; no explicit rate call in the quoted text.

items.speaker: Nomura economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated May 21, reported by Invezz May 22
items.quote: But recent data and Fedspeak make us sceptical that he will be able to convince a majority of the FOMC to go along with rate cuts in 2026.
items.summary: Nomura dropped its forecast of two cuts later in 2026 and now expects no cuts this year, citing higher inflation readings and waning support among Fed officials for easing; it doubts Warsh can win an FOMC majority for cuts.
items.score_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); no hike call on the page.
items.call: no cuts in 2026 (previously two cuts later in the year)

items.speaker: Phillip Lee
items.role: Head of Real Money Rate Sales, Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs The Markets podcast (recorded May 21, 2026), transcript PDF
items.quote: the Fed will stay on hold for a bit
items.summary: Lee (a sales-desk view, not GS Research) said the base case has moved from when and how much the Fed cuts to how long it stays on hold; he finds the roughly 30bp of hikes priced into 2027 a bit tough, though inflation keeps the Fed on hold at best.
items.score_note: Base case is a hold of uncertain length; notes hikes are priced but does not forecast them.
items.firm: Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets (rates sales)
items.call: on hold for a while; base case shifted from cuts to how long the hold lasts

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks at the swearing-in of Kevin Warsh as Fed Chair, White House
items.quote: I want Kevin to be totally independent.
items.summary: Trump said he wants Warsh to be totally independent ('don't look at me'), that the Fed lost its way in recent years, and that Warsh understands a booming economy is a good thing: 'just let it boom', 'we want to stop inflation, but we don't want to stop greatness', and economic growth does not mean inflation. He also praised Warsh's plans to curtail forward guidance and reform data and models.
items.score_note: Professes independence but argues the Fed should not tighten against strong growth; between 0 and -1, kept at -1 because the explicit message is against stifling the boom.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Speech on tax cuts and the economy, Suffern, New York
items.quote: You get the interest rates down, everybody's going to be very, very happy.
items.summary: Hours after the swearing-in, Trump said he 'had a rotten head of the fed' and now has a great one in Warsh, that housing is all about interest rates, and that 'we're going to get the rates down' very quickly, helped by falling energy prices.
items.score_note: Wants rates down and links it to the new Fed Chair, but speaks mainly of mortgage rates and makes no direct demand for a cut.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Centre for Central Banking Guest Lecture, Frankfurt School of Finance and Management: 'Policy Risks Have Changed'
items.quote: I can no longer rule out rate hikes further down the road if inflation does not abate soon
items.summary: Hawkish pivot. Inflation is 'not headed in the right direction'; he would remove the easing-bias language so a cut is no more likely than a hike, and would not hesitate to hike if expectations become unanchored. But hikes in the near future are premature and policy is still restrictive, so his position is to hold. Needs better inflation or a significant labor deterioration before considering cuts. In Q&A (Reuters) he called talk of near-term cuts 'kind of crazy'.
items.score_note: Inflation risk now dominates, pushes back on cut talk and opens the door to hikes, but explicitly says a hike now is premature, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Remarks at swearing-in ceremony, White House East Room (first remarks as Chair)
items.quote: When we pursue those aims with wisdom and clarity, independence and resolve, inflation can be lower, growth stronger, real take-home pay higher
items.summary: After taking the oath, Warsh said the mandate is price stability and maximum employment and that he will lead a reform-oriented Fed, learning from past successes and mistakes and escaping static frameworks and models. He gave no indication of the rate path or balance-sheet plans.
items.score_note: Ceremonial remarks restating the mandate and reform agenda; no stance on rates or the balance sheet.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research: 'The Opportunities and Risks AI Presents for the Economy and Financial System'
items.quote: As such, I am prepared to raise rates, if the expected disinflation does not appear in a timely manner.
items.summary: Cook said inflation is clearly moving in the wrong direction (PCE 3.8 percent, core 3.3 percent in April) on the Iran-conflict energy shock and tariffs, with AI investment demand a possible further price shock ($1.5 trillion of announced data-center plans). She favors holding now, sees risks tilted toward higher inflation, expects disinflation to resume without hikes, but is prepared to raise rates if it does not, and to ease if the labor market deteriorates. On financial stability she flagged debt-financed AI capex: hyperscaler bond deals, smaller data-center developers borrowing from private debt funds and ABS markets, and software-related redemptions at BDCs.
items.score_note: Hold is the baseline but risks are tilted to inflation and she explicitly says she is prepared to raise rates; conditional, not a call for a hike soon, so +1 not +2.
items.ai_quote: the increasing use of leverage to finance investments in an emerging technology carries risk, and a sustained boom in debt issuance could eventually represent a financial-stability concern

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Panel at the Bank of Japan IMES Conference 2026, Tokyo (excerpt of planned remarks on Chicago Fed site)
items.quote: The bigger the hype about future productivity, the more rates may need to rise to prevent overheating.
items.summary: Goolsbee repeats that unexpected productivity gains call for lower rates, but expected gains act like a wealth increase today and can overheat the economy before the boom arrives, in which case rates would likely need to rise. He says to watch stock-market wealth effects on consumption and valuation-driven capital investment.
items.score_note: Leans tighter on overheating risk from expected AI productivity; conditional, no meeting-specific call.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Kaori Enjoji at the BOJ-IMES conference, Tokyo (CNBC article, published May 27 evening ET / May 28 Tokyo)
items.quote: I don't regret dissenting at that meeting, because the inflation has not proved as temporary as was advertised at the beginning,
items.summary: Goolsbee says energy inflation from the Iran war has lasted longer than futures implied and that he does not regret dissenting against the December 2025 cut. If inflation heads back to 2 percent, rates would ultimately settle well below today's level. He warns that AI-driven equity wealth and data-center investment can overheat the economy before productivity gains arrive.
items.score_note: Inflation persistence and overheating risk dominate; long-run lower settling point is conditional.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Bernstein Strategic Decisions Conference, New York
items.quote: there will be more inflation than people expect
items.summary: Dimon repeated his view that inflation will be higher than people expect and that asset prices, including JPMorgan's stock, are high. He said clients are gung ho and there is a lot of exuberance. eFinancialCareers reports he said the next crisis will not be systemic but credit losses will be much worse than people think.
items.score_note: Inflation-higher-than-expected forecast leans tighter; no explicit call on what the Fed should do in the quotes found. His reported comments on Warsh and the Fed balance sheet could not be verified as direct quotes.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: 2026 Bank of Japan-IMES Conference, Tokyo: 'Global Economic Developments and the U.S. Economy'
items.quote: I view risks around my inflation outlook as tilted to the upside
items.summary: Prepared text: inflation moved notably higher on energy costs, risks to his inflation outlook are tilted to the upside, labor-market risks somewhat to the downside; the current stance is well positioned and he has not prejudged June. Unlike his earlier 2026 speeches, the text no longer refers to the 'extent and timing of additional adjustments'. In the Q&A (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-28/feds-jefferson-says-he-focusing-inflation-us-labour-market-very) he said the labour market has been very resilient to the shock, so it seems appropriate that the focus be on returning inflation to 2%. Delivered the morning of May 28 Tokyo time (8:00 p.m. ET May 27 per the Board's speech listing).
items.score_note: The prepared text alone reads as a hold (0), but in the Q&A he said the focus should be on returning inflation to 2% given a resilient labour market, so inflation risk dominates: +1. No call for a hike. If only the official text is to count, use 0.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Kaori Enjoji at the BOJ-IMES Conference, Tokyo (7:55 a.m. JST May 28)
items.quote: the labor market is in decent shape right now, while inflation is simply much too high
items.summary: Kashkari says he is focusing heavily on inflation, which has been above 2 percent for more than five years, while the labor market is in decent shape. The longer inflation stays high the greater the risk expectations unanchor, which would force an even more aggressive response, so the Fed is better off doing what it needs to now. Energy and fertilizer drive the current surge. On AI he is bullish long term but says it is too soon to know the policy implications. He would welcome a rethink of the dot plot.
items.score_note: Inflation clearly dominates and he talks of doing what is needed to keep expectations anchored; no explicit call to hike now, so +1 not +2. US Eastern date and time derived from the JST slot in the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF; CNBC dates the article May 28.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.occasion: Opening remarks, 'Monetary policy and imbalances' panel, Bank of Japan IMES Conference, Tokyo
items.quote: Developing a richer toolkit in calm times would support a more nimble and targeted response to any future stresses.
items.summary: Logan says the Strait of Hormuz closure has cut global oil supply by nearly 13 million barrels a day and US producers can add little near term, so consumption may need to fall further. On Treasury markets she wants the FOMC to centrally clear its open market operations and to deepen tools that separate support for market functioning from monetary accommodation, flagging levered hedge-fund positions. She also discusses falling fertility and its effect on break-even job growth and the neutral rate. No statement on the near-term rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; remarks concern energy supply, Treasury market resilience tools and demographics.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: White House press briefing
items.quote: I had breakfast with Chair Powell 41 times, and I never did that
items.summary: Bessent said he had breakfast with new Fed Chair Warsh that morning. Asked whether he pressed Warsh to lower rates, he answered that he had breakfast with Powell 41 times and never did that.
items.score_note: Denies pressing the Fed Chair on rates; no view on the rate path.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Keynote "How Should the Promise of Higher Productivity Growth Change the Reality of Monetary Policy Today?" and Q&A (moderator Claire Jones, FT), Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland
items.quote: A better policy would be to lean against demand and inflation pressures today.
items.summary: Musalem argued it would be risky to rely on future AI-driven productivity gains to solve today's inflation problem. He noted the real policy rate is below the FOMC's long-run neutral, inflation is meaningfully above target and longer-term inflation expectations are creeping higher, and said holding policy rates too low could push long-term rates up. He called for a vigilant policy focused on restoring price stability and said he would adjust only if evidence shows productivity is pulling inflation to target. In the Q&A (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-28/fed-policymakers-eye-rate-hike-scenarios-ai-debate-deepens) he said "If we don't see disinflation in the next one to two quarters, that would concern me" and that risks have tilted more toward inflation than the labor market.
items.score_note: Inflation risk dominates and he says policy should lean against demand; says the real rate is below neutral. No explicit call for a hike in the prepared text, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg TV interview with Stephanie Flanders at the Reykjavik Economic Conference (auto-generated transcript published with the Bloomberg Talks podcast clip, https://omny.fm/shows/bloomberg-talks/feds-alberto-musalem-talks-fed-policy)
items.quote: There is a scenario where inflation remains high, there's no disinflation in the next quarter or two, and in that scenario, the economy will probably require a hike.
items.summary: Musalem said the real policy rate is around 0.5%, below the 1% the Committee sees as neutral, so policy is at or slightly below long-run neutral. He supported the April hold but thought the statement's easing bias was no longer consistent with the outlook and a balance of risks that has shifted toward inflation. Hike, cut or hold depends on the scenario: no disinflation in a quarter or two would probably require a hike; a material weakening in the second half would mean no hikes, maybe a cut. He said the probability of considering a rate increase "has to be greater than zero", and that shrinking the balance sheet is better done by reducing reserve demand than by cutting supply.
items.score_note: Open to hiking and wanted the easing bias removed, but frames a hike as scenario-dependent rather than needed now; +1 not +2. Transcript is machine-generated (names are garbled in places); the quoted sentence matches the Reuters account of the interview.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Speech at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland, 'Productivity Growth and the Challenge of Real-Time Policymaking'
items.quote: Second, an increase in trend productivity growth raises real interest rates in the long run.
items.summary: A research-style speech on how shifts in trend productivity growth affect the economy and real interest rates, using historical episodes and model simulations. Williams avoided speculating on AI and gave no comment on the current stance or near-term rate path. He concluded that structural shifts are hard to identify in real time, which favors robust policy approaches.
items.score_note: No statement on the current policy stance or rate path; conceptual discussion only.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Q&A at the Reykjavik Economic Conference, Iceland (after his productivity speech)
items.quote: Right now monetary policy for the Fed is, is right where we want it to be
items.summary: In the discussion after his prepared speech, Williams said policy is slightly restrictive and well positioned to keep learning about the conflict and the data before any decision. He expects PCE inflation close to 4 percent and core above 3 percent over the next few months, easing as tariff and energy effects fade. Asked about hikes, he said persistently high inflation or rising long-term expectations would call for somewhat higher real rates, but that is not where things are today (per Reuters and MNI accounts).
items.score_note: Policy 'right where we want it'; names the condition for a hike but says it is not the current outlook. Separate item from the prepared text because the speech itself has no stance.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: Remarks before the 2026 Reagan National Economic Forum: While America Slept
items.quote: Taken together, these efforts reflect the broader principle that President Trump has articulated clearly: economic security is national security.
items.summary: Speech setting out an economic security doctrine. No Fed, interest-rate or Treasury-yield content in the published prepared text (a fireside chat with Larry Kudlow followed; no transcript found).
items.score_note: Official text with no statement on the Fed's policy rate; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Reykjavik Economic Conference 2026, Central Bank of Iceland: 'A Framework for Practical Monetary Policy Decision Making'
items.quote: Reacting to temporarily elevated energy price inflation would add unwarranted policy restraint, weighing unnecessarily on economic activity and labor market conditions.
items.summary: Lays out her conditions for cutting, hiking and holding. Calls policy moderately restrictive, supported keeping the statement's language on additional adjustments (the easing bias), and says it is appropriate to look through energy-driven inflation. But the longer the conflict and high oil prices persist, the more likely she will shift her view of the balance of risks. April core PCE 3.3 percent; ex one-offs only a bit above 2 percent.
items.score_note: Pushes back on tightening and defends the easing bias, which fits 'opposes further hikes'; the conditional hawkish caveat keeps it from -2.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (FOMC non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria' interview with Maria Bartiromo (quotes via Reuters reprint)
items.quote: there's no urgency to make an adjustment
items.summary: Daly said policy is in a good place and there is no urgency to adjust rates; any future move may hinge on when the Iran war ends. If oil futures drift up because the conflict persists, that would change her inflation outlook. She is watching whether services firms start raising prices and so far sees little of that outside fuel-intensive industries.
items.score_note: Comfortable holding while several colleagues that week talked about hikes; conditional concern on oil only.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: CNBC interview at the Reagan National Economic Forum
items.quote: Interest rates are gravity to asset prices
items.summary: Dimon said the market is exuberant, that there is hype in some of it, and that very low credit spreads are a risk. He named inflation as his most immediate concern and said it can easily hit 4% this year. He said that if something goes wrong asset prices can come down because interest rates are gravity to asset prices.
items.score_note: Inflation (could hit 4%) is his top risk and he ties higher rates to asset-price risk; leans tighter. No explicit statement on what the Fed should do.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.occasion: Korea University Distinguished Speaker Seminar, Seoul, moderated by Jinill Kim (Bloomberg report)
items.quote: I think it’s premature for me to conclude we need to be raising rates right away
items.summary: Kashkari says it is too early to conclude rates must rise and he wants to keep watching the data and the Middle East conflict before making adjustments, while keeping all options open. Reuters' version of the same remark adds that the situation makes him pay further attention to the risk that inflation keeps climbing and expectations become unanchored.
items.score_note: Pushes back on an immediate hike but the stated risk is all on the inflation side and hikes stay on the table. Torn between 0 and +1; kept +1 because the lean is tighter and only the timing is deferred. Time converted from 3:00 p.m. local in the Minneapolis Fed schedule PDF.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks to a business group in New Jersey (as reported by Reuters)
items.quote: as well as scenarios where further tightening becomes necessary
items.summary: Paulson said monetary policy is well positioned given unacceptably high inflation and economic uncertainty, and that the Fed is ready to react. She repeated that it is healthy that markets have taken on board scenarios in which the funds rate stays unchanged for an extended period as well as scenarios where further tightening becomes necessary. No official text was posted on the Philadelphia Fed site.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid

He sees the labor market in balance; inflation is his primary concern in setting policy. In comments after the speech (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-29/feds-schmid-warns-against-viewing-oil-shock-transitory) he said "We're not very restrictive at this stage" and that officials need to start considering what tools they have to make policy a little more restrictive, including looking at the balance sheet again.
items.score_note: Inflation dominates; in Q&A he said policy is not very restrictive and tools to add restriction should be considered, depending on the oil shock. Open to tightening but no call for an immediate hike; +1 rather than +2.

Solomon said the AI investment cycle is widening capital needs into infrastructure, energy and data centers, that this multi-year cycle will keep financing and capital formation elevated, that leveraged finance activity is partly tied to the AI build, and that Goldman raised $31 billion in private credit in the quarter.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: JPMorgan Chase Q2 2026 earnings call (analyst Q&A)
items.quote: The only point we're always trying to make is when there's a credit cycle, and there will be a credit cycle, how will everybody perform?
items.summary: No comment on the Fed rate path. Dimon said the weakening in credit underwriting standards is 'a very mild one' but spread across several dimensions (revenue assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants, rollover/interest-rate risk) and concentrated in some players. He also said AI capex went from about $400 billion to $700 billion and that global deficits of 4.5-5% are competing for the same capital.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Semiannual Monetary Policy Report, House Financial Services Committee
items.quote: The members of our Committee have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation.
items.summary: Prepared testimony: the June hold at 3.50-3.75% was focused on restoring price stability; activity is solid, the labor market broadly stable, and AI-driven business investment is the most striking feature of the economy. He described the five task forces, including a review of the ample-reserves regime. In Q&A (per Semafor, CNN and Bloomberg coverage) he said the soft June CPI did not mean 'mission accomplished', gave no rate signal, and said any balance-sheet change would be previewed well in advance.
items.score_note: Inflation is the dominant concern and he rejects reading the June CPI as mission accomplished; no explicit hike signal.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'Economic Outlook', The Exchequer Club of Washington D.C.
items.quote: If we do not see signs of disinflation soon, I am prepared to act.
items.summary: Cook says inflation is 'simply too high' (PCE 3.7% in the 12 months through June) and that the balance of risks has shifted to inflation, citing the Middle East energy shock and AI-infrastructure capital spending as two unanticipated price shocks. She supported the June hold to give 'a bit more time' but sees risks 'strongly weighted toward higher inflation' and declines to predict the path.
items.score_note: Conditional readiness to hike while still endorsing the June hold: leans tighter, not an explicit call for a hike. AI is cited as a demand and price shock (capex), not as a financing or credit risk, so ai_financing is not tagged ('other' = AI capex demand).

items.quote: You never want to make too much hay out of any one number,
items.summary: After June CPI eased to 3.5%, Goolsbee cautions against reading too much into one print following months of inflation going the wrong way, and notes energy costs work through the economy. He welcomes Warsh's plan to end forward guidance and voices optimism about Warsh as chair.
items.score_note: Data-dependent, no lean expressed.

items.summary: Rieder argued the funds rate is powerful but uneven: it pressures borrowers, housing and lower-income consumers while the companies behind the AI capex cycle are far less rate-sensitive, and the categories driving inflation are largely rate-insensitive. He also called the new Fed's hawkish stance very understandable given above-target inflation.
