items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Semiannual Monetary Policy Report, Senate Banking Committee (Q&A)
items.quote: these are all imperfect measures of the state of underlying inflation
items.summary: AP report of the Senate hearing (prepared remarks identical to the House text on the Fed site). Warsh played down the cooler June inflation data as imperfect measures of underlying inflation, said a one-time price change from AI infrastructure investment is not necessarily inflationary because of a supply response, deferred the temporary-versus-permanent question to the task forces, and said he was chosen as 'an independent guy'. No rate signal.
items.score_note: Refuses to take comfort from better inflation prints and repeats the no-tolerance line, but also says AI-related price rises need not be inflationary; +1 for consistency with the identical prepared text the day before.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the Partnership for New York City, 'Stability of Thy Times'
items.quote: The current stance of monetary policy is well positioned to do that.
items.summary: Williams said inflation at about 4% is unquestionably too high, driven by tariffs, Middle East energy disruptions and AI-related demand, but he sees reasons it has peaked. He backed the mid-June hold, forecast inflation near 3.25% by year-end and 2% in 2028, and said his views will follow the totality of the data.
items.score_note: Explicitly says the current stance is well positioned after the June hold; data dependent with no stated lean.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR), Stanford University: 'Navigating Economic Shocks: A Monetary Policymaker's Perspective'
items.quote: I believe that it could be appropriate to reconsider our current policy stance to ensure we fulfill our commitment to deliver price stability
items.summary: Says the June hold at 3.50-3.75% should let inflation resume falling and policy is 'well positioned', but if actual inflation does not start to cool soon it could be appropriate to reconsider the stance. Warns the quick succession of energy, tariff and AI shocks raises the risk that inflation becomes entrenched. Notes AI could raise r*, making a given funds rate more accommodative.
items.score_note: Base case is hold, but he explicitly opens the door to tightening if inflation does not cool soon and frames the main risk as entrenched inflation; conditional, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks on inflation, employment and monetary policy, Dallas Fed Houston Branch (before moderated conversation)
items.quote: I currently believe modestly higher interest rates would better balance the outlook and risks for the FOMC’s maximum employment and price stability goals.
items.summary: Logan said inflation is heading toward the mid-2s, not 2 percent, the labor market is solid, and labor, consumption and financial data show policy is not restraining the economy. She said modestly higher rates are warranted now ('Better modest restriction now than severe restriction later'), with inflation risks to the upside from energy and the AI investment surge. Delivered about a week and a half before the July FOMC.
items.score_note: Explicitly says higher rates would be better now, ahead of the July meeting where she dissented for a hike. [AI link: capex demand only] she cites AI investment as an upside inflation risk, not a credit or funding issue.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, July 28-29 meeting: opening statement
items.quote: And where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act.
items.summary: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% by 9-3 (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan preferred +25bp). Warsh said there is 'no soft inflation target', that five-plus years of above-target inflation cannot be cured in nine weeks or by one month of price declines, and that nominal and real Treasury yields rose materially over the intermeeting period as markets reacted to data without Fed guidance. He listed four questions debated, including whether AI capex-driven chip price increases signal broader inflation and how much accommodation the balance sheet provides.
items.score_note: Hold, but the framing is entirely about inflation and readiness to act; no commitment to a hike.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, July 28-29 meeting: Q&A on why no hike and the reaction function
items.quote: I wouldn’t characterize what we did as anything like a pause.
items.summary: Warsh rejected the word 'pause', called it a period of 'watchful thinking, not watchful waiting', and said if inflation stays elevated through the forecast period interest rates 'could well be part of that solution'. He described his reaction function: with the labor market near equilibrium, a central banker who sees underlying inflation moving higher is more inclined to tighten. He said the cool June CPI mattered 'not much' to the decision.
items.score_note: Openly keeps a hike on the table and denies the hold is a pause, but stops short of saying a hike is needed.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, July 28-29 meeting: Q&A on balance sheet and transmission
items.quote: The balance sheet probably works through some other channels
items.summary: On transmission, Warsh said rates work through lending, credit, confidence and FX channels while the balance sheet works through signaling and portfolio balance, and that the Committee is keeping abreast of all tools. In the opening statement he framed the open question as how much accommodation the balance sheet is providing if rates are the primary instrument. No balance-sheet action was signaled; the statement kept the ample-reserves policy.
items.score_note: Hints the balance sheet is adding accommodation, but no action or timing; scored neutral.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, July 28-29 meeting: Q&A on market-led tightening
items.quote: The markets have done quite a bit.
items.summary: Asked why rates should not be higher with the funds rate about 75bp below the two-year yield, Warsh said rates are already higher than 42 days earlier because markets tightened both nominal and real yields on their own, that the Fed observes this without taking dictation, and that tighter financial conditions gave the Committee some comfort. He said the Fed will not be constrained by market pricing of a September hike.
items.score_note: Uses market-led tightening to explain holding; neither endorses nor pushes back on hike pricing.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)

items.quote: If instead underlying inflation remains stubbornly elevated, the passage of time without progress would itself signal that more restrictive policy is needed.

Underlying inflation is 2.4-2.8% and has edged down only modestly; ready credit access is supporting robust AI investment and price pressure. She will judge by how evidence accumulates.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview on CNBC 'Squawk Box' with Steve Liesman
items.quote: If we don't see that progress, then we have to be open to recalibrating monetary policy
items.summary: Paulson said the July hold was not a close call for her: policy needs to be mildly restrictive and she thinks it has been. Underlying inflation is 2.4-2.8% and she needs to see progress from here; without it the Fed must be open to recalibrating, which could mean higher rates or the same rates for longer. She said she has an open mind on Chair Warsh's proposal to change the meeting schedule.
items.score_note: Hold was clear-cut and policy judged mildly restrictive; tightening is conditional. Scored one notch nearer zero than her same-day essay, which gives more weight to the not-restrictive-enough scenario.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: The Diary of a CEO podcast with Steven Bartlett
items.quote: There’s almost nothing that’s easier to produce than stock
items.summary: Dalio agreed that markets show classic signs of a bubble and, per Fortune's paraphrase, named two forces that typically prick one: rising interest rates that make debt costlier to service and a surge in stock issuance. No statement about what the Fed will or should do.
items.score_note: Bubble and issuance commentary only. Podcast recording date not given on the page, so the article date is used.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Kansas City Fed Agricultural Economic Summit, Omaha, Nebraska: "Agriculture, the Economy, and the Kansas City Fed"
items.quote: As such, I believe that bringing inflation down to the Fed’s 2 percent objective will require tighter policy.
items.summary: Speaking the week after the July FOMC, Schmid said inflation is too high, the labor market is in balance and growth is resilient. He does not see the current policy stance as restrictive and said getting inflation to 2 percent will require tighter policy. He also said the Fed should respond to aggregate inflation even when it comes from relative price rises tied to AI infrastructure demand.
items.score_note: Says policy is not restrictive and that tighter policy will be required: an explicit call for rate increases (made before the September hike).

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Q&A after the Agricultural Economic Summit speech, Omaha (same event as the 2026-08-04 speech item; split out for the AI-financing remarks)
items.quote: is that circle getting too leveraged?
items.summary: Reuters (Aug 6) reports that in his Tuesday appearance Schmid asked whether the way the AI industry finances itself is making it 'another too big to fail', and whether the circle of contractual commitments among data centers, energy providers and communities is getting too leveraged. This is a financial-stability remark, not a statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content in these remarks; the rate stance for this occasion is scored in the speech item of the same date.
items.ai_quote: is this industry becoming another too big to fail?

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'Outlook for the U.S. and Alaskan Economies', Anchorage Economic Development Corporation 2026 Economic Luncheon, Anchorage, Alaska
items.quote: Still, I would support an increase, if it becomes necessary to bring inflation down.
items.summary: Cook says she is 'prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary' but that a hike may not be needed because three disinflationary forces are in play (tariff effects fading, oil expected lower, AI-related goods pressure easing). She explains her July vote to hold on that basis, and warns that after five years above target 'we do not have that luxury' of waiting long.
items.score_note: Explicitly open to a hike but conditional, and she says it may not be needed: +1 rather than +2. AI again cited as a demand and price shock, not financing ('other' = AI capex demand).

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: ESRI International Conference, Tokyo: keynote on economic shocks and monetary policy
items.quote: I was completely supportive of the decision to hold rates in July.
items.summary: Daly laid out two scenarios: a modal one where tariff, energy and AI shocks fade and mildly restrictive policy is enough, and a second where overlapping shocks compound and inflation gains momentum, which would need a more aggressive recalibration. She said the two are much closer in probability than before, backed the July hold to gather information before September, and said the Fed must be very prepared to act if the second scenario emerges. Time is 5:35 p.m. PT on the SF Fed page.
items.score_note: Supports the hold with the benign scenario still modal, but risk is one-sided toward tightening; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Q&A at the ESRI International Conference, Tokyo (same event as the 2026-08-05 keynote item; split out for the AI-financing remarks)
items.quote: not of the things that happened in the financial crisis, but what could go wrong that would tip this over
items.summary: Reuters (Aug 6) reports Daly said on Wednesday that judging only by the growth rate and amount of AI investment one could call it 'very worrisome', though many commitments are still announcements rather than built assets. She said rising borrowing to fund the buildout could become an issue and the Fed should build a dashboard of what could go wrong. Not a statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; the rate stance for this occasion is scored in the keynote item of the same date.
items.ai_quote: not of the things that happened in the financial crisis, but what could go wrong that would tip this over

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: CNBC 'Closing Bell: Overtime' interview with Leslie Picker, Los Angeles
items.quote: If there's inflation, they will have to fight it.
items.summary: Asked whether the long-end selloff is a credibility test for the Fed, Dimon said the real question is whether there is inflation, noted it has been over 3% for five years, and said the Fed will have to fight it if it persists. He backed Chair Warsh's review of inflation measurement and the balance sheet and dismissed complaints about the end of forward guidance. On credit he said market leverage (margin, prime broker, hedge fund) is high but not systemic, he is not worried about private credit systemically, and hyperscaler data-center spending will 'ultimately play out and pay out' though individual data-center projects need deal-by-deal analysis.
items.score_note: Conditional statement that the Fed will have to fight inflation, paired with his view that the odds favor higher inflation and rates. Leans tighter but no call for an immediate hike.
items.ai_quote: So, in my own view, and I may be wrong, it'll ultimately play out and pay out.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box live interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin from Aspen, Colorado
items.quote: I would rather get going now in small steps than wait till later, then we have a really entrenched inflation problem and have to raise rates aggressively.
items.summary: Kashkari said strong earnings, consumers and the labor market give no evidence that policy is restrictive, so now is the time to start slowly moving rates up. He said he is not calling for a dramatic increase, did not commit to September, and said Warsh told him to do what he thinks is right.
items.score_note: Explicitly wants to begin raising rates now in small steps, one week after dissenting for a hike.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Centro de Debate de Políticas Públicas (CDPP), São Paulo, Brazil: "Monetary Policy and Productivity: Promoting Growth vs. Stabilizing Prices"
items.quote: it is crucial that monetary policy put a meaningful restraint on underlying inflation
items.summary: Musalem said the US economy is resilient, the labor market has stabilized, and inflation is well above 2% with risks tilted toward it staying above target for a year or more. He argued policy must restrain underlying inflation now rather than tolerate higher inflation in the hope of AI-driven productivity gains later. In the Q&A, per Reuters (kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-08-07/feds-musalem-says-central-bank-should-have-hiked-rates-last-meeting), he said he expressed a preference at the July meeting to raise the funds rate by 25 basis points.
items.score_note: The prepared text alone reads +1; the Q&A reported by Reuters (page opened) has him saying he preferred a 25bp hike at the July meeting, so +2 for the occasion.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Punchbowl News interview, released August 7
items.quote: It's up to him a little bit, but not completely.
items.summary: Trump said he would not criticize Warsh over rate decisions, which are 'not totally up to' the chair because 'He's got a board that's very political'. He said he wants to go back to the days when strong data meant lower rates and that the US should have the world's lowest borrowing costs.
items.score_note: Restates the wish for much lower rates but pledges not to criticize Warsh and makes no specific demand; interview date not stated, release date used.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview with Yahoo Finance
items.quote: I think that now is the time for us to start acting, to start bringing more restraint into policy
items.summary: Hammack said one 25bp move probably does not do much, so some number of increases is likely needed, though she would not prejudge how many. She said the 3.50-3.75% range is not meaningfully restricting the economy, businesses report no restraint on investment, and the weak July jobs report did not change her view because unemployment at 4.1% is near full employment.
items.score_note: Explicit call to start raising rates now and for more than one hike.

items.speaker: Cheryl Venable
items.role: Interim President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta since March 2026 (non-voter in 2026; Atlanta votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Atlanta Fed quarterly president's essay: Chocolate Factories, Small Towns, and Monetary Policy
items.quote: Will inflation then resume its moderation to 2 percent absent a change in monetary policy?
items.summary: Venable says inflation is too high and has exceeded 2 percent for more than five years, with the outlook hinging on the Middle East conflict and oil. She calls the labor market broadly stable and says there are nuanced risks on both sides of the mandate. She gives no view on whether a hike is needed.
items.score_note: Frames the hike question as open and risks as two-sided; no stated lean.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Financial Times interview (Reuters summary via Kitco)
items.quote: do see the possibility that economic conditions in the coming months will require tighter
items.summary: Collins tells the FT she would be open to backing a rate increase as soon as September if the data call for it, with lower-income households struggling as the Iran war worsens cost-of-living strains. A separate recap says she supported the July hold and calls policy mildly restrictive.
items.score_note: Conditional readiness to hike as soon as September. Quote is the clean middle of the sentence; the full Reuters sentence ends 'policy, and I would be prepared to raise rates in that context'.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'The Mysterious U.S. Economy', Greenville Chamber of Commerce, Greenville, S.C.
items.quote: Will the Fed need to raise rates further, or is inflation already on a path down to target?
items.summary: Barkin lays out both cases: inflation may fade as tariff, oil and data-center shocks pass and policy is still restrictive, or it may be more embedded and need help from weaker demand or from the Fed. He says the FOMC is committed to 2 percent and has the tools, and declines to prejudge the next move. Reuters reports he added that headlines about inflation coming down help keep expectations in check.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided and refuses to prejudge the path.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Fox News 'Special Report' interview with Bret Baier (Reuters story carried by The Star)
items.quote: The good news is the new information that's been coming in has been a little better.
items.summary: Goolsbee says inflation in the 3% range is too high but the last couple of readings have been a little better, and he is hopeful that as tariff and oil effects fade the economy returns to the 'golden path' toward 2%. He describes a stable economy where the Fed is mostly watching inflation.
items.score_note: Watching inflation with mild optimism; no call for a move either way.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the Dayton Area Chamber of Commerce, Ohio
items.quote: I think that we need to act now because I think we need to bring inflation back down to that 2% objective faster
items.summary: Hammack reiterated that the Fed should raise rates now. She said businesses are excited to borrow and invest, so policy needs some restraint to get inflation from above 3% to 2%, and that two months of better inflation data do not give her confidence. She questioned whether taking another three or four years to reach 2% is acceptable. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Explicit call to act now.

items.speaker: Jan Hatzius
items.occasion: Client note published Sunday 16 August, reported by Bloomberg (carried by The Star)
items.quote: We still think market pricing for the funds rate is too hawkish.
items.summary: Hatzius wrote that a September hike had become 'very unlikely' after softer retail sales, jobs and inflation data, and that under Goldman's baseline the inflation news is more likely to improve than deteriorate.
items.score_note: Explicit pushback against the hikes priced by the market; base case remains a hold.
items.call: September hike 'very unlikely'; hold; market pricing too hawkish

items.speaker: Donald Trump

items.quote: The problem is he has a board, and it's a political board
items.summary: Trump renewed his push for lower rates, saying Warsh's problem is a 'political board' of appointees of Obama, Biden and himself who 'vote to raise interest rates', and questioned whether they do so for policy or politics. He complained that good economic numbers now make things worse for interest rates.
items.score_note: Opposes the board's hiking bias and wants lower rates, without an explicit demand for an immediate cut in the quoted remarks.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk on the Street interview with Sara Eisen, day after Treasury doubled long-end buyback sizes
items.quote: I think that the Treasury and the Fed would work together if there was any change in the balance sheet
items.summary: Bessent said the larger long-end buybacks signal that yields 'don't reflect the underlying fundamentals' and that buybacks could exceed $4 billion per issue. He said a possible Fed hike 'has nothing to do' with the buyback decision, that Treasury would coordinate with any Fed balance-sheet run-off, that core inflation is down with no second-round effects, and that heavy AI-related corporate issuance is competing for capital.
items.score_note: Declines to address the rate path; dovish inflation narrative and yield-capping intent noted but no stance on what the Fed should do, so 0 rather than -1.
items.ai_quote: It is causing a short-term competition for capital

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television "Surveillance" interview
items.quote: seem to be signaling to us that they understand our reaction function
items.summary: Daly said policy is in a good place and that she strongly supported the July hold. She sees no evidence of an urgent need for preemptive cuts or hikes, does not see Fed credibility at risk despite higher long-term yields, and would not prejudge how the Treasury's debt-management moves affect policy. The quoted clause refers to short-dated bonds pricing some Fed tightening.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate, no urgency in either direction.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem

He confirmed he argued for a hike in July but said he keeps an open mind for the September 15-16 meeting. Full sentence in the Reuters text: 'More gradual interest rate increases are preferable, better, less disruptive than later, potentially larger, potentially more abrupt increases.' (the page has invisible characters inside it, so the quote field holds a clean fragment). The St. Louis Fed's own page for this interview is a summary without quotes.
items.score_note: Leans clearly to tightening but explicitly did not prejudge September; between +1 and +2, chose +1.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio

His fix needs spending cuts, higher tax revenue and lower interest rates at the same time, but he warned against the Fed forcing rates down. He advised being underweight bonds and holding gold.
items.score_note: He says lower rates are part of the solution but that the Fed must not push them down artificially; the two points offset, so 0. LinkedIn original not opened; quotes from CNBC.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: CBS Face the Nation interview with Margaret Brennan
items.quote: Eventually, we're going to have to do more.
items.summary: Kashkari said the Treasury market is functioning despite the rise in yields (10-year at 4.7 percent), which lets the Fed focus on the funds rate as its primary tool. He would not prejudge September but said he is not confident inflation is heading back to target soon, citing the Iran conflict and the Canada tariff standoff.
items.score_note: Leans toward more tightening but says 'I'm not sure if we're there yet' and declines to prejudge September, so +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.role: Chairman and CEO, Duquesne Family Office

The piece is aimed at Treasury and fiscal policy; the quoted passages do not say what the Fed should do with the policy rate.
items.score_note: Statement about Treasury buybacks and long yields, no usable view on the Fed rate path in the text read. WSJ original is paywalled; quotes taken from CNBC's report.

items.summary: Asked about US public debt above $40 trillion, Barkin warns of an eventual reckoning if investors stop buying. On policy, the recap says he repeated his case for holding rates steady given evidence inflation is declining, while acknowledging a hike may be needed if price pressures become embedded.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)

items.quote: Should evidence of sustained inflation progress not materialize, I believe it will be appropriate to tighten policy soon to ensure we deliver price stability in a reasonable time frame.
items.summary: Collins was comfortable with the July hold and calls policy mildly restrictive, with a baseline of gradual disinflation. But keeping the range unchanged requires continued evidence that inflation is coming down; otherwise she would favor tightening soon. She sees upside inflation risks from supply shocks and stronger activity, noting the AI build-out is lifting core goods prices.
items.score_note: Conditional but explicit readiness to tighten soon; inflation is her stated focus.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)

items.quote: My modal scenario does continue to have that gradual disinflation,
items.summary: Collins calls the July PCE report mixed: the headline was higher than expected but driven by a patchwork of items such as portfolio management fees, with market-priced components near 2%. Her modal outlook remains gradual disinflation under a slightly restrictive rate, though she is ready to raise rates if it does not materialize. She is watching the rise in bond yields.
items.score_note: Says the data alone should not push the Fed toward a hike while keeping the conditional hike option; chose 0 over +1.

items.speaker: Beth Hammack
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Interview on Fox Business Network during Jackson Hole week
items.quote: My forecast is that inflation is going to end this year around 3%

Reuters reported that she reiterated her belief that a rate hike is needed. Other outlets attribute similar same-week remarks to CNBC and Bloomberg interviews (see unverified).
items.score_note: The direct quote is a forecast, but Reuters reports in the same piece that she reiterated a rate hike is needed, consistent with her dissent and her August 10 and 13 remarks.

items.role: Chief Investment Officer of Global Fixed Income, BlackRock
items.occasion: BlackRock CIO Perspective, 'AI, the Fed and Market Opportunities'

items.summary: Rieder said inflation is moderating, consumer credit stress is concentrated among weaker borrowers, and higher rates hurt those borrowers while having limited influence on the AI-driven corporate investment cycle. He wrote that the AI build-out is becoming a test of financing and cash-flow durability, with AI-related IG issuance meeting weaker sponsorship.
items.score_note: Argues for patience; leans against hikes on distributional grounds but gives no directional call. Torn between 0 and -1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid

items.occasion: CNBC "Squawk Box" interview from the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium
items.quote: I don't know what we're restricting currently with the rate policy that we're at today
items.summary: Schmid said inflation is still stubborn and sticky and that he does not see what the current policy rate (3.50% to 3.75% at the time) is restricting. He stopped short of endorsing a hike at the September 15-16 meeting, saying he needs a little more information on the demand side.
items.score_note: Policy may not be restrictive enough and inflation dominates, but he explicitly withheld a September hike call.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at Jackson Hole
items.quote: For me I think it might be accommodative on the short end
items.summary: In a separate Jackson Hole interview Schmid told Bloomberg TV that policy might be accommodative at the short end and added 'So we've got work to do'. Bloomberg groups him with officials who say rates are not restraining the economy.
items.score_note: Says policy may be accommodative and there is work to do; no explicit hike call in the quoted words.

items.speaker: Barclays economists (unnamed in report)
items.occasion: Client note on Friday 28 August after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, reported by Reuters (carried by The Star)
items.quote: unfavorable base effects will work against progress by those metrics through year-end.
items.summary: Barclays switched from no change through year-end to 25bp hikes in September and December, calling Warsh's speech notably hawkish and an implicit case for further tightening. It still expects monthly inflation readings to be much softer than the longer-horizon measures Warsh emphasised.
items.score_note: Moves from hold to two hikes starting at the next meeting.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium speech, 'In Our Time'
items.quote: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed.
items.summary: Warsh said the economy has strengthened, the labor market is consistent with full employment, and PCE inflation is 3.7% (six-month 4.1%), so the Fed's predominant focus should be prices. He said he would be hard pressed to call broad financial conditions restrictive (tight credit spreads, easy bank lending standards, strong issuance) and that summer inflation readings do not show underlying improvement. He set the standard quoted here, adding 'Otherwise, we have work to do', and said he is 'committed to a discipline, not to a decision'. He also argued against routine forward guidance and said unconventional tools should be used sparingly.
items.score_note: Sets a conditional bar that points to tightening and says conditions are not restrictive, but explicitly declines to commit to a decision.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk on the Street interview with Sara Eisen from the G20 finance ministers meeting, Asheville
items.quote: traditionally, you don't raise until a supply shock unless you see second or third order effects
items.summary: Three days after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, Bessent refused to speculate on a September hike but said the economy has seen a supply shock, that one does not traditionally raise rates into one absent second-round effects, and that core inflation remains very restrained. He defended the buyback increase as slowing a one-way move in yields and dismissed the idea that AI build-out financing is crowding out other borrowers.
items.score_note: Lays out the case against hiking into a supply shock without explicitly telling the Fed to hold.
items.ai_quote: we keep hearing about, oh, this AI build out, the financing for that is crowding, is creating a crowding problem

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Sara Eisen at the G20 finance meeting, Asheville
items.quote: I won't speculate on Fed rate decisions.
items.summary: Asked whether raising rates now would be right, Solomon declined to speculate, saying only that Chair Warsh is focused on inflation while data-dependent and that policy rates and the long-term premium follow different dynamics. He said a 5% long yield is not a calamity and reflects fundamentals. On debt-financed AI capex he said it bears monitoring but he sees no systemic risk now because most issuance comes from large companies with strong cash flow, though some areas will overextend and need recalibration.
items.score_note: He explicitly declines to give a view on the Fed. Goldman's page is dated Sept 3 and states the interview was recorded Aug 31.
items.ai_quote: Over time, it is something to monitor: the total size of the investment and how much of it is debt-financed.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Oval Office remarks to reporters, first comments after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech
items.quote: I think our interest rates are too high.
items.summary: Trump said he has a lot of respect for Warsh and 'he'll do what he has to do' on possible hikes, while saying US interest rates are too high. CNN reported that in the same Monday Oval Office session he called talk of raising rates 'ridiculous' because growth does not cause inflation.
items.score_note: Says rates are too high but gives Warsh a pass on hiking; between -1 and -2, the nearer-to-zero level is used.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: G20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting, Asheville: opening plenary remarks
items.quote: If I were to try to characterize this moment, it would be one of a global investment surge
items.summary: Reuters report of rare public remarks by a Fed chair at a G20 plenary. Warsh said the old 'global savings glut' has given way to a global investment surge, that secular stagnation no longer applies, and that the key question is underlying growth potential and productivity. No comment on the rate path in the quoted remarks.
items.score_note: Growth and productivity framing only; no usable rate-path content.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Unlocking Opportunities for Workers and Entrepreneurs with a Criminal Record', Second-Chance Lending Forum, Washington, D.C.
items.quote: However, if inflation appears not to be moderating sufficiently, then I think we should act decisively to raise rates.
items.summary: In a short outlook passage Barr says inflation 'remains too high' after shocks from tariffs, the Middle East conflict and the rapid AI buildout, with a risk of broader price pressures. Ahead of the September FOMC he sets a two-way condition: more time if data show inflation moderating toward 2 percent, a decisive hike if not.
items.score_note: Conditional two-way statement before the September meeting (more time vs. decisive hike): open to hiking with inflation risk dominating, not an unconditional call. AI buildout cited as a price shock, not financing ('other').

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Fortune interview with Eleanor Pringle (after Jackson Hole)
items.quote: so it makes sense to wait and see if this has legs, or is just a blip.
items.summary: Goolsbee says he was comfortable holding rates in July because recent inflation data had improved, and wants to see whether that lasts. He agrees with Warsh that inflation is the challenge, says the real economy is stable and inching toward overheating, and warns the data-center boom is close to turning from sector rebalancing into aggregate overheating.
items.score_note: Wait-and-see on the hold, with overheating concern; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Interview on CNBC
items.quote: depend on the data and depend on some of the risks to achieve our goals
items.summary: Ahead of the September 15-16 meeting, Williams said the decision will depend on the data and the risks, and that there is no clear science saying policy is in the right position. He attributed the rise in long-term yields to a strong economy fueled by investment in AI and data centers rather than inflation fears, and called recent inflation data encouraging but not yet enough. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Undecided and data dependent two weeks before the September hike; no stated lean.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Reuters NEXT Newsmaker Interview, Washington: prepared opening remarks 'The Economic Outlook and Some Comments on My Policy Communication'
items.quote: If there is continued progress toward our 2 percent goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level.
items.summary: Says recent data finally show signs of disinflation (3-month core PCE down from 4.76% in February to 3.05% in July) and he is inclined to hold on September 15-16 if August inflation confirms it; if inflation comes in hot he would consider a hike, since policy is 'only slightly restricting' demand. Describes this as his reaction function, not forward guidance.
items.score_note: Explicitly conditional both ways with the base case a hold; torn between 0 and +1 (he says it would not take much to move him to hike), chose the level nearer 0. Markets cut September hike odds after the remarks.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Reuters NEXT Newsmaker Interview, Washington: moderated Q&A with Reuters (same event as the prepared remarks)
items.quote: Give disinflation a chance
items.summary: In the Q&A he urged patience: wait and see whether the next inflation report extends the improvement rather than hike prematurely, though not 'until next year'. AP separately quotes him from the same Reuters interview: willing to 'sit and wait and be patient', but if inflation reverses 'it's time to pull the trigger and hike rates' (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/fed-governor-waller-muddies-outlook-on-possible-rate-hike-later-this-month).
items.score_note: Same occasion as the prepared remarks (Q&A portion), kept separate because the wording differs; patience is the lead message with a hike as the conditional alternative, so 0.

items.speaker: Andrew Hollenhorst and Veronica Clark
items.occasion: Client note on Friday 4 September after the August jobs report, reported by Reuters (carried by Devdiscourse)
items.quote: unemployment rate was unchanged and labor force participation rebounded noticeably,
items.summary: Citi pushed its next cut from October 2026 to June 2027, saying the labor data suggest policymakers will view employment as broadly stable and focus on inflation. Per Stocktwits' account of the same note the new baseline is three 25bp cuts in June, September and December 2027.
items.score_note: Still no hike in the forecast and the next move is a cut, but it is pushed out by eight months; hold through 2026 scored 0.
items.call: No change in 2026; next cut June 2027 (was Oct 2026)

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post after the August jobs report, twelve days before the September FOMC
items.quote: LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT
items.summary: After a strong August payrolls report raised hike odds, Trump threatened to stop trading with countries that run surpluses with the US unless the Fed lowers rates, argued a stronger country means a lower interest rate, and said the Fed Board 'with its great new leader, must get smart'.
items.score_note: Explicit ultimatum demanding a rate cut.

items.speaker: Jonathan Pingle and Abigail Watt
items.occasion: UBS note after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech and the August jobs report, reported by Investing.com (carried by Hellenic Shipping News)
items.quote: we expect he has little choice but to put his monetary policy where his mouth is,
items.summary: UBS forecast quarter-point hikes in September and December, saying every point in Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks supported hikes and his credibility is on the line. It called the forecast not high conviction and the September decision a close call.
items.score_note: Two hikes starting at the next meeting, though flagged as low conviction.
items.call: Sep +25bp and Dec +25bp ('not high conviction'; September a close call)

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.role: Chairman and CEO, Duquesne Family Office
items.occasion: Private remarks at a Piper Sandler investor event in New York, reported by the Financial Times
items.quote: Committee members on the Fed who keep saying Fed fund rates are restrictive are just ridiculous
items.summary: According to FT-based reports, Druckenmiller told a closed-door audience that US borrowing costs remain a little low, that rate cuts are no longer needed, and that officials who call the funds rate restrictive are ridiculous given asset prices worldwide. He called Warsh a great Fed chair and said he is no longer allowed to speak with him.
items.score_note: Says policy is not restrictive and yields are too low, which pushes back on easing; no explicit call for hikes in the quoted text. Secondary source (Yahoo/TheStreet citing Investing.com and the FT); the FT original was not opened. Event date Sept 10 per PrimeXBT and Newsquawk reports of the same remarks.

items.speaker: David Mericle
items.role: Economist, Goldman Sachs (as described by Reuters)
items.occasion: Client note on Friday 11 September, reported by Reuters (carried by The Edge Malaysia)
items.quote: We think that the FOMC will be reluctant to surprise
items.summary: Goldman abandoned its call for unchanged rates and now expects a 25bp hike at the September 15-16 meeting after hot August CPI and PPI. In a separate Sunday note it still expected two cuts in 2027, later than before, seeing the hike as driven more by market pricing than inflation fundamentals.
items.score_note: Switch from hold to a hike at the next meeting, but framed as a market-pricing-driven single move with cuts still pencilled in for 2027; chose +1 rather than +2.
items.call: Sep +25bp (was: no change); still two cuts in 2027, later than before

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.role: Lead economist on the note, J.P. Morgan (as described by Reuters)
items.occasion: Client note after August CPI/PPI, reported by Reuters on 14 September (carried by The Edge Malaysia)
items.quote: a firm enough set of inflation readings to make a rate hike at next week's FOMC meeting more likely than not
items.summary: JPMorgan now forecasts quarter-point hikes in both September and December and raised its long-run policy rate estimate to 3.25%, saying the inflation data cast doubt on a sustained disinflation trend.
items.score_note: Two hikes, starting at the next meeting.
items.call: Sep +25bp and Dec +25bp; long-run policy rate estimate raised to 3.25%

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley economists (unnamed in report)
items.occasion: Client note on Monday 14 September, reported by Reuters (carried by Kitco)
items.quote: the balance of risks now argues for a somewhat more restrictive policy
items.summary: Morgan Stanley switched to forecasting 25bp hikes in September and December, saying disinflation has been slower and less convincing than policymakers need. It cited second-round effects from energy, strong demand tied to AI-related investment, a possibly higher neutral rate and credibility concerns.
items.score_note: Moves from hold to two hikes starting at the next meeting.
items.call: Sep +25bp and Dec +25bp (was: hold through 2026)

items.speaker: David Mericle
items.occasion: Client note after the September FOMC decision, reported by Stocktwits citing The Fly
items.quote: more hawkish than expected in a few ways
items.summary: Mericle said the statement and projections were more hawkish than expected: a 16-2 majority projecting another 2026 hike, no dissent, an elevated median path through 2029 and a neutral-rate dot up to 3.25%. Goldman now expects a second 25bp hike in October instead of September being the only hike; further hikes are possible but not the base case.
items.score_note: Adds a hike at the very next meeting.
items.call: Oct +25bp (second hike; was: September only); additional hikes possible but not base case

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Yahoo Finance interview after the September FOMC hike
items.quote: It's not clear to me we've slayed inflation
items.summary: Hours after the Fed raised rates, Dimon said he is not convinced inflation is beaten and that every business should be prepared for volatility in interest rates. Per Yahoo he said persistent inflation, global deficits and heavy capital demand, including for AI, could keep upward pressure on rates, while low unemployment and corporate profits show the economy is not near a downturn; rising unemployment is what would bring consumer and corporate credit losses.
items.score_note: Sees the inflation fight as unfinished and rates biased higher, without calling for a specific further hike.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: CNBC 'Closing Bell' interview after the September FOMC 25bp hike
items.quote: I would have just done the 50 and then see what the data does
items.summary: Gundlach said the Fed should have hiked 50bp ('stun and done') because the 2-year yield was more than 100bp above the funds rate and the inflation problem is not fully respected. He called Warsh's press conference thin and opaque and criticized the Fed task forces. DoubleLine's recap adds that AI-related investment-grade bonds have widened about 50bp while the rest of IG barely moved.
items.score_note: Would have dissented for a larger hike.
items.ai_quote: does not believe the ratings that are on these AI bonds

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Thoughts on the Market podcast with Matthew Hornbach after the September FOMC, 'One Fed Hike—Or More to Come?' (transcript)
items.quote: I strongly believe the committee as a whole is thinking in terms of more than one move.
items.summary: Gapen said the committee is thinking of a series of moves, probably at a slower, roughly quarterly pace rather than three or four meetings in a row, and that if disinflation continues the cycle could still end up looking like one and done. He noted wage income is decelerating, so the labor market is not a source of inflation pressure.
items.score_note: Expects more than one hike but stresses a slow pace and the chance the Fed stops early; chose +1 over +2.
items.call: More than one hike likely, at a roughly quarterly pace; could end as one-and-done if disinflation continues

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts, 'September Fed Hike May Be More Than a Risk Management Exercise'
items.quote: it may be sensible for central banks to lean in a more hawkish direction to ensure their inflation-fighting credibility remains intact.
items.summary: PIMCO said the projections send a strong signal that the September hike will very likely be followed by another this year and possibly one more in 2027 if inflation does not moderate fast enough. It stressed this is not 2022: labor is not driving inflation and wage growth has decelerated.
items.score_note: Endorses a hawkish lean and expects another hike, but frames the labor backdrop as benign.
items.call: Another hike in 2026 very likely; possibly one more in 2027

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Truth Social post about two and a half hours after the FOMC raised rates 25bp
items.quote: Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR
items.summary: Hours after the September hike to 3.75-4.00%, Trump posted that US rates should be 1% or less and demanded 'LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!'. He tied the demand to trade deficits and did not name Warsh.
items.score_note: Explicit demand for large, fast cuts right after a hike.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks to reporters on arriving in North Carolina for a campaign trip, hours after the September rate hike
items.quote: And I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter.
items.summary: Trump said he had talked to Warsh and told him he might as well vote with the board, and called the board 'very hostile' and 'very political', saying 'They’re doing the wrong thing.' He said he still had confidence in Warsh. CNBC's account of the same remarks adds that he said the board is raising rates to make him do as badly as possible.
items.score_note: Calls the hike the wrong thing on the day it was delivered; blame is directed at the board rather than Warsh.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, September 15-16 meeting: opening statement
items.quote: So we removed a dose of accommodation.
items.summary: FOMC raised the target range 25bp to 3.75-4.00% by 12-0. Warsh said the economy is strengthening, the labor side of the mandate is in good shape, inflation is too high and has been for too long (PCE about 3.6% in August), and the Jackson Hole standard 'has not been satisfied'. He said the Committee widely shared his view that financial conditions were not restrictive. SEP median funds rate 4.1% for end-2026 and end-2027; he again submitted no projection.
items.score_note: Announces and justifies a hike he voted for and says the standard for confidence on inflation is not met; no pre-commitment to more.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, September 15-16 meeting: Q&A on whether more hikes follow
items.quote: not going to prejudge any future decisions we make
items.summary: Asked whether the hike starts a sequence, Warsh said he is 'not in the forward guidance business' and would not prejudge future decisions; the SEP forecasts are his colleagues', not his. He said the action 'starts to show we're serious' and that it was the Fed's own decision, not a market-led one.
items.score_note: Declines to signal either a follow-up hike or a stop.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, September 15-16 meeting: Q&A on restrictiveness and neutral
items.quote: my colleagues were hard pressed to describe it that way, too
items.summary: Asked whether rates are now restrictive, Warsh repeated that he was hard pressed to call financial conditions restrictive and said colleagues agreed; the hike removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions are more consistent with the mandate. He said the neutral rate has no operational effect on decisions, and that he does not believe the Fed needs to harm the labor market to reach its objective.
items.score_note: Describes pre-hike policy as accommodative and gives no sign that 3.75-4.00% is restrictive; leans tighter without committing.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, September 15-16 meeting: Q&A on rising long-term yields and AI capex funding
items.quote: the so-called hyperscalers are out in the market raising funding
items.summary: Asked what higher long-term yields signal, Warsh gave three reasons: economic strength, competition for capital from the capex surge with hyperscalers raising funding, and geopolitics (energy and commodity prices, crack spreads). He said he wants bond prices to tell their own story.
items.score_note: Explains why yields rose; states no stance on the policy rate path.
items.ai_quote: the competition for capital is real, and I think it partly explains the increase in yields

items.speaker: Andrew Sheets
items.role: Global Head of Fixed Income Research, Morgan Stanley
items.occasion: Thoughts on the Market podcast, 'Why the Fed May Have Further to Go' (transcript)
items.quote: Morgan Stanley's economists now expect two additional quarter point rate hikes in December and March
items.summary: Sheets said that after the September meeting Morgan Stanley's economists expect two more hikes, in December and March, to 4.25-4.5%, with rates staying there through the rest of 2027. Reasons: the Fed does not see policy as restrictive, inflation trends are too high, and geopolitics and oil second-round effects. The Fed could stop earlier if energy prices fall.
items.score_note: House forecast of two further hikes.
items.call: Dec +25bp and Mar 2027 +25bp to 4.25-4.50%; hold through rest of 2027

items.speaker: Jeffrey Gundlach
items.occasion: DoubleLine client event at the Plaza Hotel, New York (conversation with Jeffrey Sherman)
items.quote: In the next recession, long term rates will go up
items.summary: Gundlach said long-term rates will rise even in a recession as the deficit heads toward 12% of GDP, and expects more government intervention starting with a larger Operation Twist. DoubleLine's summary says he sees cracks in credit, with AI-related bonds widening well beyond the market and private credit marks in question; he called rating agencies' investment-grade stamps a price list. A Yahoo report of the same event quotes him saying defaults will start coming in fast and furious.
items.score_note: Long-rate and credit views; nothing on the next Fed move in the text read (his view on the hike is in the Sept 16 CNBC item).

items.speaker: Wells Fargo Economics (Wells Fargo Research Team)
items.occasion: Wells Fargo monthly U.S. Economic Outlook, 'Economic resilience raises the rate floor', as republished by FXStreet
items.quote: We expect the Fed to hike one more time.
items.summary: Wells Fargo changed its fed funds forecast to 4.00-4.25% by year-end 2026 with no changes in 2027, saying it is hard to justify hiking beyond that when excess inflation is largely supply-driven and the labor market is not overheating.
items.score_note: One more hike, then a hold through 2027.
items.call: One more hike to 4.00-4.25% by year-end 2026; no changes in 2027

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Lord Mayor's luncheon, Mansion House, London: 'The Final Chapter on Modernizing Bank Regulatory Stress Testing'
items.quote: Today, my remarks will highlight our work to enhance and improve the bank regulatory stress test framework.
items.summary: Speech on stress test reform, two days after the September hike. No monetary policy content.
items.score_note: No statement on the policy rate path; official speech included for coverage.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Lord Mayor's luncheon, Mansion House, London: 'Initial Findings from Independent Review of Silicon Valley Bank'
items.quote: Today I am announcing the initial findings of the independent review of the failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB).
items.summary: Announces findings of the independent SVB review (second text posted for the same Mansion House event). No monetary policy content.
items.score_note: No statement on the policy rate path; official speech included for coverage.

items.speaker: Kristy Akullian
items.role: Head of iShares Investment Strategy, Americas, BlackRock
items.occasion: BlackRock 'Inside the market' article, 'First Fed rate hike in years: What it may mean for investor portfolios'
items.quote: While this hike is significant, we don’t believe this is the start of an aggressive hiking cycle.
items.summary: The iShares strategy team's baseline is one more hike in 2026 as the Fed seeks to reduce inflation at sufficient speed; it noted futures priced 4.25% by year-end.
items.score_note: One more hike, explicitly not an aggressive cycle.
items.call: One more hike in 2026; not an aggressive hiking cycle

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Independent Community Bankers of Colorado 53rd Annual Convention, Vail, Colorado: "The Strategic Imperative of Instant Payments for Community Banks"
items.quote: With the labor market in balance and growth resilient, inflation is my primary concern as I think about the correct course for monetary policy.
items.summary: Two days after the September FOMC raised the policy rate, Schmid said he supported the decision, describing it as a response to inflation that has been too high for too long and is trending above 3 percent. He called the hike a step toward the work the Fed has to do on inflation. The rest of the speech is about instant payments.
items.score_note: Supports the hike and calls it 'a step' with inflation the primary concern, but does not explicitly ask for another increase in this text; nearer-0 choice between +1 and +2.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Fox News 'Sunday Morning Futures' interview (days after the September 16 hike)
items.quote: in terms of where the economy is going, inflation is still too high
items.summary: After voting for the September hike, Kashkari said inflation is too high even excluding energy and food and is present in all aspects of the economy, including services. He said the Fed has tools to bring it down and will do its part. The Hill article is dated Sept 21; the interview aired Sunday Sept 20.
items.score_note: Inflation-focused and supportive of tightening, but no statement on the timing or number of further hikes in the quoted remarks.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box interview with Joe Kernen, first interview after the September 16 hike
items.quote: Yeah, I'm not going to talk about whether I agree with it or not.
items.summary: Asked whether he agreed with the 25bp hike, Bessent declined to say, voiced 'great confidence' in Warsh on behalf of himself and the president, and said core inflation has been quiescent with everything in the headline number. He said long yields are highly correlated with crude and crack spreads and that 'rates should come down' once the Iran conflict ends.
items.score_note: Explicitly neutral on the hike; the quiescent-core and yields-will-fall remarks lean dovish but he gives no direction for policy.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: Associated Press interview after the September FOMC (AP story carried by the Boston Globe)
items.quote: I did not see the inflation progress I was hoping to see,
items.summary: Collins says she agreed with the September quarter-point hike because inflation progress did not materialize, energy pressures from geopolitics could continue, and stronger hiring suggests the economy can withstand higher rates. The AP reports she expects the Fed to keep rates unchanged next year. A recap of the AP interview adds that she penciled in a second hike for later this year.
items.score_note: Supported the hike on inflation grounds; no explicit call for more at this point.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: OMFIF event 'Monetary Policy in an Uncertain World', London (prepared remarks; also reporter Q&A)
items.quote: if demand overheats, there is no ambiguity about how the Fed needs to respond
items.summary: Goolsbee argues central banks should not look through persistent supply shocks: if shocks are large and recurring, the only way to bring inflation down is to raise rates, though the response need not be as large as for demand overheating and will not be painless. He is watching services inflation and AI data-center construction spilling into aggregate demand. AP and Axios report he told reporters the fight would be painful and that one hike likely would not be enough if inflation is demand-driven. Reuters also reports he rejected the idea of cutting rates to help finance government debt as the classic argument for central bank independence.
items.score_note: Case for tightening against persistent supply shocks and overheating; conditional on evidence, no explicit call for the next meeting.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: CNBC-TV18 interview on the sidelines of the JPMorgan India Conference
items.quote: there's a chance it won't, and it may even go up a little bit
items.summary: Dimon said he hopes price pressure eases but it may not and could rise, and (per CNBC's paraphrase) that the Fed should stick to its 2% inflation target. He said hyperscaler AI spending could reach $1 trillion next year, adds about 1% to GDP each year and may add a little to inflation, and that capital demand from infrastructure, remilitarization and deficits may be pushing interest rates higher.
items.score_note: Inflation risk seen to the upside and the Fed should hold to 2%; no explicit call for a further hike. Article timestamp is 01:30 UTC Sept 22 (Sept 21 ET); the interview took place in India time.
items.ai_quote: may add a little bit to inflation

items.speaker: Mike Wilson
items.role: CIO and Chief U.S. Equity Strategist, Morgan Stanley
items.occasion: Thoughts on the Market podcast, 'Market Resilience Isn’t Complacency' (transcript)
items.quote: A few additional hikes over the next year are unlikely to end this bull market if earnings remain strong.
items.summary: Wilson said the September hike can enhance credibility and lower uncertainty and term premium, and that the rate hike is not his concern. The bigger unknown is how a Warsh-led Fed handles the balance sheet, money supply and credit growth; an overly restrictive approach to liquidity could matter more than the policy rate.
items.score_note: Treats a few more hikes as the working assumption and as benign; not a house rate forecast.
items.call: A few additional hikes over the next year assumed; main risk is balance sheet/liquidity policy, not the funds rate

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview
items.quote: earlier and incremental policy firming is better and less disruptive than later and larger and potentially more abrupt policy action
items.summary: Five days after the September hike Musalem said that without further policy restraint inflation is more likely to be substantially above 2% in 18 months than at target, that inflation 'is not a risk. It's there', and that underlying inflation is moving in the wrong direction. Reuters reads this as more hikes likely needed. Interview date (Monday Sept 21) is from the Reuters URL listed by the St. Louis Fed and from Bloomberg's same-day report; the copy opened was published Sept 22-23.
items.score_note: Argues for further and earlier firming right after a hike.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'Why Hike?', CFA Society Baltimore, Baltimore, Md.
items.quote: The risks to inflation outweigh the risks to maximum employment.
items.summary: Barkin defends the September 25bp hike: inflation is more than a point above target and broad-based, shocks are not proving short-lived, and firms are more willing to pass on costs, while demand and the labor market are solid. On further hikes he says 'We'll see', noting inflation could fall quickly or prove more stubborn so that one move might not be enough. In Q&A (wire recap) he said he would like this cycle to resemble a 1990s-style mid-cycle adjustment and would not yet make an overheating case.
items.score_note: Supports the hike and says inflation risks dominate; open to more but not committed.

items.speaker: Susan Collins
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (non-voter in 2026)
items.occasion: LinkedIn post after the September FOMC (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: more restrictive federal funds rate will help ensure that inflation durably returns to target.
items.summary: Collins writes that she supported the September hike, now sees an increased likelihood of scenarios in which inflation stays notably above 2%, and that with the labor market on a better footing policy can focus on a timely return to price stability. Reuters notes she did not say whether she wants rates to go up again.
items.score_note: Backs the hike and a more restrictive stance; no explicit call for another move.

items.speaker: Howard Marks
items.occasion: Oaktree memo 'Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics - Part III'
items.quote: arguing against the likelihood of a decline in interest rates anytime soon
items.summary: Marks argued that long-term yields reflect fundamentals (inflation well above target, which is why the Fed hiked the prior week, no fiscal discipline, and heavy capital demand from the AI buildout) and that Treasury buybacks treat the symptom. He wrote that the goal should not be to get interest rates down but to address what is pushing them up, and that net Treasury issuance plus AI capital needs argue against lower rates soon.
items.score_note: Forecast that rates will not fall soon and endorsement of the reasons for the September hike; mostly about long yields, no call on the next FOMC move. credit_view left null because he treats AI financing only as a source of capital demand, not as a credit-quality judgment.
items.ai_quote: the AI buildout is likely to cost trillions of dollars

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York: 'Discount Window Modernization and Treasury Market Functioning'
items.quote: The discount window also helps respond to sudden tightening in money markets
items.summary: Speech on discount window operations and Treasury market resilience. Mentions more discount window use around quarter-end money market pressure. Nothing on the rate path, given six days after the September hike.
items.score_note: No statement on the policy rate path; official speech included for coverage.

items.speaker: Seth Carpenter
items.role: Global Chief Economist and Head of Macro Research, Morgan Stanley
items.occasion: Thoughts on the Market podcast, 'Why Central Banks Are Raising Rates Again' (transcript)
items.quote: we now expect two additional rate hikes, in December and in March
items.summary: Carpenter said Morgan Stanley had thought for much of the year the Fed might avoid hiking, but now expects December and March hikes to a 4.25-4.5% terminal rate. He called it a recalibration rather than a fundamental shift and said the market may have overestimated how much hiking is left.
items.score_note: Two further hikes forecast; note he also says markets may price too much hiking, which argues for +1, but the stated call is two hikes.
items.call: Dec +25bp and Mar 2027 +25bp; terminal 4.25-4.50%

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: Remarks at the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 'Do You Remember?'
items.quote: Put simply, the evolution of financial market structure leads to the evolution of how we carry out monetary policy effectively.
items.summary: Speech on monetary policy implementation: the ample-reserves framework, ON RRP and standing repo operations, and how tools must evolve with market structure (central clearing, stablecoins). No comment on the rate path or the economic outlook.
items.score_note: Implementation and market-structure speech with no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'A Long-Term View on the Costs of Shelter', Housing Affordability 2026: A Community Development Summit, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
items.quote: In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion.
items.summary: First remarks after the September 16 hike. Barr says he supported the increase because 'we were out of position', that inflation risks have increased while labor-market risks have receded, and that in his base case more adjustments are likely needed. The rest of the speech is on housing affordability.
items.score_note: Says further tightening is likely needed in his base case one week after a hike, which matches 'says more hikes are needed'. Hedged ('base case', 'likely', no timing), so a reader could argue +1.

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts, 'A Recalibration, Not a Rate-Hike Cycle'
items.quote: And our base case is that the FOMC will likely deliver one or two more 25-bp rate hikes through this year and into early next.
items.summary: PIMCO reads the September hike as aimed at preventing financial conditions from easing further rather than as the start of a cycle. As tariff, energy and AI-related computing-equipment price effects fade, further adjustments beyond one or two more hikes may not be necessary.
items.score_note: One or two more hikes, explicitly not a cycle; chose +1 over +2.
items.call: One or two more 25bp hikes through 2026 and into early 2027; then likely stop

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Economic Club of Washington, D.C., conversation with Barbara Humpton (reported by Fortune)
items.quote: then you have to look in the mirror and say inflation looks like it’s been here for a while.
items.summary: Barkin explains the September hike by pointing to persistent tariff costs, higher gasoline prices and a wave of AI investment pushing up some equipment prices; if inflation is not coming down quickly, the Fed has to accept it has been here a while. He says the 'AI apocalypse' for jobs has not arrived.
items.score_note: Justifies the hike on inflation persistence; no explicit call for further hikes.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Opening remarks at the Philadelphia Fed 10th Annual Fintech Conference
items.quote: Looking ahead, if conditions evolve as I expect, some modest further tightening may be warranted.
items.summary: Paulson said she supported the 25bp hike at the September meeting because inflation risks were growing: underlying inflation is stuck at 2.5-3% and price pressure from the Middle East conflict and the AI buildout grew. She called returning inflation to 2% non-negotiable and said some modest further tightening may be warranted.
items.score_note: Conditional signal of modest further tightening ('may be warranted'); leaning tighter rather than calling for an immediate hike.

items.speaker: John Williams

items.quote: I have always thought there is a higher chance than other people.
items.summary: Asked about a 6% 10-year yield and the Fed hiking a few more times, Dimon said he would never take that off the table, that it could come from strong capital demand or from sticky inflation, and that he sees a higher chance of it than others while stressing it is preparation, not a prediction. He said JPMorgan is tightening up on credit because terms have become a little loose, and that shrinking the Fed balance sheet will require changes (to liquidity rules). In the earnings release he listed large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices and rising interest rates as risks; to reporters he said a move from 5% to 6% would hurt more than 4% to 5% (CNBC live blog).
items.score_note: Assigns above-consensus odds to further Fed hikes and higher long rates but explicitly declines to predict them. The quote sits in the transcript data embedded in the Fortune/Quartr page (inside a script block).

items.speaker: Paul Tudor Jones
items.role: Founder and CIO, Tudor Investment Corporation
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' interview
items.quote: And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path.
items.summary: Jones compared conditions to the period just before the dot-com bust, citing debt-financed AI capex and sovereign debt, said 2027 will be very challenging for stocks and that he will be short all year, and expects the bond market to force fiscal change followed by a TARP-style bailout. He put 60-40 odds that the market is already at that tipping point. CNBC's Oct 30 recap quotes him saying AI-related issuance as a share of GDP is 50% more than railroads.
items.score_note: No statement on the Fed rate path in the text read (CNBC live blog entry and later recap; no full transcript found).

items.summary: Dalio wrote that the Treasury selloff is far from over because debt supply from the government, companies and the AI buildout outstrips demand, and (per the report) that the cycle is unlikely to stabilize until high borrowing costs weaken the economy enough to rebalance supply and demand.
items.score_note: Forecast of higher market rates until the economy slows; about bond yields rather than the funds rate, so +1. LinkedIn original not opened; post date per Stocktwits (Oct 13) and 24/7 Wall St ('Tuesday'). AI-debt figures are paraphrased on the page, so no ai_quote.

Bloomberg's accessible text does not quote him on the timing of the next hike.

items.summary: Williams reaffirmed that one more hike in 2026 may be appropriate and said he currently has no reason to believe more would be needed in 2027, though data could change that. He still sees disinflationary forces, expects inflation near 2% for 2027 as a whole, and said the economy is not overheating overall.
items.score_note: Still leans to one more hike this year but explicitly sees no need for further tightening in 2027; mild tightening lean.

Reuters also reports she said the Fed looks at the capital going into data center construction from banks and other funding sources (paraphrase, not a direct quote).

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)

items.quote: We are more likely than not to need additional adjustments, but the timing of those adjustments to me is something we’re still deliberating
items.summary: Daly said further rate increases are more likely than not but she feels no urgency to decide at the October 27-28 meeting on limited information. She said the CPI report shows inflation risk remains elevated, that reacting to risk when there is time is imprudent, and that markets understand the Fed's reaction function.
items.score_note: Expects more hikes but explicitly not urgent; between +1 and +2, chose +1.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: CNBC interview from Goldman's Builders and Innovators Summit, San Francisco
items.quote: The anomaly is zero interest rates, not a 5% 10-year Treasury.
items.summary: Solomon noted a hot inflation print and that four rate hikes are priced in, but gave no view on what the Fed should do. He said the world is absorbing the move in the 10-year reasonably well, that AI capital demand is competing with heavy government borrowing and puts some pressure on rates, and that he is not scared by it. He disagreed that capital is a choke point for the AI buildout, while granting some crowding-out at the margin.
items.score_note: Describes market pricing of hikes without endorsing or forecasting. Page states it was recorded Oct 14.

items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: NPR 'All Things Considered' interview with Scott Detrow after September CPI
items.quote: are we reentering a very persistent inflation environment which is going to require more aggressive action to get us back to where we need to be?
items.summary: Goolsbee calls the CPI report disheartening, with services inflation distressingly high, and says the danger is that inflation is shifting from temporary tariff and oil effects to old-fashioned demand overheating linked to the AI buildout. He defends central bank independence against political pressure.
items.score_note: Inflation dominates and he raises the prospect of more aggressive action, framed as a question.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Yahoo Finance interview with Jennifer Schonberger after September CPI
items.quote: If we get more months like this where you got core inflation on a monthly basis coming in above 4%, that's totally unacceptable.
items.summary: Goolsbee finds the CPI report discouraging, with services inflation above 5% and goods still above 3%. He says there is no ambiguity about how a central bank responds when the real economy is solid and inflation is above target and going the wrong way. Asked whether more hikes are needed, he says the Fed does not yet know but must get back on a path to 2%.
items.score_note: One-sided inflation problem with clear tightening implication; stops short of calling for a specific hike.

items.speaker: Larry Fink
items.occasion: BlackRock Q3 2026 earnings call
items.quote: we are going to have structurally higher interest rates for longer, and especially out the curve
items.summary: Fink said that for the first time in his 50-year career he sees genuine shortages of capital, with record federal deficits competing against private demand including the AI build-out, and that this means structurally higher interest rates for longer, especially at the long end. He said bespoke deals cannot raise the trillions needed for data centers and that a new securitized financing market for compute and chips is needed.
items.score_note: Higher-for-longer forecast aimed mainly at long rates; he does not predict a specific Fed move, so +1. Quote is in the transcript data embedded in the Fortune/Quartr page (script block).
items.ai_quote: I do not see us having the ability to raise trillions and trillions of dollars of bespoke transactions related to data centers.
