items.speaker: Ted Pick
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Q3 2026 earnings call
items.quote: And I think it is probably a longer odds bet that we are going to have a low interest rate, low inflation, non-recessionary environment.
items.summary: Pick said the quarter split in two: a risk-on July and August, then higher rates globally from Labor Day as central banks moved to keep inflation at bay. He said the Fed is focused on managing long-term inflation expectations, that higher rates are fine if they reflect productivity and growth but not if they reflect lost control of inflation expectations, and that he would not bet on a return to low rates and low inflation. Hyperscaler capex is running around $1 trillion a year and the cycle is still early.
items.score_note: He bets against a return to a low-rate, low-inflation setting, which pushes back on easing expectations; no call on the next meeting. Quote is in the transcript data embedded in the Fortune/Quartr page (script block).

He called the AI investment cycle real and sustained, with hyperscaler capex near $1 trillion a year, and said Morgan Stanley is not seeing troubling leverage in its equities financing book.
items.score_note: Describes the Fed's focus and a risk scenario but gives no view on what the Fed will or should do. Morgan Stanley's page is dated Oct 16; the interview aired the morning of the Oct 14 results (Fortune transcript date for the call, CNBC live blog for the reporting day).

items.speaker: Mohamed El-Erian
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' interview ahead of the October FOMC
items.quote: My problem is that it's the wrong policy measure right now.
items.summary: El-Erian expected the Fed to hold in October with hawkish language because inflation data came in hot, and expected more monetary tightening to follow. He called further hikes the wrong tool, said the answer to inflation and high Treasury yields should be fiscal containment, and warned tightening would hit housing and consumer loans while tech is barely affected.
items.score_note: Opposes further hikes as the wrong instrument but does not ask for cuts. His forecast, by contrast, is a hold now and more tightening later.

items.speaker: Michael Gapen

items.summary: Gapen expected a hold in October with rates going higher later, at a more gradual pace because back-to-back hikes risk too much tightening in financial conditions. He said six or seven total hikes back to 2023 levels would cause concern, and that energy markets will dictate whether an every-other-meeting pace is affordable.
items.score_note: Hold now, further hikes ahead at a gradual pace.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent

He said future hikes would not necessarily be a mistake because the Fed sees the economy accelerating, and warned against slowing growth enough to cut energy demand. He called stress in AI-related junk debt not problematic.
items.score_note: Urges an open mind on a transitory supply shock and invokes the ECB 2008 error, while declining to call further hikes a mistake.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, October 27-28 meeting: opening statement
items.quote: The information we receive over the coming period will help us determine where we want policy to be.
items.summary: FOMC held at 3.75-4.00% by 10-2 (Cook and Hammack preferred +25bp). Warsh said growth has strengthened, employment conditions are quite positive, and inflation is too high with energy prices up again. Since the September hike financial and credit conditions have tightened for some borrowers; he is 'unwilling and unable' to call them tight. He said the Committee has shown its willingness to act, and announced that from 2027 one of eight meetings (two in 2028) will be strategy-only with no rate vote.
items.score_note: Rhetoric still centers on inflation and readiness to act, but he chose to wait against two hawkish dissents and says tightening is working; torn between 0 and +1, so 0.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, October 27-28 meeting: Q&A on a December hike
items.quote: I also don’t believe in prejudging meetings.
items.summary: Asked why not hike now and whether colleagues still back another hike this year, Warsh said quashing inflation is not about a fixed calendar date, that the 'new monetary medicine' is starting to work with inflation compensation and expectations moving the right way, and that there are 'no firm conclusions' on whether the current rate is the right one. He called the period ahead information rich and said the Committee will be better positioned in six weeks.
items.score_note: Leaves December open both ways and stresses signs that policy is working.

items.speaker: Kevin Warsh
items.occasion: FOMC press conference, October 27-28 meeting: Q&A on AI investment, credit conditions and rate sensitivity
items.quote: You’ve seen credit spreads for certain assets widen out, gap out.
items.summary: Asked whether AI-driven demand is insensitive to rates, Warsh said he was skeptical of that view: rates 'get in the cracks', and since early September investors inside and outside the technology complex have become more discriminating, with credit spreads on some assets gapping wider. He said capex strength is broadening beyond AI, most colleagues do not judge the economy to be running too hot, the goal is not to 'throw sand in the gears', and tighter financial conditions tell him policy is working.
items.score_note: Says the hike is biting on AI-related financing and is comfortable with that; does not call for more or for a stop.
items.ai_quote: Interest rates have had an effect.

items.summary: Asked how further balance-sheet shrinkage would avoid disrupting foreign Treasury holders and dollar funding, Warsh said the question sits with the Balance Sheet Task Force, whose recommendations should reach the FOMC probably early in the first quarter of 2027, and that any change is unlikely to have a material effect on the current policy conjuncture.
items.score_note: Rules out near-term balance-sheet tightening as a policy lever; neutral for the rate path.

He says AI investment is adding demand-side inflation the Fed can lean against and that lived inflation feeds future inflation unless the Fed acts.

His more likely scenario has inflation staying meaningfully above 2% without more tightening; a less likely one has it falling on its own (energy, productivity, or an AI/data-center spending slowdown). He noted credit spreads have widened, especially for AI-infrastructure borrowers, but is not overly concerned by tighter financial conditions.

He said current shocks are not so far spilling into expectations or wages, did not discuss the next move, and said the last FOMC statement rightly concluded it was appropriate to collect more information. (Reuters via SRN News.)
items.score_note: Strong inflation language but no comment on the next move and an endorsement of gathering more information; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Tom Barkin
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Speech 'The Rooms Driving the Economy', Greater Greer Chamber of Commerce, Greer, S.C.
items.quote: Should the economy remain on its current path, the risk lies on the inflation side of our dual mandate.
items.summary: Barkin says that with demand healthy and inflation stubbornly elevated the appropriate direction of policy is relatively straightforward, but demand risks are easy to envision so policy should move with care. He flags AI as the key swing factor: if it underdelivers, investment, stock prices and asset-fueled spending could pull back; if it overdelivers, job displacement could hit spending. In Q&A (wire recap) he said he has no base case for the December meeting and that the policy rate is around or slightly below neutral.
items.score_note: Direction is toward tightening, at a careful pace; not an explicit call for a hike at the next meeting.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Council on Foreign Relations, C. Peter McColough Series, Washington: 'The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy'
items.quote: This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent.
items.summary: Supported the October hold to assess the September hike; now says inflation is more persistent than she expected and broadening (core PCE likely 3.3% in October), the labor market is firming, and she is more attentive to the inflation side. But financial conditions have tightened, so the benefit of additional tightening must be weighed against costs for rate-sensitive sectors, and she wants clarity on AI financing conditions; flags AI-related debt on track to exceed $800 billion and off-balance-sheet structures as a risk to activity and financial stability. Identical remarks were given the same day at an Unleash Prosperity Now virtual event (18:30 ET per the Fed index).
items.score_note: Inflation is the priority and 'there is still work to do', but she stops short of endorsing a December hike and stresses tightening costs and AI-financing risks; +1 not +2.
items.ai_quote: Greater clarity on AI-related financing conditions and the sustainability of AI investments should increase my confidence in future policy decisions.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Council on Foreign Relations, C. Peter McColough Series, Washington: moderated Q&A with John Lipsky and audience (same event as the speech)
items.quote: I gave an indication today that I think addressing inflation is the right move for us
items.summary: Said that with the labor market stabilized she is shifting her focus to inflation, which is not on a downward trend, and that this 'should give us some pause as we think about the need to address inflation, and at what pace, and on what timeline'. Asked by the WSJ about colleagues calling for faster tightening, she let their statements speak for themselves. Compared the path to last year's gradual cuts with a pause, 'in the same way that we may work to address inflation in the coming months'. Longer-term expectations are very well anchored but do not control her thinking; she needs AI-buildout and Middle East risks to abate before being confident in her 2027 disinflation forecast.
items.score_note: Clear lean toward tightening ('addressing inflation is the right move') but gradual and with no commitment on December size or timing; +1. Q&A portion of the same occasion as the prepared speech.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: PBS News Hour interview with Geoff Bennett after October CPI
items.quote: we must get inflation back down to target, and it's going the wrong way at this point
items.summary: Goolsbee calls the CPI report distressing, 'borderline disturbing', with services inflation not coming down and AI build-out demand drifting into broader overheating. Asked about a possible half-point hike in December (the host cites Waller), he declines to be specific but says everything is on the table and inflation is going the wrong way.
items.score_note: Does not rule out a larger hike and stresses inflation, but avoids committing; +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Economic and monetary policy outlook, 11th joint Dallas Fed / Kansas City Fed energy conference, Houston
items.quote: It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall.
items.summary: Logan said inflation is trending meaningfully above 2 percent, October CPI was higher than expected, and the real funds rate (78bp by her staff's estimate) is below the lowest neutral estimate. She repeated that at least two more 25bp hikes are needed and added that the pace could be faster this winter, then a pause to assess.
items.score_note: Explicit call for at least two more hikes and an open door to a faster pace. [AI link: market volatility around the technology investment outlook cited for the October skip; AI capex also described as a demand driver].
items.ai_quote: Financial markets had been volatile in the weeks before the meeting in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments.

items.speaker: Matthew Hornbach
items.role: Global Head of Macro Strategy, Morgan Stanley
items.occasion: CNBC interview after October CPI, reported by Stocktwits
items.quote: To my mind, that's taking it too far.
items.summary: Asked about a 50bp hike, Hornbach said that would be going too far. He said the more immediate question is whether the Fed moves from quarterly 25bp hikes to hiking at consecutive meetings, and questioned how many more elevated readings the Fed would tolerate before accelerating.
items.score_note: Expects continued 25bp hikes and possibly a faster cadence, but rejects 50bp.
items.call: 25bp hikes continue; 50bp in December 'too far'; open question is quarterly vs consecutive-meeting pace

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: 'Economic Outlook' speech at the Philadelphia Fed 81st Annual Field Meeting Capstone, Conshohocken, Pa.
items.quote: For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate.
items.summary: Paulson said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive, that she supported the September hike and the October hold, and that skipping a meeting is a matter of pace, not direction: there is likely more work to do. She prefers gradual tightening but would act more quickly if inflation expectations drift up, wage pressures build or underlying inflation moves higher. Underlying inflation is stuck at 2.5-3%.
items.score_note: States that further tightening is appropriate and that there is likely more work to do, which is an explicit call for more hikes, albeit at a gradual pace.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)

The report says he views the rate as still too loose and reads his remarks as part of a chorus pointing to hikes.
items.score_note: Calls policy fairly accommodative with demand strong; the hike implication is the reporter's framing, so +1 not +2.

items.summary: PIMCO said October CPI and Waller's comments strengthen the case for a December hike; its baseline is not yet 50bp but could shift if Williams and Jefferson echo Waller. It still calls the tightening a recalibration, not a new cycle, and says higher yields plus recent weakness in credit and equity markets are already doing some of the Fed's work, so a dramatically higher policy rate is not necessarily needed.
items.score_note: Adds a January hike to December, with risk of March and an open door to 50bp.
items.call: Dec +25bp and Jan 2027 +25bp; some risk of Mar 2027 hike; 50bp in Dec not baseline

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Bank of England Watchers Conference, King's Business School, London: 'The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism'
items.quote: I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting
items.summary: Says further tightening is needed 'sooner rather than later'. He held in October only because signaled hikes were already priced, and those hikes must be delivered. Would back a 25bp hike in December even if October CPI improves; if core CPI is again around 0.3% or higher, a 50bp hike should be considered because 25bp would put credibility at risk. September inflation was 'bad' and broad (over 70% of core services components above 3%). In later remarks the same morning (Newsquawk wrap, paraphrase with quoted fragments) he said that at a minimum the Fed needs to take back the three insurance cuts, but that he is not "super hawkish" and is not looking to tighten by 150-200bp (https://www.newsquawk.com/headlines/newsquawk-us-market-wrap---hawkish-waller-and-hot-cpi-ignite-fed-50bps-rate-hike-bets).
items.score_note: Explicit support for a December hike and conditional support for 50bp.

items.speaker: Howard Marks
items.occasion: Oaktree memo 'A Layman Thinks About AI'
items.quote: Lenders will have to be exceptionally vigilant regarding the creditworthiness of the borrowers they back and the structure/terms through which they do it.
items.summary: No view on the Fed. Marks wrote that hyperscalers are spending their cash and borrowing more, asked whether their creditworthiness and ratings could change, flagged out clauses in data-center leases, circular vendor financing and off-balance-sheet vehicles, and said lenders to AI face debt concentrated in one industry. He added that rate-insensitive hyperscaler borrowing could be lifting the rates the government pays. He does not call AI a bubble and says whether returns will justify the spending is largely a matter of faith.
items.score_note: Credit and AI-financing content only; interest rates appear only as a consequence of capital demand.

items.speaker: Mary Daly

She was comfortable with the September hike and has a bias toward further tightening, but said how much and when need not be decided today, and that tighter financial conditions are welcome and aligned with where policy needs to be. AI is not the main inflation driver but adds pressure; investors re-pricing the risk of AI firms' borrowing strategies is healthy. Time is 10:10 a.m. PT on the SF Fed page.

He will not commit on a 50bp hike but says every possibility is on the table and the pace depends on inflation. With progress, rates could eventually settle well below current levels. She favors smaller, more frequent increases as less disruptive, does not think the Fed is behind the curve today, and would consider more aggressive moves only if it falls behind. She stressed these are conditional expectations, not forward guidance. (Reuters via Kitco.)

She will not get ahead on how high or how fast; her best case is a careful adjustment, though some scenarios could change that. She says financial markets are functioning well.

He does not commit to a hike but says the Fed has work to do to re-establish credibility and that conventional wisdom is to prevent demand overheating.

Says inflation trajectory is the more important signal for the stance; further adjustments depend on data. AI investment demand is pushing up resource utilization and prices now, with supply gains later.
items.score_note: Explicitly puts inflation ahead of employment as the signal for policy and describes persistent price pressures, but does not commit to a December hike; +1.

items.score_note: Rate stance is a brief restatement of the Nov 10 speech inside a balance-sheet and money-market speech; scored +2 because she says outright that policy must become more restrictive. Main content is tools.

She sees two-sided risks, including that higher medium and longer-term borrowing costs may restrain demand more than assumed, but says recent price data and a firmer labor market mean the rate path may end up somewhat higher than she expected. He says he is less concerned about direct losses given still-limited debt, but warns that hedge fund leverage and opacity could amplify a repricing. He also covers AI in trading, cyber risk, consumer finance and AI-agent-driven deposit runs. He says the Board does not target market levels and makes no comment on rates.

items.speaker: Cheryl Venable
items.role: Interim President, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta since March 2026 (non-voter in 2026; Atlanta votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Atlanta Fed quarterly president's essay: Formulating Good Monetary Policy Requires Lots of Listening
items.quote: Energy prices and the AI buildout continue to fuel inflation that remains well above the Federal Open Market Committee's 2 percent goal.
items.summary: Venable says inflation is still too high, driven by energy and the AI buildout, while growth holds up on consumption and AI infrastructure investment and the labor market is stable but low-hire, low-fire. Higher mortgage rates weigh on housing. She states no rate-path preference; the essay is mostly about regional outreach (Louisiana, Miami, Nashville).
items.score_note: Inflation described as well above goal but no policy prescription; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: John Williams
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FOMC Vice Chair, permanent voter)
items.occasion: On-stage interview at the Axios BFD summit, New York
items.quote: If those continue, I think that's a factor that will argue that we may need to raise rates more
items.summary: Williams said the AI investment surge and stock-market wealth are strengthening the economy and, if they continue, may require raising rates more next year; AI is the more persistent inflation factor. He said the situation does not call for dramatic action, pushing back on a 50bp December move. He said the Fed is watching the fast-growing structured finance funding the AI boom but does not see a financial stability risk yet.
items.score_note: Conditional signal of more hikes ('may need to raise rates more') combined with a rejection of a larger step; lean tighter.
items.ai_quote: We are definitely seeing structured finance of the type we saw in housing finance, so that's why we're paying attention to that

items.speaker: Michael Barr
items.occasion: Speech 'Investing in America's Underserved Communities', Making Missing Markets conference, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
items.quote: If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people.
items.summary: In a short outlook passage Barr says the economy is strong with low unemployment and robust business investment, but inflation is too high and must come back to 2 percent 'in a timely way'. He expects further rate increases to be appropriate if the economy evolves as he forecasts, while continuing to watch the data. The rest of the speech is on community investment.
items.score_note: States that he expects further rate increases to be appropriate under his forecast, three weeks before the December meeting. No specific meeting named.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Virtual conversation at a St. Louis Fed conference (day the October FOMC minutes were released)
items.quote: This measured approach we've been taking, and I would be supportive of continuing to take, is the right way to go
items.summary: Stocktwits reports Daly said further rate increases will be required to return inflation to 2% but favored a measured pace, citing uncertainty over tariffs, the Iran conflict and AI capital spending. The article contrasts her with Waller's call for a 50bp move in December.
items.score_note: More hikes needed per the report, but the direct quote argues for a measured pace and against larger moves; +1.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Steve Liesman (reported by Reuters)
items.quote: then you have to go 50 in December
items.summary: Says inflation is 'heading in the wrong direction and it is spreading out' into services, and businesses are starting to treat 3% as normal, so the Fed needs aggressive action: either a 50bp hike on December 8-9 or a 25bp hike with a very clear signal (statement or press conference) of another hike in January. Per Stocktwits' account of the same interview he said last year's three 'insurance cuts' should be reversed, 'three hikes plus maybe some more', and that he sees no AI bubble but the Fed is examining banks' leveraged lending to AI firms (https://stocktwits.com/news-articles/markets/equity/fed-s-waller-stresses-on-the-need-for-half-point-rate-hike-in-december-says-i-am-very-concerned-about-inflation/cNbg5eSR9LV).
items.score_note: Explicitly wants a larger or faster sequence of hikes starting in December.

items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Moderated Q&A at the Economic Club of Indiana luncheon, Indianapolis (Reuters story carried by The Star)
items.quote: The Fed's job is to prevent this thing from overheating the economy,
items.summary: On the day of Anthropic's record IPO, Goolsbee says data-center construction and consumers spending out of future wealth can easily overheat the economy and that the Fed's job is to prevent that. Wire recaps add that he called the job market stable, inflation way above 2% and tariff effects more persistent than expected.
items.score_note: Overheating and inflation dominate; no explicit hike call in the quoted text.

items.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (non-voter in 2026, votes in 2027)
items.occasion: Conference call with reporters (Reuters via Kitco)
items.quote: The evidence does not suggest we're on a path back to 2%.
items.summary: Goolsbee says the AI boom is contributing to potential overheating, likening near-unprecedented business investment to 'a pig through the python', and that inflation is borderline disturbingly high. The steepness of the rate path should depend on whether inflation returns to 2% on its own, and the evidence says it is not. He would not say whether he backs a half-point December hike but said all options are on the table; a recap says he is unsure how the financial sector would handle a major AI-related equity correction.
items.score_note: All options open and inflation not on path; no commitment to a hike size or timing.

items.summary: Short panel remarks restating his shock framework: energy shock creates an inflation/employment tradeoff, and a stronger reaction is warranted if expectations risk becoming unanchored; the AI buildout is currently adding to demand and inflation. No comment on the December decision or the rate path.
items.score_note: Framework remarks with two-sided conditional statements and no rate-path lean; scored 0 rather than +1 because nothing is said about the next move.

items.summary: Rules out discussing a different inflation target or a target range until 2% has been achieved for a durable and extended period, calling the target critical as a nominal anchor and for accountability and credibility. Comes as the Fed reviews parts of its policy framework.
items.score_note: About the framework (2% target), not the rate path, so not scored; directionally it rejects accommodating higher inflation. Article body is paywalled, so the occasion is not confirmed.

items.speaker: Anna Paulson
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Speech at Money Marketeers of New York University, 'Monetary Policy Communication: Do We Understand Each Other?'
items.quote: I see holding rates steady in October as a matter of pace, not direction
items.summary: A speech on Fed communication, reaction functions and credibility. In the text Paulson repeated that she supported the September hike and the October hold and that the pause was not a stop because markets expected further tightening. In the Q&A afterwards, as reported by Reuters (https://srnnews.com/feds-paulson-says-understanding-not-guidance-drives-effective-communication/), she said the way to bring inflation down is by having higher rates, that there is more tightening to do, and that slow and steady increases give the economy time to adjust.
items.score_note: The prepared text alone would be +1 (restates direction), but in the Q&A at the same event she said there is 'more tightening to do' (Reuters direct quote), which is an explicit statement that more hikes are needed. The machine-checkable quote is from the official text.

items.speaker: Scott Bessent
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk on the Street interview with Sara Eisen
items.quote: So, I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards.
items.summary: Asked whether a 50bp December hike floated by a governor would be a mistake, Bessent called that governor's shift 'peripatetic', said crude and gasoline have had some of their biggest drops in history since the election, and urged the Fed to look forward rather than at noisy headline inflation.
items.score_note: Argues against a large December hike on falling energy prices; does not call for cuts.

items.speaker: Lisa Cook
items.occasion: Speech 'The U.S. Economy in Global Context', XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
items.quote: I am skeptical that September's single 1/4 point rate increase will be enough to change the path of inflation.
items.summary: Cook's first public explanation of her October dissent. Two reasons: financial conditions are too accommodative with no clear disinflation (the policy stance is not curtailing the AI buildout and equity prices support spending, so holding implies a widening positive output gap), and urgency after more than five and a half years above target, since waiting 'risks getting behind the curve' and could require larger hikes later that stress the financial system. PCE inflation was an estimated 3.8% and core 3.2% in October; data since September 'fail to provide' evidence of a return to a sustainable path.
items.score_note: Explains a dissent for a hike and says one hike is unlikely to be enough. ai_financing tag is a borderline call: she ties accommodative financial conditions and the policy stance to the AI buildout, but does not mention AI debt or credit explicitly.
items.ai_quote: The current stance of policy does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout, and equity prices continue to support consumer spending.

items.speaker: Donald Trump
items.occasion: Remarks to reporters at a White House news briefing, first Fed comments found after the midterms
items.quote: Interest rates are too high because we have a very political Fed, and I'm not blaming the chairman, by the way
items.summary: With a December hike priced, Trump said interest rates are too high because of a 'very political Fed', explicitly not blaming Warsh. He said the Fed should lower rather than keep raising rates when the numbers are strong, that the US should have the lowest rate in the world, and that lower rates would help pay off the debt.
items.score_note: Explicit call to lower rates and stop raising them, less than three weeks before the December FOMC.

coverage_notes.A1: Warsh: 23 items from 11 occasions (4 press conferences split into opening statement plus Q&A signals as instructed, 2 Fed speeches, House and Senate testimony, Sintra panel, G20 Asheville remarks, Bangkok IMF chat, 1 press-release statement). The Fed speech index (json/ne-speeches.json) and testimony index list only two Warsh speeches and one testimony since June; Reuters (Jul 1) confirms Sintra was his first public appearance after the June 17 press conference, so June has only the press conference. No Warsh media interview was found in any month; searches by month for August (pre-Jackson Hole), early October and November 17-23 returned nothing beyond the items here. He mentioned a central bank meeting in Basel in early September; it was closed-door and no remarks were found. Powell: 0 items. The Fed speech index has no Powell entry after his May 31 award remarks (20:30 EDT, one day before the window; federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/files/powell20260531a.pdf), and no interview, panel or statement on policy was found for June-November. He did not speak at the June 2 Brookings retrospective on his chairmanship (transcript checked). FOMC minutes show Powell voted with the majority at all four meetings (June hold, July hold, September +25bp, October hold); neither Warsh nor Powell dissented, so there are no dissent items. time_et: speech and testimony times are the Fed index listing times (ET); the July 9 time is the release time on the page; all others null. The Bangkok item is dated Oct 15 because the remarks were made before 23:51 ET on Oct 15 (Oct 16 morning local). Quote matching: press conference quotes are copied from the PDF text layer and use typographic apostrophes (U+2019); the Oct 28 opening-statement quote wraps across a line break in the PDF, all other PDF quotes sit on one line. The PBS page (Sintra) encodes the apostrophe in the quote as an HTML entity in raw source. Blackout dates come from the Atlanta Fed page because the Board calendar page does not list them and the Board blackout-calendar PDF returned 404. FOMC facts: the 2027 schedule released Nov 12 lists Jan 26-27 as the next meeting after December and makes Oct 26-27, 2027 a strategy-only meeting.
coverage_notes.A10: Method: every quote was checked programmatically as an exact substring of the fetched page text. Scoring convention for forecasts: +2 = hike forecast at the next meeting or two or more further hikes; +1 = one more hike later or a tightening bias; 0 = hold (including hold with cuts a year or more out); -1 = explicit pushback against priced hikes or cuts seen as the next move. Rieder's essays are normative and carry score_basis 'should'. Extra top-level key call_history_no_quote holds dated calls that were readable on a page only in the journalist's words (each is also listed in unverified, per rule 3); page_text there is a verbatim sentence from that page. Thin or missing: (1) June: no Goldman/JPMorgan/Morgan Stanley reaction to the June 17 FOMC with a direct quote was found; the Reuters post-June and post-July brokerage tables were not found on an open page. (2) Post-October-28 FOMC: no brokerage round-up dated after the meeting was found; the last Reuters table is dated Oct 28 (pre-decision). kfgo/whbl/wtvbam copies of Reuters factboxes return 403. (3) November: no dated post-CPI forecast update found for Morgan Stanley, Citi, Barclays, Nomura, UBS Global Research or Wells Fargo. (4) Blocked sources: ubs.com (403 to scripts), advisorperspectives.com (403), citigroup.com transcripts (503), Bloomberg/CNBC video interviews (no transcripts). (5) Bruce Kasman: nothing in window. Jan Hatzius: four notes and two TV appearances seen, only one with a direct policy quote. (6) Wells Fargo items use the firm's text as republished by FXStreet (tier official_text); the bank's own site was not opened. AI/credit as a reason: only Rieder (27 Aug, 17 Nov) explicitly ties AI capex financing to the rate question, as a reason hikes bite weak borrowers but not the AI investment cycle while financing terms tighten. BofA (13 Nov) and PIMCO (10 Nov) name tighter financial conditions or credit-market weakness as something that could shorten the hiking path; Deutsche Bank's 10 Nov note, per FXStreet's paraphrase, says an AI-valuation sell-off that has widened credit spreads could make the Fed hesitate. No house has a cut as its next move as of November; Goldman is the only one with a dated first cut (Dec 2027), Citi sees cuts from June 2027. Inconsistency noticed on a source page: Stocktwits (17 Sept) says August core inflation eased to 2.4%, which conflicts with other pages describing core PCE above 3%.
coverage_notes.A11: RESULT: no new verifiable items. The first-pass gaps for these three speakers are almost entirely real silences, not missed occasions. All 26 first-pass items for the three speakers already verify as exact in ledger.json. Evidence by speaker follows. KASHKARI: (1) The Minneapolis Fed publishes his full monthly schedule (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/about-us/leadership/presidents-schedule); the June, July, August and September 2026 PDFs were opened. Every public or media entry in them is already in A5: June 2 Bank of Korea panel, June 26 Bloomberg interview (Catarina Saraiva) and Aspen panel, June 29 NPR, August 5 CNBC Squawk Box, August 23 CBS Face the Nation, the Fox 'Sunday Morning Futures' interview, September 30 CFR. July has no interview, speech or public event at all (employee town halls, a Helena, Mont., business roundtable, internal calls), so he said nothing in public before the July 28-29 dissent. September has nothing before the Fox interview. The only other entry is a five-minute welcome at the bank's Bank Holding Company Executive Conference on August 25 (not published). The October and November schedules are not posted yet (404). (2) For October 2 to November 23 I used the Newsquawk headline sitemaps (all 7 files, about 30 Kashkari entries), the SRN News archive of Reuters stories (WordPress search API, all posts since June 1), month-by-month web searches, Bloomberg Law/BGOV and Kitco searches, and the CBS Face the Nation transcripts for October 4, 11, 18, 25 and November 1, 15 (the November 8 and 22 pages returned 404). Newsquawk's November 18 primer says his previous remarks were 'at the end of September, before the October FOMC'. So between the October 1 interviews and November 18 no policy remarks by him were reported: no reaction to the October 28 hold, and nothing on December until the FinRegLab conversation, which is video only (see unverified, with caption text). The Minneapolis Fed people page still lists only four events in the window and one essay (July 31). LOGAN: the Dallas Fed retrospective calendar (https://www.dallasfed.org/fed/leadership/logan/calendar, read through a page-summary tool because the raw HTML served only placeholder data; it runs to September 29) shows no interview entry in 2026 and no remarks, speech, panel or moderated conversation in August or September: only attendance at the Aspen Institute Program on the World Economy (August 23-24), Jackson Hole (August 28-29) and the North Capital Forum in Mexico City (September 27), plus business roundtables and a UT Austin class visit. The speeches page has nothing beyond the nine texts A5 opened (latest November 13); the releases page has only the July 31 dissent statement. Newsquawk and SRN show no Logan headline outside those occasions except an October 6 moderator slot. No Logan media interview was found in any month. PAULSON: the Philadelphia Fed speeches-and-essays page has nothing between May 19 (Atlanta Fed conference, outside the window) and August 4, and nothing between September 24 and November 10. Its press-coverage page lists, for the window, only NJBIZ (June, unreadable), Reuters and CNBC on August 4, CNBC on September 24 (a report on the fintech speech, same occasion as A4) and the Wellsboro local story (October 1 visit, no policy content). Newsquawk has no Paulson headline between May 29 and August 4 or between September 24 and November 10, and its November 10 primer says her previous remarks were in late September. The November 20 Newsquawk headline already in A4's unverified list (open to consecutive hikes) still has no direct-quote page; the CNBC November 20 article on Fed communication quotes only her November 19 speech, so the headline may be a late item from the November 19 Q&A (inference, not confirmed). coverage_notes.B1: Window 2026-01-01 to 2026-05-31. POWELL: complete for official occasions. federalreserve.gov lists only three Powell texts in the window (Jan 11 statement, Mar 21 and May 31 award remarks) and the Board calendar adds one moderated discussion (Harvard, Mar 30), which is sourced to a news page because no official text exists. The three FOMC press conferences come from the official transcripts (one opening-statement item plus two or three Q&A items each). The balance sheet and AI-related credit did not come up as questions in any of the three press conferences; the only AI remarks were on jobs, productivity and (March) data-center construction pushing up inflation and the neutral rate at the margin, which is not a financing link, so no ai_financing tag was used anywhere in this file. There was no semiannual Monetary Policy Report testimony in the window: the Board's MPR page lists only a July 2026 report for 2026 and the testimony list has no Powell entry for January to May. WARSH: he made no public policy remarks as nominee before the April 21 Senate Banking hearing that I could find (the wire feed shows only third-party comments between January 30 and April 20), and no statement by him on nomination day was found. Hearing items rely on CNN's rush transcript (10:00-11:30 ET segments only) plus a Reuters article for the balance-sheet answer; the rest of the hearing is in the unverified list. After the May 22 swearing-in remarks there were no further Warsh remarks through May 31 on the Board calendar or speech list. MIRAN: both official speeches, all three FOMC dissents, the resignation letter and the May 15 statement with Bowman are from federalreserve.gov. No separate Miran dissent statement exists on the Board site, so dissent quotes are the Committee statement's wording, not his own words. Interviews and panel remarks are from news pages with direct quotations (CNBC, Fox Business, Reuters via Kitco or Yahoo, Bloomberg via Bloomberg Law/Bloomberg Government mirrors that show only the opening paragraphs, MNI, BU Today) and one full transcript (The Peg). Thin spots: late April to mid-May (May 1, May 8 and May 14 television interviews are unverified), and the Jan 30 CNBC page gives excerpts rather than a full transcript. SCORING NOTE for Miran: -2 whenever the page shows an explicit call for cuts on that day; -1 where the visible text is a revision toward fewer cuts or an argument about inflation measurement without an explicit cut call. His path shrank over the window (150 bp in early January, about 100 bp from mid-February, neutral rather than below neutral from March, three or four cuts in April, 75 bp in mid-May); the five-point scale does not capture that drift, so use the summaries if the trend matters. TIMES: time_et is filled only where the source page itself states a time (FOMC statements, 2:00 p.m.). Scheduled start times from the Board's speech list and calendar feed are given separately under scheduled_times and are not on the source pages. ACCESS: banking.senate.gov blocked both curl and the browser (bot challenge, not bypassed). Bloomberg and Reuters originals were not opened; syndicated copies were used. Machine check: every quote and source_url in this file was matched against the downloaded page with the project's own pipeline.check() and returned 'exact'. CONTEXT CHECK: the Board's May 22 release says the President nominated Warsh on March 4, 2026 (the formal transmission to the Senate; the public announcement was January 30) and that the Senate confirmed him to the Board on May 12 and as Chair on May 13. Miran's resignation letter is dated May 14 and was effective on or shortly before Warsh's swearing-in. On May 15 the Board named Powell chair pro tempore until Warsh was sworn in, with Bowman and Miran not supporting the open-ended designation. The April 29 vote was 8-4 with three hawkish dissents over the statement's easing bias (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) in addition to Miran. Nothing else contradicted the brief's context section.
coverage_notes.B10: Sources actually opened: Reuters copies on Kitco (off-the-wire sitemap scanned for all of Jan-May 2026) and BNN Bloomberg (daily sitemaps Jan-May), The Standard HK, The Star, Invezz, Hellenic Shipping News (Investing.com reprints), FXStreet (Wells Fargo research), investingLive (weekly sitemaps W01-W23; its bank-by-bank FOMC previews of Jan 28 and Mar 18 carry direct quotations, none found for Apr 29), and firm pages: jpmorgan.com Global Research Fed page via four Wayback versions, morganstanley.com Thoughts on the Market transcripts, pimco.com post-FOMC notes, goldmansachs.com insights and transcript PDFs. Timeline of the turn as supported by the items: J.P. Morgan had no 2026 cuts from Jan 9 (next move a Q3 2027 hike) and did not change through May. Goldman: Mar/Jun -> Jun/Sep (Jan 11) -> Sep/Dec (Mar 11) -> Dec 2026/Mar 2027 (May 8); it dropped 2026 cuts only on Jun 9, outside the window. Morgan Stanley: Jan/Apr -> Jun/Sep (Jan 9) -> Sep/Dec (Mar 19) -> no 2026 cuts (Apr 29). Barclays: Mar/Jun -> Jun/Dec (Jan 12) -> Sep only (Mar 13) -> no 2026 cuts (May 4). BofA: Jun/Jul (Jan through Mar 18) -> first cut September (date not found) -> no 2026 cuts, Jul/Sep 2027 (May 8). Citi: Mar/Jul/Sep (Jan-Feb) -> Apr/Jul/Sep (Mar 18) -> Jun/Jul/Sep (date not found) -> Sep/Oct/Dec (Apr 3), still cutting in 2026 at end-May. Wells Fargo Economics: Mar/Jun (Jan 14) -> Sep/Dec (by Apr 8); Wells Fargo Investment Institute separately went to no cuts (Apr 6). Nomura: Jun/Sep -> Sep/Dec (Apr 8, paraphrase only) -> no 2026 cuts (May 21). UBS GWM: cuts later in 2026 (Apr 10; Sep/Dec per Reuters) -> Dec 2026/Mar 2027 (May 12). No house in this set had a 2026 HIKE as its base case inside the window; the most hawkish were J.P. Morgan (2027 hike) and commentary that hikes were 'feasible' (BofA, May 19) or debated (Deutsche, mid-March). Scoring convention used for forecasts: base case with a 2026 cut that is not at the next meeting = -1; hold through 2026 with next move a cut = 0; next move a hike but distant = +1; an explicit call for cuts now = -2 (only Rieder, scored as 'should'). Dates: where the page gives the note date it is used (date_basis event); otherwise the article date. Several Reuters poll quotes carry the poll publication date. Quotes from Kitco pages are deliberately cut to spans that contain no zero-width characters (Reuters copies embed U+200B/U+2060 inside sentences), so some quotes are clauses rather than full sentences. The Goldman Mar 11 quote is from a Hong Kong reprint that uses British spelling ('labour'); the Nomura May 21 quote likewise ('sceptical'). Two Goldman-arm items come from transcript PDFs, and the investingLive preview pages wrap quotations across lines, so those quotes are kept to a single text line. Thin coverage: Deutsche Bank (3 items, no dated change of its one-cut-in-September call found), Nomura (3), UBS (2, wealth management only; no UBS Global Research item), BlackRock (1 Rieder item; his March 25 Bloomberg remarks are paywalled), and February in general (no forecast changes; the Feb 6 factbox shows calls unchanged after the January FOMC). No CNBC or Bloomberg TV transcript was opened. Items labelled Goldman Sachs Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets (rates sales), J.P. Morgan Wealth Management and Wells Fargo Investment Institute are other arms of those firms, not the research house call; filter on firm if only the sell-side economists are wanted. Roles verified on opened pages: Michael Feroli chief U.S. economist (J.P. Morgan), Michael Gapen chief U.S. economist and Seth Carpenter global chief economist (Morgan Stanley), David Mericle chief US economist (Goldman Sachs; Jan Hatzius is named as team lead by Bloomberg), Aditya Bhave head of U.S. economics (BofA), Matthew Luzzetti chief U.S. economist (Deutsche Bank Securities), Jonathan Millar senior U.S. economist (Barclays; Stocktwits names Marc Giannoni as chief U.S. economist), Jeremy Schwartz senior U.S. economist (Nomura), Tiffany Wilding economist (PIMCO), Rick Rieder head of global fixed income (BlackRock). Not verified from any opened page: chief economists of Citi (Reuters copy via Bloomberg names Andrew Hollenhorst as a Citigroup economist), UBS, Wells Fargo.

coverage_notes.B6: Window 2026-01-01 to 2026-05-31. Barkin: April has only the Reuters interview published April 1 and May only the May 21 speech; no late-April or early-May appearances were found. Bostic: most January-February appearances are video or audio only, so 6 items against 7 unverified. Venable: one item, the May 12 essay; the Atlanta Fed feed lists no speeches or interviews by her from March to May and wire searches return nothing. Goolsbee: the Chicago Fed media list snapshot ends April 17, so May interviews were found through news listings only and some may be missing; about 16 TV, podcast and paywalled appearances are in the unverified list. Quote caveats. Kitco copies of Reuters stories from March onward contain zero-width characters inside sentences; quotes from Kitco were chosen from clean spans (the pipeline's normaliser also strips them). SRN News and the Boston Globe use curly apostrophes, quoted as on the page. Collins speech quotes are from the official PDF texts. The Yahoo Finance April 14 transcript is auto-generated. The Chicago magazine Q&A URL on the Chicago Fed list redirects to chicagotribune.com, which is the URL used. Dates. AI: Goolsbee, Barkin and Collins discuss AI investment, data-center demand and productivity as demand or overheating drivers; none links policy to AI debt financing or private credit in the pages opened, so this is tagged 'other' or 'growth', never 'ai_financing'. coverage_notes.B8: Sources and method. Trump: (1) every Truth Social post in the window that mentions Powell, the Fed, Warsh or interest rates, read in full on the trumpstruth.org archive (timestamps are US Eastern); (2) Roll Call Factba.se full transcripts of speeches, interviews and press gaggles. Factba.se transcript pages are rendered by JavaScript, so source_url for those items is the site's own JSON endpoint that the page loads (rollcall.com/api/factbase/transcripts?person=trump&slug=...), where the quote can be matched as plain text; the human-readable page is rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/<slug>/. These are third-party transcripts, labelled official_transcript only for want of a closer tier. (3) CNBC transcripts on the Versant press room. Bessent: all Treasury press releases sb0340-sb0560 were scanned by title; CNBC transcripts from the Versant press room; Reuters reports republished by SRN News (found through the site's WordPress search API for 'Bessent' over the window); Semafor. Thin spots. Bessent in March: the March 16 CNBC interview has no Fed content (only that inflation expectations are anchored) and was left out; Fox Business March 19 is covered only through a Reuters report. Bessent in May: the May 20 remarks on Treasury yields could not be opened (see unverified). Fox News, Fox Business, NBC, CBS and ABC interview transcripts for Bessent were not found as full texts, so those occasions rest on Reuters direct quotes or are missing. Bloomberg, WSJ and FT were not opened (paywall). Trump occasions were limited to those where he said something about rates, the Fed Chair or the Powell probe; passing mentions of the Fed building alone (for example March 24, March 26 Fox 'The Five', March 31 remarks, April 25, April 30 Newsmax, May 19) were not itemised. On days with several occasions (January 13, January 29, April 23, May 22) each occasion is a separate item, so same-day duplicates should be averaged before use. Scoring conventions. Posts or remarks that only attack Powell or discuss the Fed Chair choice are scored null. 'Too late' or 'rates too high' without an explicit demand is -1; an explicit call to cut now or for lower rates is -2. Balance-sheet-only remarks: the January 9 MBS comment is null, the February 8 forecast is 0 with score_basis 'forecast'. Dating notes. The CNBC Halftime excerpts page prints 'February 6, 2025' in its header but the body and video link show February 6, 2026. The Factba.se slug for the Kudlow interview ends in 2023 but the record is dated February 9, 2026. The Trump CNBC Davos interview is listed by Factba.se as airing on 'The Exchange' and by CNBC as airing during 'Closing Bell', both January 21. Discrepancy. The January 8 Bessent text on treasury.gov does not contain the line 'the Fed should not delay' that CNBC-based press reports quote from the remarks; see that item's score_note. The ai_financing tag is used twice: April 15 (Bessent on private credit, saying Treasury's work shows no systemic problem) and March 3 (liquidity rules reducing bank lending to AI hyperscalers). Neither links AI or private-credit stress to the policy rate.
coverage_notes.B9: Window 2026-01-01 to 2026-05-31. Every quote and ai_quote was re-checked by substring match against its page, both with a browser-style fetch and with the same curl method pipeline.py uses (89 of 89 exact on 2026-11-23). Gaps: David Tepper, no on-topic statement found in the window (0 items). Paul Tudor Jones, only the Apr 28 podcast and the May 7 CNBC interview; no CNBC full-transcript page found and nothing for January to March. Howard Marks, the two memos only; a Mar 17 fireside chat and a May 5 podcast are in unverified. Bill Ackman, January only. Ken Griffin, Davos Jan 21 and Milken May 5 only. Ted Pick, Davos and Apr 15 Bloomberg interviews are video-only. Gundlach's Mar 10, Mar 18 (FOMC day) and Mar 26 appearances have no open direct quote. El-Erian weekly notes for Jan 25, Apr 26, May 3, May 24 and May 31 were not located. Steve Cohen, nothing found. Scoring: 57 of 89 items are unscored because they address only credit stress, AI financing or Fed independence. Judgment calls to review: Gundlach Mar 23 (+1 rests on DoubleLine's recap, the quote is about credit), Gundlach Jan 13 (0 from a paraphrase), Dimon Apr 28 (+1 leans on Fortune's report of the same event), Ackman Jan 11 (+1 for fewer cuts than priced, although he also expects the Fed to drop the 2% goal), Dalio Jan 8 and May 7 (set to null by the lead collector: long-run debt-monetization thesis, not a rate-path call). Private-credit warnings tied to AI disruption of software loans are tagged ai_financing. Where score is null and the sub-collector left score_basis empty it was filled with 'forecast' as a placeholder. Dates: Dimon's Shanghai Bloomberg interview is dated May 20 ET (aired May 21 local time). Fink's letter page has no date; Mar 23 comes from the Reuters release report (date_basis article). The Apr 29 El-Erian item uses X's syndication JSON URL as source_url. One Gundlach X post in unverified carries a placeholder date (2026-01-31) because only the month is known. Nothing found contradicts the context section of the brief.
